topics.title: useReducer
topics.description: useReducer(reducer, initialState, init?) centralizes state transitions in a pure function. React owns the queue; you own the logic.
keyConcepts: When it's better than useState
The next state depends on the previous state in several places (a state machine, a wizard, a form with cross-field rules).
You want every transition named and logged (the action log is a free audit trail and makes debugging much easier).
You want to co-locate related state that must change together.
You want to test transitions as a pure function without rendering anything.
Why the discriminated union matters
Reducer rules
Must be pure: no mutation of state or action, no network calls, no Date.now()/Math.random() inside (put them in the action payload).
Must be complete: every action handled, with assertNever for exhaustiveness.
dispatch is stable for the component's lifetime. Never put dispatch in a dependency array (harmless but noise), and never rely on dispatch changing to trigger an effect.
init runs once and must be pure; use it to avoid re-creating the initial state.
Lazy initialization: useReducer(reducer, expensiveArg, init) beats useReducer(reducer, expensiveArg()).
commonMistakes: side effects inside a reducer; Date.now() in a reducer (breaks replayability); mutating state instead of returning a new object; expecting the reducer to be called once per dispatch in dev; using a reducer where a ref would do.
practiceTasks: Model a 4-step checkout wizard as a reducer with an explicit state union, guards for "can go back", and a MAX_STEPS-aware progress field. Then write unit tests that drive the reducer directly with action sequences — no rendering — including illegal transitions.

interviewQuestions.text: When do you choose `useReducer` over `useState`?
Why must reducers be pure, and what breaks if they aren't?
Is `dispatch` referentially stable? What does that enable?
How do you get exhaustive type checking on actions?
What's the `init` third argument for, and when does it matter?
Why is `status: 'loading' | 'done'` better than two booleans?
When would you reach for a state machine library instead?
How would you implement undo/redo with `useReducer`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Keep a history array in state: { past: State[], present: State, future: State[] }. On each action, push present to past, set present to the new state, and clear future. Undo pops from past into present and pushes the old present onto future. Redo is the mirror. Keep the history bounded (last N) so memory doesn't grow, and skip entries for high-frequency, non-meaningful changes like a text field keystroke — or coalesce them by action type."

topics.title: useRef
topics.description: useRef(initial) returns a stable { current } object that lives for the component's lifetime. Mutating .current does not trigger a render.
keyConcepts: Legitimate uses
DOM references (ref={node => ...} or useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)), used for measurement, focus, scroll, imperative third-party libraries.

Mutable values that shouldn't cause renders: the latest props in an async callback (4.1.6), a timer id, an AbortController, a WebSocket instance, a "have we mounted" flag, a previous-value tracker for comparing in an effect.
Storing an instance of a non-React system where a state variable would be wrong (a <canvas> context, an animation controller).
Anti-uses
As state (it doesn't render — you'll read ref.current in render and get a stale value).
To "avoid re-renders" for values the UI must display.
To replace useState for things that need to trigger renders.
Ref identity and rules
The ref object is created once per component instance (per fiber), so it's stable across renders and safe in dependency arrays.

Don't write ref.current during render and read it in the same render — under concurrent rendering and StrictMode's double-invoke, render runs twice and the second run sees your mutation. If you need "the value from the previous committed render", write in useLayoutEffect or useEffect, or use React's official "adjust state in an effect" pattern:
Don't pass the same ref to two nodes (last write wins) and don't write and read .current in the same render.
commonMistakes: useRef for displayed data; reading .current in render; expecting useRef(fn()) to be lazy (it's not lazy — the argument is evaluated every render, so pass useRef(null) and set it in an effect, or use useState(() => fn())); returning a ref object from a custom hook and exposing it where a value is expected.
practiceTasks: Build useLatest, usePrevious, useIsMounted, and useEventCallback (a stable callback that always calls the latest version — the workhorse for event handlers passed to memoized children), and write a test for each showing it doesn't cause re-renders.

interviewQuestions.text: Why doesn't mutating a ref cause a render? Where does React read it?
When is a ref better than state?
What's wrong with writing `ref.current` during render?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Because render can run twice (StrictMode) and can be interrupted and restarted, anything a render writes could be written twice or read from a discarded render pass. Refs are mutable boxes with no corresponding Fiber update, so writing to them during render breaks the model that render is pure computation over props and state. The safe place is after commit: useLayoutEffect (before paint) or useEffect."

interviewQuestions.text: How do you track the previous value of a prop?
Should you ever put React state in a ref?
interviewQuestions.answer: Yes, for "is this the initial value" guards and for values that must be read synchronously in a callback, but you must be careful: state changes won't re-render, so it's for bookkeeping, not display.

interviewQuestions.text: How do you forward a ref to a DOM node from a function component?
When would you need a ref to an object (not a DOM node)?

topics.title: useLayoutEffect
topics.description: useEffect — passive effect, runs *after* the browser has painted (usually).
keyConcepts: When you need useLayoutEffect
Reading layout after mutation and synchronously re-rendering: measure an element, then set state to adjust a tooltip position, a carousel translate, or a virtualized scroll offset.
Preventing a visual jump: for example, resetting scrollTop to 0 on route change after the new content has been committed.
Keeping two DOM nodes in sync imperatively where a state update would be too slow.
Why this works where useEffect doesn't
The infinite useLayoutEffect loop
useLayoutEffect and SSR
Do not measure in render
Measurement toolbelt
commonMistakes: using useLayoutEffect for anything that isn't synchronous layout work (it blocks paint, hurting INP); measuring during render; storing DOM nodes in state; ignoring SSR warnings; layout effects with heavy computation or network calls.
practiceTasks: Build a tooltip, a sticky header that toggles a shadow at scrollY > 8, and a virtualized list that must read scrollTop synchronously. Implement each with useLayoutEffect and explain, in terms of paint timing, what a visible flash would look like with useEffect.

interviewQuestions.text: `useLayoutEffect` vs `useEffect` — when each?
Why does measuring a tooltip cause a flash with `useEffect`?
Why can't you call `useLayoutEffect` on the server?
Your layout effect runs forever. Diagnose and fix.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Most likely I call setState with a fresh object each time, so the state identity always changes and re-triggers the effect. Fixes: return the previous state when the value is effectively unchanged (a functional update with a tolerance check), depend on primitives rather than objects, or move the whole thing to an event handler with requestAnimationFrame."

interviewQuestions.text: Why should you avoid measuring during render?
When do you need `useInsertionEffect`, and who should actually use it?
When is ResizeObserver better than a resize listener?
interviewQuestions.answer: "ResizeObserver fires when an element's box changes for any reason — content, siblings, CSS load, font load, container queries, orientation — and it fires before paint. A resize listener only fires on window resize, fires *after* layout in a way that's easy to thrash, and needs debouncing."

interviewQuestions.text: What's the cost of a `useLayoutEffect` that does heavy work?

topics.title: useTransition/useDeferredValue
topics.description: useTransition/useDeferredValue within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: The problem being solved
useTransition
startTransition(scope) marks all state updates inside scope as transition updates (same lane).

The input's own setQuery is urgent; the expensive setDeferredQuery is not. React renders the urgent update first, so typing stays at 60fps, and the results update after (or are interrupted and restarted when the next keystroke arrives).

isPending is true from the moment the transition starts until the transition's render *commits* — a genuinely reliable "loading" flag, unlike isLoading state you manage yourself (it flickers if you forget to reset it).

Rule: the transition scope must be synchronous. No await inside it — you cannot startTransition(async () => {...}). For async work, either set pending state in an event handler before awaiting, or wrap the state updates *after* the await:

Rule: you cannot transition a controlled input's own value to something slower. If setQuery itself triggered an expensive synchronous render, typing would still block. Transitions only help if the urgent part is cheap.
useDeferredValue
Suspense + transitions
Measurement
commonMistakes: wrapping everything in startTransition including the input's own value; awaiting inside a transition in React 18; assuming isPending is a network flag (it's a render-scheduling flag); using a transition where the change must be reflected synchronously (e.g. a destructive confirm); assuming transitions work without createRoot.
practiceTasks: Build a filter panel over a 20,000-row list with a text input, a facet select, and a sort dropdown. Use a transition for the results, useDeferredValue for the query, and render a subtle "updating…" affordance instead of a spinner (which is the better UX). Then type as fast as you can and record dropped renders in the Profiler and INP.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem do transitions solve that `useState` + `isLoading` doesn't?
Why can't you put `await` in a transition scope (React 18)? What changes in React 19?
`useTransition` vs `useDeferredValue` — when each?
interviewQuestions.answer: "They're two sides of the same idea. useTransition is for state you own: you wrap the expensive state update and get a pending flag. useDeferredValue is for a value you don't own — a prop, a store value, a URL param — where you want the expensive part of the tree to render against a slightly stale version instead of blocking. Use both together when you control the input and also want to derive expensive content from it."

interviewQuestions.text: Why can't you make a controlled input's value itself a transition?
What does `isPending` guarantee that a `loading` boolean doesn't?
How do transitions interact with Suspense?
Does `startTransition` make the work faster, cheaper, or just later?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Later, and interruptible. Total work is unchanged, but because it's interruptible React can throw away a render that has already been invalidated by a newer keystroke, so under fast typing the expensive tree effectively renders less often. That's a real CPU saving, not just a reordering. But the urgent render must still be cheap, or the input will lag."

interviewQuestions.text: What would you do if the urgent render itself is expensive?

topics.title: Suspense and error boundaries
topics.description: Suspense and error boundaries within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: Error boundaries
They must be class components (React 19 adds no hook equivalent — this is a well-known API gap). A framework may offer one (Next.js error.tsx, Remix ErrorBoundary).
They catch errors thrown during render, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of children — including errors thrown inside a component rendered within them.

They do not catch: errors in event handlers, in async code/setTimeout, in promise rejections handled elsewhere, errors thrown in the boundary itself, and errors during SSR (the boundary runs on the server).
Event handler and async errors must be caught at the source (try/catch) and reported to your error tracker.

Where to place them: at meaningful feature boundaries (per route, per widget), with a top-level fallback as the last resort. A boundary that wraps the entire app is a fallback of last resort only; it will hide most bugs.
Report to Sentry with the componentStack and a user-action breadcrumb trail (Phase 4.6).
Suspense

A component suspends by throwing a promise (React 19 also supports throwing an async function's promise with use(); data frameworks like Relay/Apollo/SWR adapters, and Next.js's <Suspense> + streaming RSC, use this).
Only the nearest boundary shows a fallback. Nested boundaries let you keep the shell interactive.

use(promise) (React 19) reads a promise or context during render and suspends on a pending promise. The promise must be created outside the component (or be cached) — creating it inside the component loops.

Transitions + Suspense = no fallback flash. Wrapping a state update in startTransition means React keeps showing the old content instead of swapping to a spinner. This is the main UX reason for both APIs.
commonMistakes: wrapping the whole app in one boundary; expecting boundaries to catch fetch errors; putting a data-fetching side effect in a component that suspends without a cache; using Suspense for sub-100ms loads; forgetting key to reset a boundary's error state (a common pattern: reset on navigation).
practiceTasks: Build a QueryErrorBoundary with: reset(), retry-with-backoff, a "report" affordance that sends the componentStack, and a resetKeys prop so navigation clears the error. Simulate a thrown error in a child, then in an event handler (show that the boundary does *not* catch it), then in an async callback.

interviewQuestions.text: Why must error boundaries be class components, and what is the React 19 state of play?
What do error boundaries *not* catch?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Not event handler errors, not errors inside setTimeout or promise callbacks that you don't rethrow during render, not errors thrown by the boundary itself, and not server-render errors. Those must be caught with try/catch at the call site and reported. The reason is that the boundary mechanism is implemented by React's render/commit machinery: it can only catch a throw that happens while React is rendering a child fiber."

interviewQuestions.text: Where would you place boundaries in a real app?
Why is a top-level boundary alone insufficient?
How does Suspense + `startTransition` avoid spinners?
interviewQuestions.answer: "A transition update is non-urgent, so if the new content suspends, React can keep showing the existing UI and keep the main thread responsive to input, instead of committing a fallback. Without a transition, React must show the fallback immediately, which is why typing in a search box with a Suspense boundary produces a flash of spinner on every keystroke. That's the canonical 'Suspense + transition' pairing."

interviewQuestions.text: What throws a promise in a Suspense world?
Suspense vs a `loading` state variable?
How does Suspense help SSR/TTFB?

topics.title: Portals
topics.description: Portals within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: Portals

Events bubble through the React tree, not the DOM tree. A click inside a portal rendered deep in your tree will bubble to ancestors in React even though the DOM parent is document.body. This is a classic bug ("my outside-click handler fires when I click the modal") — stop propagation, or check e.currentTarget vs e.target.
document doesn't exist during SSR — guard with a mounted check, or render null on the server and mount on the client (hydration-safe if you don't render content that differs).
Server rendering portals needs a framework-provided target.
Refs, three flavors
forwardRef (and React 19's ref-as-prop)
useImperativeHandle
commonMistakes: forgetting the focus trap; not restoring focus; no aria-modal; portal content without scroll-lock compensation (layout shift when the scrollbar disappears); assuming document exists on the server.
practiceTasks: Build a portal-based modal that is fully keyboard accessible, restores focus, locks scroll without layout shift, closes on backdrop click, and announces its title. Then a tooltip positioned via getBoundingClientRect in useLayoutEffect inside a portal so it escapes clipping and overflow.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem do portals solve?
Do events inside a portal bubble to the React parent? Why does that surprise people?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Yes. React attaches its event listeners at the root container and simulates propagation using the *React* tree, so a click inside a portal bubbles to the React ancestors of the component that created the portal, even though its DOM parent is document.body. That's why an overlay-level click-outside handler in the tree will fire for clicks inside the portal. Fix: check e.target === e.currentTarget for backdrop clicks, or call stopPropagation inside the portal content."

interviewQuestions.text: What must you handle when opening a modal?
interviewQuestions.answer: focus move, focus trap, Escape, restore focus, scroll lock, `aria-modal`, labelling, inert background, portal target on SSR

topics.title: Strict Mode
topics.description: Strict Mode within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: StrictMode
Re-renders components an extra time (render-phase double invocation).
Re-runs effects an extra time: mount → cleanup → mount.
Re-runs reducers and (in dev) re-runs some initializer functions.
Why
Purify your render phase
Date.now(), Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID() in render → use useState(() => ...) for a once-per-instance value, or move to an effect.
Mutating props or state objects.
Reading and writing refs during render (4.1.8).
Dispatching to a store during render.
Network calls or logging with side effects (logging is fine but noisy).
Hydration
commonMistakes: treating the double-invoke as a bug to suppress; adding a didMount ref guard around every effect instead of cleaning up properly; using suppressHydrationWarning on a wrapper element to hide structural mismatches; reading window in render in an SSR app.
practiceTasks: Take an SSR-rendered page and intentionally introduce four hydration mismatches (a timestamp, a localStorage read, a navigator.userAgent branch, and invalid nesting). Observe each error message, then fix all four properly and explain why suppressHydrationWarning is not the answer.

interviewQuestions.text: Why does StrictMode double-invoke effects, and what bug class is it designed to expose?
My API call fires twice in development. Is it a StrictMode bug? What is the real fix?
interviewQuestions.answer: "StrictMode is doing its job: it remounts effects so that a missing cleanup shows up. The real bug is that my effect performs a non-idempotent side effect with no cleanup. If the effect created a subscription, timer, or socket, StrictMode's cleanup would tear it down and it would be recreated — fine. My fetch had no abort, so both calls completed. The fix is to make the effect abortable and idempotent, and for writes to carry an idempotency key. Production StrictMode does not double-invoke, so this only shows up in development, which is exactly why it is valuable."

interviewQuestions.text: Why is reading `Date.now()` in render a bug even though it "only happens in dev twice"?
What causes hydration mismatches? Which fix is legitimate and which is a hack?
interviewQuestions.answer: "In order of likelihood: time- or locale-dependent rendering, direct window/localStorage/navigator reads during render, invalid HTML nesting the parser repairs, and content that depends on client-only feature detection. The legitimate fix is to make the first client render match the server — defer browser-only reads to an effect, pass server-resolved values down, or render a stable placeholder. suppressHydrationWarning is legitimate for a single genuinely unavoidable value like a formatted timestamp on a text node; using it broadly hides real bugs, and it does not fix mismatched attributes or extra/missing elements."

interviewQuestions.text: What does `suppressHydrationWarning` actually do, and when is it acceptable?
How do you reduce hydration cost?
Should you ship StrictMode to production? What does it do to your bundle?

topics.title: The rendering model: elements, phases, reconciliation, and Fiber
topics.description: *Rendering* in React means calling your component functions to produce a tree of React elements, comparing that tree with the previous one, and committing the minimal set of DOM mutations. *Reconciliation* is the algorithm for that comparison. *Fiber* is the data structure and scheduling engine that make it possible to interrupt, resume, and prioritize that work.
keyConcepts: Step 1: elements, not DOM
Step 2: the component types
Function components are called and return elements. They may also be async in a Server Component context only.
Class components are instantiated (new) and have lifecycle methods; React still re-renders them with this.setState.
Host components are lowercase strings and map to DOM/host elements.
React.Fragment/<> groups children without adding a node.
memo(Component) returns a special element type; React skips re-invoking it when props are shallow-equal.
forwardRef(fn) wraps a function component so it receives ref as a third argument.
Context providers/consumers are also element types and participate in the tree.
Step 3: the two-phase commit

Render must be pure. Since the render phase can run twice (StrictMode, or after an interruption in concurrent mode), side effects in render will happen twice. Never mutate external state, never fetch, never write to a ref that render reads.

Render can be aborted. A transition (4.1.12) may start, get interrupted by a higher-priority update, and re-render. So the same component function can run with the same props twice and produce different results *only* if it read something impure like Date.now() or Math.random().
commonMistakes: treating effects as lifecycle hooks; doing data fetching and derived-state work in effects; assuming useMemo makes things fast without measuring; putting a console.log in render and trusting its count.
practiceTasks: Build a 10,000-row list and profile it: (a) with plain setState on every keystroke, (b) with a debounced filter, (c) with a manual useMemo filter, (d) virtualized with a fixed row height. Record commit counts and long-task durations using the React DevTools profiler and performance.measure.

interviewQuestions.text: What is the virtual DOM, and is it the reason React is fast?
interviewQuestions.answer: "The virtual DOM is an in-memory description of what the UI should be, as plain objects. It lets React compute a diff against the previous description and apply only the real DOM mutations needed. It's not the reason React is fast — React is fast because it batches multiple state updates into one commit, avoids interleaved read/write layout thrash, and skips DOM writes entirely for unchanged subtrees. For a single text-node update, direct DOM manipulation is faster than a React render."

interviewQuestions.text: Describe the render and commit phases. What can happen in each?
Can rendering be interrupted? Can it be discarded? Why does that matter for purity?
What are the reconciliation rules when types differ?
What is a Fiber, and what does it buy us?
Why can a render run twice in development but not production?
What's the difference between "re-render" and "re-mount"? Which is more expensive and which bugs are more subtle?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Re-render means React calls the component function again and diffs the returned elements; state and DOM nodes are preserved. A re-mount means React throws away the old fiber and its state and creates new instances, which loses state, refires effects, and is far more expensive. Remount bugs are nastier because they usually come from unstable keys, changing element types in a position (a <div> becoming a <span>), or conditional rendering, and they show up as 'my form state resets' or 'this effect runs way too often' rather than as an obvious error."

interviewQuestions.text: Where do refs get attached, and why does that make `useRef` in an effect always non-null?

```
 /props│ 2. walk down: render components, build the work-in-    │
 change│    progress tree; call component fns; diff children;    │
       │    call hooks in order; collect effects                 │
       └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
      commit phase (synchronous, not interruptible)
      ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │ 3a. before-mutation lifecycle (getSnapshotBeforeUpdate)│
       │ 3b. DOM mutations (insert/update/remove nodes, refs)   │
       │ 3c. layout effects (useLayoutEffect) — sync, before    │
       │     paint; can read layout, blocks paint               │
       │ 3d. paint (browser renders)                             │
       │ 3e. passive effects (useEffect) — async, usually after │
       │     paint; can be interrupted                          │
       └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

topics.title: Keys and identity: why index keys break
topics.description: Keys and identity: why index keys break within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: What a key is
The rule
Why index keys break
Input values "follow the row" instead of the item.
Animations and CSS transitions apply to the wrong nodes.
Checked/focused state sticks to a position.
With AnimatePresence-style libraries, elements exit with the wrong content.
The subtler case: item IDs that aren't stable
Keys and conditional rendering
Keys in lists that reorder often: alternatives
Sort/compare by a stable identity column.
Use a Map keyed by id and pass the item in as a prop instead of relying on position.
commonMistakes: index keys in sortable/filterable lists; random keys; reaching for key={Math.random()} to force a remount instead of restructuring; copying keys from the array index because "the order never changes" and then adding sorting.
practiceTasks: Write a sortable, filterable, addable/deletable list twice — once with index keys, once with id keys — and add two uncontrolled inputs per row. Show the bug, then fix it. Then explain which state was destroyed by the remount and how you would preserve it.

interviewQuestions.text: What is a key for, and what breaks without one?
Why is `key={index}` worse than no key at all in a reorderable list?
Why is `key={Math.random()}` catastrophic?
Do keys need to be globally unique?
How do you force a component to remount on purpose?
A child component's input loses its text when the parent reorders a list. Diagnose it.
interviewQuestions.answer: "The parent is likely using index keys, so after the reorder React matched the fiber at position 0 — which used to be item A — to item C. Because inputs are uncontrolled, their DOM value (and focus) lives on that reused node, so the text sticks to the position instead of the item. Fix: key by a stable item.id. Then check whether the id is truly stable (don't derive it from the array index anywhere upstream)."

topics.title: What actually causes a re-render
topics.description: A re-render is React calling your component function again and diffing the new output. It happens when React has new work for a fiber: a state update on that fiber, a props change from the parent, or a context read that changed.
keyConcepts: The complete list of triggers
setState (or a dispatch) in this component.

A parent re-renders and creates new props for this element. (Note: a parent re-render does *not* by itself force children to re-render if they are memo'd and props are shallow-equal. But an unmemoized child *always* re-renders when its parent re-renders, even if props are identical objects.)
useContext returning a new value (see 4.1.14) — this propagates to all consumers below the provider, bypassing memo.
A store subscription in the component (Zustand, Redux useSelector, Jotai) emits a value that changed for that slice.
The root re-renders (new element from root.render, or a parent of the tree).
forceUpdate (class) / useReducer dispatch.
useSyncExternalStore detects a store change.
HMR in development.

Mutating an object or array in place (items.push(x) then setItems(items)): the identity is unchanged, so Object.is says "equal" and React bails out. This is why "mutate then set" bugs feel random — other triggers (parent render) later expose the change, so it looks non-deterministic.
Re-rendering because of an useMemo recompute — a memo recompute causes no re-render; it's just a cache miss.
An effect running. Effects *follow* renders.
commonMistakes: assuming memo stops the parent from re-rendering; assuming one log line equals one render; using an object/array literal as a prop or in a context value and then wondering why memo doesn't help; treating context reads as scoped.
practiceTasks: Take any 200-line component and count renders for every component on: initial mount, a state update, a context value change, a parent-driven prop change with identical values, and a store update. Write down which triggers which, and confirm with React DevTools' "why did this render".

interviewQuestions.text: List every thing that causes a re-render.
My `setState` with the same value still logs a render. Why?
interviewQuestions.answer: "React enqueues the update and compares the next state with the current state using Object.is. If they're equal it bails out of re-rendering that subtree. But the spec allows React to render the component one more time before bailing out — it 'may still need to render that specific component again before bailing out' — so you can see one extra render. Also, in StrictMode dev, renders are intentionally double-invoked. So one extra render log is normal; a loop is not."

interviewQuestions.text: Why do memoized children re-render when the parent re-renders?
Mutating an array and calling `setState` doesn't update the UI. Explain.
Does a context consumer re-render if the provider value is `Object.is`-equal but a new object?
How do you find why a component re-renders, precisely?
What's the cost of a re-render, really?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Re-running a component function is cheap: it's a plain function call plus a diff of the returned elements. What costs is the subtree below it and whatever you compute during render. So the optimization question isn't 'how do I stop this render' but 'is this subtree expensive, and if so is it expensive because of an O(n) computation, an unmemoized child, or a large DOM update'. Measure with the Profiler, then decide."

topics.title: useState: queue, updater, bailout, equality, batching
topics.description: useState creates a single state slot whose value persists across renders and is private to the component (or shared only via props/context).
keyConcepts: Creates an update object {lane, payload} and appends it to fiber.updateQueue (a circular list with next/circle pointers).
Schedules work on the fiber.
During the next render, React processes the queue from the position it last stopped at (baseQueue for skipped updates), computing newState = reducer(prevState, action).
Compares newState with memoizedState using Object.is. Equal → bailout. Different → new memoizedState, mark children for update, re-render.
Key rules that follow from that mechanism
State is a snapshot. The variable in your closure is the value from *that* render. setN(n + 1) three times in one handler sets the same value three times.
Functional updates are queued and applied in order. Use them whenever the next value depends on the previous one, especially inside async callbacks, intervals, and event handlers that may batch.
Batching. React 18+ auto-batches updates from promises, timeouts, and native event handlers, not just React events. Updates in the same tick produce one render.
Lazy initial state. useState(() => expensive()) runs the initializer exactly once. useState(expensive()) runs it on *every* render and throws the result away.
Equality is Object.is, not shallow equality. NaN equals NaN under Object.is (unlike ===); +0 and -0 differ. There is no built-in deep comparison, and you should not want one — see 4.1.7.
State must be immutable. Mutating nested objects in place is the same bug as mutating arrays: the identity of the state object is unchanged, so Object.is bails out and the UI never updates.

Setting state on an unmounted component. React 18 removed the warning; the update is simply ignored. It no longer warns, but you can still leak if the async work itself holds resources — use AbortController in 4.1.5.
commonMistakes: useState(new Date()) (runs every render); useEffect(() => setX(props.x), [props.x]) loops; treating state as mutable; assuming setState returns the new value synchronously; mixing n and p => p styles in one place.
practiceTasks: Implement a useReducer-free counter hook with: increment(), incrementBy(n), reset(), and history via undo. Write it twice — once naively with object state, once with independent slots — and compare re-render behavior with the Profiler.

interviewQuestions.text: Why does `setN(n + 1)` three times only increment once?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Because state is a snapshot, n is the value from this render and doesn't change until the next render. All three calls enqueue the same computed value, n + 1. React coalesces them into one render. If I need the accumulated result, I pass an updater function, and React applies each updater to the latest state in the queue in order, giving n + 3."

interviewQuestions.text: When does the initializer of `useState` run?
What is `Object.is` and why does React use it? Why no deep compare?
How does batching work in React 18 vs 17, and how do you opt out?
Why can't you mutate state? What exactly goes wrong?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Two failures. First, Object.is(next, current) is true when you mutate in place, so React bails out and never re-renders. Second, even if a render happens for another reason, the previous element tree references the *same* objects, so the diff sees no change and the DOM isn't updated. It works until the day it doesn't, which is worse. Immutability also gives you structural sharing for free, cheap change detection via ===, and undo/redo."

interviewQuestions.text: When would you use `useReducer` instead of `useState`?
What happens if you `setState` after unmount?
Multiple `useState` in a component — how does React know which one to update?

topics.title: useEffect: mental model, dependencies, cleanup, when *not* to use it
topics.description: useEffect(effect, deps) schedules a *side effect* after React commits: it runs after the DOM is updated, and React runs cleanup before re-running it and again on unmount.
keyConcepts: The mental model that makes effects click
Timing, precisely
Cleanup functions and their three jobs
Undo the effect: unsubscribe, clearInterval, close(), abort().
Reset state before the next run so you don't get a race (see stale responses below).
Guard against races with a cancelled/ignore flag or AbortController.
The dependency array
Omitted → runs after every render.
[] → runs after the first render only, cleanup on unmount. "Mount/unmount", not "first time the value is truthy".
[a, b] → runs when the identity of a or b changes (Object.is per slot) *compared to the last committed render*, and cleanup runs before re-running.
Missing deps → stale closure (4.1.6).
Extra deps → effect churn: a new object/array/function identity every render re-runs the effect every render (a subscription leak, a re-animation, an infinite loop).
commonMistakes: fetching in effects without cancellation; returning an object from cleanup (React throws); async cleanup functions (they're ignored — you must not await in cleanup); forgetting to remove event listeners; using effects as lifecycle equivalents of class componentDidMount for data derivation; using an effect for analytics on every render instead of on the specific action.
practiceTasks: Write five effects: (1) a resize observer with correct cleanup, (2) an interval with a pause/resume control, (3) a debounced search with AbortController and stale-response protection, (4) a document-title sync that you'd argue should be an effect, and (5) a document-title sync that you first write as an effect and then rewrite as *not* one. For each, name the external system and what happens without cleanup.

interviewQuestions.text: When exactly do effects run relative to paint?
What is a cleanup function for? Give three reasons.
Why do I need to clean up a subscription? What breaks if I don't?
What does `[]` actually mean? Is it "run once forever"?
interviewQuestions.answer: "[] means 'this effect has no dependencies, so run it after the first commit and never re-run for state/prop changes'. Cleanup still runs on unmount. It is not 'run once per component instance forever' in the sense of ignoring all future renders — it *is* run after every commit where dependencies changed, and with [] dependencies never change. Under StrictMode in dev, React mounts, unmounts, and remounts to surface missing cleanups, so you'll see it run twice."

interviewQuestions.text: Why did my effect run twice even with `[]`?
How do I write an effect that doesn't loop forever?
What causes an infinite effect loop and how do I debug it?
Should I `await` inside an effect?
interviewQuestions.answer: "You can, but if you await in the body the cleanup function can't be returned, so you lose cancellation and unmount safety. Options: define an inner async function and call it, returning the cleanup synchronously; or use AbortController. And in most production apps the right answer is a data-fetching layer (4.4) that handles caching, dedupe, retries, and staleness — because hand-rolled effects re-implement all of it badly."

interviewQuestions.text: Why is an effect not a good place to derive state?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Because an effect writes state *after* render, you get an extra render pass and a frame where the UI shows stale data. If a value is derivable from props and state, deriving it during render is synchronous, correct under concurrent rendering (which can re-run render), and cheaper. Effects are for synchronizing with systems outside React, not for computing values inside it."

interviewQuestions.text: How do I fetch data in an effect, and what's the modern answer?

topics.title: Stale closures and how to fix them
topics.description: A stale closure is when a callback (timer, event listener, subscription, async continuation) captures a render's props/state variables, and by the time it runs, those values are from an older render — so it reads old data.
keyConcepts: Why it happens
The four fixes, and when each is right
Functional update (setCount(c => c + 1)) — best when you only *write*. No extra deps, no re-subscription.
Functional ref (read the current value at invocation time) — best when you need to *read* too:
Include the dependency and re-subscribe — correct but costly; don't re-subscribe every second just to see the new count. Fine for cheap subscriptions (a media query).

useEffectEvent (experimental) / an event-scoped callback — the React team's preferred end state: effects declare *what* they depend on for lifecycle, but read values through a stable "event" function. In React 19 this is still experimental, so pattern 2 is the practical answer today.
The classic stale-closure bugs
Detection
commonMistakes: adding every variable to the dependency array to "fix" staleness and unknowingly tearing down a subscription every render; reading e.target asynchronously; capturing a whole object and depending on its identity; using a ref during render to initialize state.
practiceTasks: Build a 200-line "live dashboard" with: a 1s poller, a resize listener, a keyboard shortcut, and a debounced input. Force each callback to log its captured values; demonstrate the staleness; then fix all four with functional updates / latest-value refs / stable subscription deps, and explain each choice.

interviewQuestions.text: What is a stale closure and what causes it?
Your `setInterval` always increments by the wrong amount. Explain and fix two ways.
interviewQuestions.answer: "The interval callback was created during the first render, so it closes over count === 0. Every tick it computes 0 + 1. Two fixes: use a functional update, setCount(c => c + 1), so I never read the outer variable; or keep a ref holding the latest count and read countRef.current inside the callback. Adding count to the deps would technically fix correctness but would clear and re-create the interval every second, resetting the timer and possibly skipping ticks — that's a bug factory."

interviewQuestions.text: Why doesn't adding `count` to the dependency array fix it well?
What is a ref-based "latest value" pattern and when is it the right fix?
`useEffectEvent` would change which rule?
How do you avoid the stale `e.target.value` in a debounce?
Why can you never just "fix it by adding deps" for a chat message handler?

topics.title: Effects vs events, and "you might not need an effect"
topics.description: Effects vs events, and "you might not need an effect" within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: The shift in thinking
Effects are for synchronizing with systems outside React. External stores, subscriptions, timers, the document, the network, imperative libraries.
Events are for responding to user actions. A click, submit, keystroke. The handler runs, and any state updates it causes are React's business.
Rendering is pure. Compute derived values during render.
The pattern table
The "adjusting state when a prop changes" problem
The 7 anti-patterns to recognize on sight
Transforming data for rendering.
Handling a user event (a reset button shouldn't need an effect).
Prop-driven state (reset with key).
Resetting state with a prop (same fix).
Adjusting state when a prop changes (prev-value pattern).
commonMistakes: the "fetch and setState" effect copied from 2018 tutorials; using an effect to reset a form; using an effect to log an analytics event that fires on every render; arguing that effects are "bad" rather than "scoped".
practiceTasks: Take any component with ≥2 effects and classify each: external system / event / derivation / anti-pattern. Rewrite the anti-patterns. For each rewrite, state how many renders you removed and what bug class you eliminated (flash, double fetch, lost input, stale UI).

interviewQuestions.text: Why is `useEffect` a poor replacement for lifecycle methods?
Give four examples of "you might not need an effect" with the fix for each.
How do you reset state when a prop changes? Give three approaches and their trade-offs.
When *is* setting state during render allowed?
Your component connects a WebSocket twice. Explain.
Where should analytics `track()` calls live?
interviewQuestions.answer: "In the handler that represents the user's intent, not in an effect. If the semantic action is 'user clicked Save', track it in onSave. If the semantic action is 'the item became persisted', that's a state transition, and an effect keyed on the persisted value is defensible — but then dedupe it and make sure it fires once per transition, not once per render. The rule of thumb: if you can't name the user intent, you probably shouldn't be tracking it."

interviewQuestions.text: How do you decide effect vs event at design time?
Why does "extra render" matter for performance and for correctness?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Correctness first: an effect writing state means the UI has already committed with the old value, so anything reading the DOM or the screen reader sees the stale state, and you get a visible flash plus a double commit. Performance second: each such effect adds a render pass, and a chain of them can cascade into several renders per interaction. Correctness is the real argument; the render count is a symptom."

topics.title: useRef: the mutable box
topics.description: useRef(initial) returns a stable { current } object that lives for the component's lifetime. Mutating .current does not trigger a render.
keyConcepts: Legitimate uses
DOM references (ref={node => ...} or useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)), used for measurement, focus, scroll, imperative third-party libraries.

Mutable values that shouldn't cause renders: the latest props in an async callback (4.1.6), a timer id, an AbortController, a WebSocket instance, a "have we mounted" flag, a previous-value tracker for comparing in an effect.
Storing an instance of a non-React system where a state variable would be wrong (a <canvas> context, an animation controller).
Anti-uses
As state (it doesn't render — you'll read ref.current in render and get a stale value).
To "avoid re-renders" for values the UI must display.
To replace useState for things that need to trigger renders.
Ref identity and rules
The ref object is created once per component instance (per fiber), so it's stable across renders and safe in dependency arrays.

Don't write ref.current during render and read it in the same render — under concurrent rendering and StrictMode's double-invoke, render runs twice and the second run sees your mutation. If you need "the value from the previous committed render", write in useLayoutEffect or useEffect, or use React's official "adjust state in an effect" pattern:
Don't pass the same ref to two nodes (last write wins) and don't write and read .current in the same render.
commonMistakes: useRef for displayed data; reading .current in render; expecting useRef(fn()) to be lazy (it's not lazy — the argument is evaluated every render, so pass useRef(null) and set it in an effect, or use useState(() => fn())); returning a ref object from a custom hook and exposing it where a value is expected.
practiceTasks: Build useLatest, usePrevious, useIsMounted, and useEventCallback (a stable callback that always calls the latest version — the workhorse for event handlers passed to memoized children), and write a test for each showing it doesn't cause re-renders.

interviewQuestions.text: Why doesn't mutating a ref cause a render? Where does React read it?
When is a ref better than state?
What's wrong with writing `ref.current` during render?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Because render can run twice (StrictMode) and can be interrupted and restarted, anything a render writes could be written twice or read from a discarded render pass. Refs are mutable boxes with no corresponding Fiber update, so writing to them during render breaks the model that render is pure computation over props and state. The safe place is after commit: useLayoutEffect (before paint) or useEffect."

interviewQuestions.text: How do you track the previous value of a prop?
Should you ever put React state in a ref?
interviewQuestions.answer: Yes, for "is this the initial value" guards and for values that must be read synchronously in a callback, but you must be careful: state changes won't re-render, so it's for bookkeeping, not display.

interviewQuestions.text: How do you forward a ref to a DOM node from a function component?
When would you need a ref to an object (not a DOM node)?

topics.title: useReducer: when state transitions are complex
topics.description: useReducer(reducer, initialState, init?) centralizes state transitions in a pure function. React owns the queue; you own the logic.
keyConcepts: When it's better than useState
The next state depends on the previous state in several places (a state machine, a wizard, a form with cross-field rules).
You want every transition named and logged (the action log is a free audit trail and makes debugging much easier).
You want to co-locate related state that must change together.
You want to test transitions as a pure function without rendering anything.
Why the discriminated union matters
Reducer rules
Must be pure: no mutation of state or action, no network calls, no Date.now()/Math.random() inside (put them in the action payload).
Must be complete: every action handled, with assertNever for exhaustiveness.
dispatch is stable for the component's lifetime. Never put dispatch in a dependency array (harmless but noise), and never rely on dispatch changing to trigger an effect.
init runs once and must be pure; use it to avoid re-creating the initial state.
Lazy initialization: useReducer(reducer, expensiveArg, init) beats useReducer(reducer, expensiveArg()).
commonMistakes: side effects inside a reducer; Date.now() in a reducer (breaks replayability); mutating state instead of returning a new object; expecting the reducer to be called once per dispatch in dev; using a reducer where a ref would do.
practiceTasks: Model a 4-step checkout wizard as a reducer with an explicit state union, guards for "can go back", and a MAX_STEPS-aware progress field. Then write unit tests that drive the reducer directly with action sequences — no rendering — including illegal transitions.

interviewQuestions.text: When do you choose `useReducer` over `useState`?
Why must reducers be pure, and what breaks if they aren't?
Is `dispatch` referentially stable? What does that enable?
How do you get exhaustive type checking on actions?
What's the `init` third argument for, and when does it matter?
Why is `status: 'loading' | 'done'` better than two booleans?
When would you reach for a state machine library instead?
How would you implement undo/redo with `useReducer`?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Keep a history array in state: { past: State[], present: State, future: State[] }. On each action, push present to past, set present to the new state, and clear future. Undo pops from past into present and pushes the old present onto future. Redo is the mirror. Keep the history bounded (last N) so memory doesn't grow, and skip entries for high-frequency, non-meaningful changes like a text field keystroke — or coalesce them by action type."

topics.title: useMemo, useCallback, memo: cost, benefit, and measurement
topics.description: React.memo(Component, areEqual?) — skips re-rendering the component when props are shallow-equal (or equal per areEqual).
keyConcepts: What memo actually does
The cost model — you must know this to use these correctly
When memoization genuinely helps
Expensive computation that runs on every render of a hot component:
Stable identity to prevent effect churn: passing a stable submit to a <form onSubmit> that a child subscribes to; a memoized context value (4.1.14); a stable object passed to a dependency array.
memo on a genuinely expensive leaf whose props are usually stable — a chart, a markdown renderer, a big table, a third-party widget.

Referential stability as an API contract: a context value, a store selector, a useSyncExternalStore snapshot, a Map/Set you return from a hook. If consumers compare with Object.is, you must return a stable reference.
When it does not help (and hurts)
Props that change identity every render (style={{}}, inline arrow functions, data={[1,2]}). memo will compare and fail every time — pure overhead plus code noise.
A cheap component. memo makes it slower.
A component that reads context whose value changes often (4.1.14): the bailout is skipped.
As a substitute for fixing an architecture problem: a 5,000-row list of unmemoized rows and one memoized wrapper is not a performance strategy.
commonMistakes: wrapping everything in memo; useCallback for a function used once; memoizing a cheap filter; unstable props defeating memo; useCallback(fn, []) capturing stale props; memoizing an effect's dependency instead of the value; assuming useMemo guarantees referential stability (React may discard the cache in the future — it's a performance hint, not a semantic guarantee; if you *need* stability, build it yourself).
practiceTasks: Take a search page with 5,000 rows. Measure: (a) baseline, (b) useMemo the filter, (c) memo the row, (d) both, (e) virtualize. Record commit counts and durations. Then find the point where the cost of memoization exceeds the benefit, and explain why in numbers.

interviewQuestions.text: What is `memo`, `useMemo`, and `useCallback`, and how do they differ?
Why does `useCallback` need a deps array if it just returns the function?
My `memo` component re-renders anyway. List every possible reason.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Any of: the props aren't actually equal — an inline object/array/function literal; the component reads a context whose value changed (context propagation skips the memo bailout); there is a pending state update inside the memoized subtree; the component type changed (a new component identity, e.g. defining it inside another component); the parent itself re-rendered and the element's type is different from last time; StrictMode is double-invoking in dev; or you're looking at a remount caused by a key change rather than a re-render."

interviewQuestions.text: Is `useMemo` free? What does it cost?
When is memoization the wrong tool?
How do you decide whether a component is worth memoizing?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Measure. React DevTools Profiler with 'record why each component rendered' tells me whether a component is re-rendering at all and why. If it's not in the commits, it's fine. If it is, I check whether its render is slow or it's just re-rendering a cheap subtree — because an expensive *DOM update* below it won't be helped by memo. Then, and only then, I memoize the specific expensive computation or wrap the specific expensive leaf."

interviewQuestions.text: Why does the React team recommend against default memoization?
What's the difference between memoizing a value and memoizing a component?
Explain `areEqual` and its risks.
What does React Compiler change about this?
interviewQuestions.answer: "React Compiler does automatic memoization at build time: it inserts the equivalent of useMemo/useCallback/memo where it can prove they're correct, based on its rules of React. So the manual effort mostly goes away for code that compiles cleanly. Until then — or for code the compiler bails on (violating the rules, side effects in render, mutating props) — manual memoization still matters, and you still have to know *why* you're adding it."

topics.title: useLayoutEffect, useInsertionEffect, and measurement
topics.description: useEffect — passive effect, runs *after* the browser has painted (usually).
keyConcepts: When you need useLayoutEffect
Reading layout after mutation and synchronously re-rendering: measure an element, then set state to adjust a tooltip position, a carousel translate, or a virtualized scroll offset.
Preventing a visual jump: for example, resetting scrollTop to 0 on route change after the new content has been committed.
Keeping two DOM nodes in sync imperatively where a state update would be too slow.
Why this works where useEffect doesn't
The infinite useLayoutEffect loop
useLayoutEffect and SSR
Do not measure in render
Measurement toolbelt
commonMistakes: using useLayoutEffect for anything that isn't synchronous layout work (it blocks paint, hurting INP); measuring during render; storing DOM nodes in state; ignoring SSR warnings; layout effects with heavy computation or network calls.
practiceTasks: Build a tooltip, a sticky header that toggles a shadow at scrollY > 8, and a virtualized list that must read scrollTop synchronously. Implement each with useLayoutEffect and explain, in terms of paint timing, what a visible flash would look like with useEffect.

interviewQuestions.text: `useLayoutEffect` vs `useEffect` — when each?
Why does measuring a tooltip cause a flash with `useEffect`?
Why can't you call `useLayoutEffect` on the server?
Your layout effect runs forever. Diagnose and fix.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Most likely I call setState with a fresh object each time, so the state identity always changes and re-triggers the effect. Fixes: return the previous state when the value is effectively unchanged (a functional update with a tolerance check), depend on primitives rather than objects, or move the whole thing to an event handler with requestAnimationFrame."

interviewQuestions.text: Why should you avoid measuring during render?
When do you need `useInsertionEffect`, and who should actually use it?
When is ResizeObserver better than a resize listener?
interviewQuestions.answer: "ResizeObserver fires when an element's box changes for any reason — content, siblings, CSS load, font load, container queries, orientation — and it fires before paint. A resize listener only fires on window resize, fires *after* layout in a way that's easy to thrash, and needs debouncing."

interviewQuestions.text: What's the cost of a `useLayoutEffect` that does heavy work?

topics.title: Concurrent React: useTransition, useDeferredValue, startTransition
topics.description: Concurrent React: useTransition, useDeferredValue, startTransition within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: The problem being solved
useTransition
startTransition(scope) marks all state updates inside scope as transition updates (same lane).

The input's own setQuery is urgent; the expensive setDeferredQuery is not. React renders the urgent update first, so typing stays at 60fps, and the results update after (or are interrupted and restarted when the next keystroke arrives).

isPending is true from the moment the transition starts until the transition's render *commits* — a genuinely reliable "loading" flag, unlike isLoading state you manage yourself (it flickers if you forget to reset it).

Rule: the transition scope must be synchronous. No await inside it — you cannot startTransition(async () => {...}). For async work, either set pending state in an event handler before awaiting, or wrap the state updates *after* the await:

Rule: you cannot transition a controlled input's own value to something slower. If setQuery itself triggered an expensive synchronous render, typing would still block. Transitions only help if the urgent part is cheap.
useDeferredValue
Suspense + transitions
Measurement
commonMistakes: wrapping everything in startTransition including the input's own value; awaiting inside a transition in React 18; assuming isPending is a network flag (it's a render-scheduling flag); using a transition where the change must be reflected synchronously (e.g. a destructive confirm); assuming transitions work without createRoot.
practiceTasks: Build a filter panel over a 20,000-row list with a text input, a facet select, and a sort dropdown. Use a transition for the results, useDeferredValue for the query, and render a subtle "updating…" affordance instead of a spinner (which is the better UX). Then type as fast as you can and record dropped renders in the Profiler and INP.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem do transitions solve that `useState` + `isLoading` doesn't?
Why can't you put `await` in a transition scope (React 18)? What changes in React 19?
`useTransition` vs `useDeferredValue` — when each?
interviewQuestions.answer: "They're two sides of the same idea. useTransition is for state you own: you wrap the expensive state update and get a pending flag. useDeferredValue is for a value you don't own — a prop, a store value, a URL param — where you want the expensive part of the tree to render against a slightly stale version instead of blocking. Use both together when you control the input and also want to derive expensive content from it."

interviewQuestions.text: Why can't you make a controlled input's value itself a transition?
What does `isPending` guarantee that a `loading` boolean doesn't?
How do transitions interact with Suspense?
Does `startTransition` make the work faster, cheaper, or just later?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Later, and interruptible. Total work is unchanged, but because it's interruptible React can throw away a render that has already been invalidated by a newer keystroke, so under fast typing the expensive tree effectively renders less often. That's a real CPU saving, not just a reordering. But the urgent render must still be cheap, or the input will lag."

interviewQuestions.text: What would you do if the urgent render itself is expensive?

useSyncExternalStore
useImperativeHandle
useDebugValue

interviewQuestions.text: Why can't you use a counter or random number for element IDs in SSR?
What problem does `useSyncExternalStore` solve?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Concurrent rendering can interleave and retry renders, so a component might read a store during a render that gets thrown away and another component might read it after it changed — that's tearing, where the tree shows inconsistent data. useSyncExternalStore makes React re-check the snapshot after commit and re-render if it changed, so every component in a pass agrees on one value, and it provides the getServerSnapshot hook needed for SSR."

interviewQuestions.text: When do you need `useImperativeHandle`?
What's wrong with exposing everything through a ref handle?
interviewQuestions.answer: "A ref handle is an escape hatch from controlled React. If you put state or data in it, callers can desync the UI from the source of truth, and the component's invariants (validation, formatting, state machines) get bypassed. Handles should expose *commands* — focus, scrollTo, open, reset, measure — and the component should remain the source of truth."

topics.description: Context: propagation, performance, and splitting within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: A context value change re-renders every consumer below the provider, even across memo boundaries. memo does not stop context propagation.
The value is read during render (useContext / use(Ctx)), so consumers always see a consistent value for that render pass.
Splitting contexts works because each Provider is a separate fiber: <ThemeProvider> and <AuthProvider> are separate nodes, so a theme change doesn't touch auth consumers.
The classic performance bug
Select from a store instead of context — Zustand/Redux with selectors means a component only re-renders for the slice it reads. This is why state libraries exist alongside context.
Don't put frequently-changing state in a high-level provider. Put it as low in the tree as possible.
Context vs state library vs props
Also
commonMistakes: one giant app context; putting dispatch and state in the same value; useMemo with an object literal in the deps; assuming memo shields consumers; context for form input state.
practiceTasks: Build an app with a 30-component tree consuming one context, and instrument render counts. Refactor to three split contexts plus a Zustand-style selector store; record the render-count reduction. Explain which refactor gave the win and why useMemo alone was insufficient.

interviewQuestions.text: How does React know a context consumer needs to re-render?
Does `memo` protect a component from context updates?
Why does creating the value object inline destroy context performance?
How many contexts do you need, and how do you decide to split?
Context vs a state library — when each?
Why is context bad for high-frequency updates (e.g. mouse position)?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Every context value change marks every consumer for update, and React re-renders those subtrees. If the value changes per mouse-move event, that's a React render per event at 60–120Hz, plus a diff of the whole subtree. A ref updated in the event handler (no render) or a transient subscription (useSyncExternalStore with a selector, or a third-party observable) is the right tool. Context is for relatively rare, meaningful changes."

interviewQuestions.text: How do you pass a lot of values through many layers without prop drilling?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Three options, in preference order: compose components so you don't need to pass anything (children/slots), pass the data through a single useMyThing() hook backed by a module-scoped store or context (so each component asks for what it needs), or split and memoize the context value. Prop drilling through five layers is a signal that a boundary or abstraction is missing — not that props are the wrong tool."

keyConcepts: Portals

Events bubble through the React tree, not the DOM tree. A click inside a portal rendered deep in your tree will bubble to ancestors in React even though the DOM parent is document.body. This is a classic bug ("my outside-click handler fires when I click the modal") — stop propagation, or check e.currentTarget vs e.target.
document doesn't exist during SSR — guard with a mounted check, or render null on the server and mount on the client (hydration-safe if you don't render content that differs).
Server rendering portals needs a framework-provided target.
Refs, three flavors
forwardRef (and React 19's ref-as-prop)
useImperativeHandle
commonMistakes: forgetting the focus trap; not restoring focus; no aria-modal; portal content without scroll-lock compensation (layout shift when the scrollbar disappears); assuming document exists on the server.
practiceTasks: Build a portal-based modal that is fully keyboard accessible, restores focus, locks scroll without layout shift, closes on backdrop click, and announces its title. Then a tooltip positioned via getBoundingClientRect in useLayoutEffect inside a portal so it escapes clipping and overflow.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem do portals solve?
Do events inside a portal bubble to the React parent? Why does that surprise people?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Yes. React attaches its event listeners at the root container and simulates propagation using the *React* tree, so a click inside a portal bubbles to the React ancestors of the component that created the portal, even though its DOM parent is document.body. That's why an overlay-level click-outside handler in the tree will fire for clicks inside the portal. Fix: check e.target === e.currentTarget for backdrop clicks, or call stopPropagation inside the portal content."

topics.title: Error boundaries and Suspense
topics.description: Error boundaries and Suspense within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: Error boundaries
They must be class components (React 19 adds no hook equivalent — this is a well-known API gap). A framework may offer one (Next.js error.tsx, Remix ErrorBoundary).
They catch errors thrown during render, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of children — including errors thrown inside a component rendered within them.

They do not catch: errors in event handlers, in async code/setTimeout, in promise rejections handled elsewhere, errors thrown in the boundary itself, and errors during SSR (the boundary runs on the server).
Event handler and async errors must be caught at the source (try/catch) and reported to your error tracker.

Where to place them: at meaningful feature boundaries (per route, per widget), with a top-level fallback as the last resort. A boundary that wraps the entire app is a fallback of last resort only; it will hide most bugs.
Report to Sentry with the componentStack and a user-action breadcrumb trail (Phase 4.6).
Suspense

A component suspends by throwing a promise (React 19 also supports throwing an async function's promise with use(); data frameworks like Relay/Apollo/SWR adapters, and Next.js's <Suspense> + streaming RSC, use this).
Only the nearest boundary shows a fallback. Nested boundaries let you keep the shell interactive.

use(promise) (React 19) reads a promise or context during render and suspends on a pending promise. The promise must be created outside the component (or be cached) — creating it inside the component loops.

Transitions + Suspense = no fallback flash. Wrapping a state update in startTransition means React keeps showing the old content instead of swapping to a spinner. This is the main UX reason for both APIs.
commonMistakes: wrapping the whole app in one boundary; expecting boundaries to catch fetch errors; putting a data-fetching side effect in a component that suspends without a cache; using Suspense for sub-100ms loads; forgetting key to reset a boundary's error state (a common pattern: reset on navigation).
practiceTasks: Build a QueryErrorBoundary with: reset(), retry-with-backoff, a "report" affordance that sends the componentStack, and a resetKeys prop so navigation clears the error. Simulate a thrown error in a child, then in an event handler (show that the boundary does *not* catch it), then in an async callback.

interviewQuestions.text: Why must error boundaries be class components, and what is the React 19 state of play?
What do error boundaries *not* catch?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Not event handler errors, not errors inside setTimeout or promise callbacks that you don't rethrow during render, not errors thrown by the boundary itself, and not server-render errors. Those must be caught with try/catch at the call site and reported. The reason is that the boundary mechanism is implemented by React's render/commit machinery: it can only catch a throw that happens while React is rendering a child fiber."

interviewQuestions.text: Where would you place boundaries in a real app?
Why is a top-level boundary alone insufficient?
How does Suspense + `startTransition` avoid spinners?
interviewQuestions.answer: "A transition update is non-urgent, so if the new content suspends, React can keep showing the existing UI and keep the main thread responsive to input, instead of committing a fallback. Without a transition, React must show the fallback immediately, which is why typing in a search box with a Suspense boundary produces a flash of spinner on every keystroke. That's the canonical 'Suspense + transition' pairing."

topics.title: Lists, virtualization, and large forms
topics.description: Lists, virtualization, and large forms within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: Lists
Reduce the data — pagination, infinite scroll, filters.
Reduce per-row cost — memoized row, no inline objects, CSS containment (contain: strict), fixed row height, will-change used sparingly.
Virtualize — render only the visible window plus overscan.
Keys for lists
Forms at scale
Uncontrolled + refs + FormData on submit (best for large forms).
Field-level subscriptions: a form library that only re-renders the changed field (RHF's register, Formik's useField).
Split components per field so each field's state change re-renders only that subtree.
Schema validation on blur and on submit, not on every keystroke (Phase 4.4).
For very large forms: dynamic import per section, virtualization of non-field sections, and progressive disclosure.
Uncontrolled form + FormData
commonMistakes: key={index} in an infinite list; unbounded DOM growth; auto-loading with no button fallback; measuring row heights in useEffect instead of useLayoutEffect (causes a jump); keeping a controlled form for 500 fields.
practiceTasks: Implement a virtualized list from scratch (fixed height), then a dynamic-height version using ResizeObserver, then wire it to a cursor-paginated API with an IntersectionObserver sentinel, a Load more button for keyboard users, and a "select all 10,000" checkbox that operates on the data model rather than the DOM.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is a 10k-row list slow? Name the three costs.
What does virtualization buy, and what does it cost (a11y, find-in-page, print, dynamic heights)?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Virtualization removes DOM nodes, which reduces memory, style recalculation, layout, and paint. The costs are: only rendered rows exist in the accessibility tree and for find-in-page; dynamic row heights need measurement; scroll position can jump when content above changes size unless you anchor; print/export and "select all" need full-data handling; and server-side rendering the whole list isn't possible. So it's a rendering optimization, not a data model change — keep the full array in memory and render a window."

topics.title: StrictMode, hydration, and the double-invoke
topics.description: StrictMode, hydration, and the double-invoke within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: StrictMode
Re-renders components an extra time (render-phase double invocation).
Re-runs effects an extra time: mount → cleanup → mount.
Re-runs reducers and (in dev) re-runs some initializer functions.
Why
Purify your render phase
Date.now(), Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID() in render → use useState(() => ...) for a once-per-instance value, or move to an effect.
Mutating props or state objects.
Reading and writing refs during render (4.1.8).
Dispatching to a store during render.
Network calls or logging with side effects (logging is fine but noisy).
Hydration
commonMistakes: treating the double-invoke as a bug to suppress; adding a didMount ref guard around every effect instead of cleaning up properly; using suppressHydrationWarning on a wrapper element to hide structural mismatches; reading window in render in an SSR app.
practiceTasks: Take an SSR-rendered page and intentionally introduce four hydration mismatches (a timestamp, a localStorage read, a navigator.userAgent branch, and invalid nesting). Observe each error message, then fix all four properly and explain why suppressHydrationWarning is not the answer.

interviewQuestions.text: Why does StrictMode double-invoke effects, and what bug class is it designed to expose?
My API call fires twice in development. Is it a StrictMode bug? What is the real fix?
interviewQuestions.answer: "StrictMode is doing its job: it remounts effects so that a missing cleanup shows up. The real bug is that my effect performs a non-idempotent side effect with no cleanup. If the effect created a subscription, timer, or socket, StrictMode's cleanup would tear it down and it would be recreated — fine. My fetch had no abort, so both calls completed. The fix is to make the effect abortable and idempotent, and for writes to carry an idempotency key. Production StrictMode does not double-invoke, so this only shows up in development, which is exactly why it is valuable."

interviewQuestions.text: Why is reading `Date.now()` in render a bug even though it "only happens in dev twice"?
What causes hydration mismatches? Which fix is legitimate and which is a hack?
interviewQuestions.answer: "In order of likelihood: time- or locale-dependent rendering, direct window/localStorage/navigator reads during render, invalid HTML nesting the parser repairs, and content that depends on client-only feature detection. The legitimate fix is to make the first client render match the server — defer browser-only reads to an effect, pass server-resolved values down, or render a stable placeholder. suppressHydrationWarning is legitimate for a single genuinely unavoidable value like a formatted timestamp on a text node; using it broadly hides real bugs, and it does not fix mismatched attributes or extra/missing elements."

interviewQuestions.text: What does `suppressHydrationWarning` actually do, and when is it acceptable?
How do you reduce hydration cost?
Should you ship StrictMode to production? What does it do to your bundle?

topics.title: REAL-WORLD DEBUGGING SCENARIOS
topics.description: REAL-WORLD DEBUGGING SCENARIOS within React Concepts.
keyConcepts: "The page re-renders 20 times when I open it." Likely: state mirroring props in an effect, unstable context value, a store selector returning a new object, an effect setting state unconditionally. Investigate: Profiler "why did this render", count commits. Fix: derive instead of sync, memoize/split context, memoize the selector output. Prevention: a render-count test for critical components, lint rule.

"Infinite loop of renders." Likely: setState in render, effect without a guard, dep identity changing every render. Investigate: the error boundary stack, React's "Maximum update depth" message. Fix: functional update + previous-value ref, or derive. Prevention: exhaustive-deps lint, review rule against setState in render.

"Input loses focus on every keystroke." Likely: the input is being remounted — a changing key, a conditionally-rendered parent, or an inline component type (const Input = () => ... inside another component). Investigate: React DevTools highlight update to see if the node is replaced. Fix: hoist the component type, use a stable key. Prevention: ESLint rules that flag components defined inside components.

"The modal closes when I click inside it." Likely: a backdrop onClick firing for inner clicks (check e.target === e.currentTarget), or a portal bubbling click to an outside-click handler in the React tree. Fix: target check or stopPropagation inside the portal. Prevention: shared useOnClickOutside hook with documented portal caveat.

"Effect runs on every keystroke and re-subscribes." Likely: an unstable dep (object/array/function literal). Fix: primitives as deps, useMemo the object, useEventCallback for handlers. Prevention: exhaustive-deps lint, review checklist.

"Data fetched twice for the same query." Likely: missing dedupe in a custom hook, two effects (StrictMode double-invoke revealing no abort), or two components each fetching the same thing. Fix: a query layer with in-flight dedupe, or lift the fetch. Prevention: contract test asserting one network request.

"The app is janky while typing in a large list." Likely: filtering a 10k array per keystroke, unmemoized rows, layout thrashing from measurement inside a render-time loop. Fix: useDeferredValue or debounce, memoize the row and the filter, virtualize, batch reads/writes. Prevention: INP budget and a perf test in CI.

"State resets when navigating between two users' detail pages." Likely: no key on the component that should reset when the route param changes. Fix: key={id}. Prevention: a test asserting state resets on id change.

"LocalStorage-persisted state flashes the wrong theme." Likely: reading storage during render causes hydration mismatch; fix: read in an effect, or initialize from an inline script in the document head to avoid flash. Prevention: SSR-safe persistence hooks.

"Memory grows every time I open a route with a chart." Likely: a subscription without cleanup, an event listener not removed, a library instance not destroyed, or a growing cache keyed by request. Fix: return cleanups, dispose instances, bound caches. Prevention: heap snapshot in a regression test.

"Context consumers re-render even though nothing changed." Likely: new value object each render, or one provider holding high-churn state. Fix: split contexts, memoize value, move state to a store with selectors. Prevention: render-count assertions.

"Optimistic UI shows the wrong thing after a failed save." Likely: rollback isn't restoring the previous snapshot, or the cache key doesn't match, or the error path forgets to invalidate. Fix: use the data library's mutation lifecycle (onMutate snapshot, onError rollback, onSettled invalidate). Prevention: test the failure path explicitly.
