topics.title: App Router vs Pages Router
topics.description: The App Router (introduced in Next 13, default since 14) is a server-first, nested router built on React Server Components; the Pages Router is the legacy getServerSideProps / getStaticProps router. Almost every React developer has shipped on one of them, but few can articulate *why* the App Router changed data fetching, caching, and layout nesting. It also tests whether you can migrate a codebase rather than just scaffold one.

interview.whyAsked: Almost every React developer has shipped on one of them, but few can articulate *why* the App Router changed data fetching, caching, and layout nesting. It also tests whether you can migrate a codebase rather than just scaffold one.

topics.title: SSR vs SSG vs ISR vs CSR
topics.description: Four strategies for *when* and *where* HTML and data are produced, and therefore how fresh, how cacheable, and how cheap the response is.

topics.title: React Server Components vs Client Components
topics.description: A Server Component renders to HTML on the server (or at build time) and its code never reaches the browser. A Client Component is normal React: it ships JavaScript, runs in the browser, and can use state, effects, and event handlers. "use client" is a *module directive*, not a component decorator. It marks the file and every module it imports as part of the client bundle. Everything a module transitively imports becomes client code. This single fact explains most "why did my bundle explode" incidents.

topics.title: Server Actions
topics.description: A Server Action is an async function marked "use server" that runs on the server, invoked directly from client code or from a form, with the framework handling the network protocol. The directive at file scope makes every exported async function an action endpoint. Next builds a reference for it, embeds an encrypted action ID in the client bundle, and sends the ID plus the serialized arguments over POST to the same route. On the server, Next validates the origin, deserializes arguments, invokes the function, and returns the serialized return value. This is why actions work without any fetch code and why they also work with JavaScript disabled.

topics.title: Data fetching and caching
topics.description: The set of distinct caches between your server and your users, and the rules that decide which one a given read hits.

topics.title: Streaming and Suspense
topics.description: Streaming SSR sends the shell of the page as soon as it is ready and flushes subsequent HTML as Suspense boundaries resolve, so the browser can paint and become interactive before the slowest data has arrived.
keyConcepts: What it buys you
TTFB drops to roughly the time to render the shell, not the slowest query.
Out-of-order completion: boundary 3 can finish and flush before boundary 1, so a fast widget is not held hostage by a slow one.

Progressive rendering and fewer spinners in the user's perception, but a caveat: <Suspense> shows a fallback for boundaries that are *not yet resolved in that navigation*. Already-resolved boundaries (for example, cached RSC payloads from the Router Cache) do not flash a fallback on client-side navigation.
Fewer data waterfalls when you hoist fetches into sibling Suspense boundaries that run in parallel, since React starts them all as it renders.
Cost and gotchas
Streaming requires a server (it is the opposite of static export). With output: 'export' there is no runtime to stream from.
A slow boundary without a fallback is just a blank region; put fallbacks where layout matters.

Streaming interacts with error boundaries: an error thrown inside a streamed boundary arrives *after* the shell, so error.tsx must be present or the user sees a half-rendered page with a broken region. Use error.tsx per segment.
Streaming does not help SEO negatively (crawlers read the completed HTML), but it does complicate "wait for full load" tooling.

With Suspense, React can commit a fallback and later swap in content — a form of state you must design for, especially inputs (unmounting a focused input loses focus and value; use key carefully and keep state lifted).
useTransition (see 4.1) plus streaming gives you non-blocking navigation: set a pending state, stream the new route, keep the old UI visible.
commonMistakes: one giant top-level <Suspense> that defeats streaming; no error.tsx for streamed regions; using loading.tsx for a region that should keep showing stale content; assuming loading.tsx is required for client-side navigation (it is for dynamic routes; for static routes the prefetched payload may make it flash or not appear); measuring TTFB only and missing that FCP/LCP depend on the *first* region completing.
practiceTasks: build a page with three suspense-wrapped regions backed by routes with 50ms, 400ms, and 1500ms artificial delays. Measure TTFB, FCP, and LCP with the browser's performance panel before and after adding <Suspense>; note the difference. Then make the slow region fail and observe the escalation behaviour with and without a nested error.tsx.

interviewQuestions.text: What does streaming SSR change about perceived performance?
What is out-of-order completion?
What does `loading.tsx` do under the hood?
Why can a streamed error appear after a good-looking page?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* A page streams its shell and three data regions; one region's query rejects after 2 seconds. *Decision.* Every data-dependent region needs its own boundary pair: a <Suspense> for the pending state and an error.tsx (or a nested <ErrorBoundary>) for the rejection. *Reasoning.* With streaming, the response is committed to the client in pieces. The shell is already sent when the failing region rejects, so the browser has a complete, valid document with a hole in it. The error is not a page-level failure; it is a *region* failure, and without a boundary at that region React cannot attribute it and will escalate to the nearest enclosing boundary — ultimately global-error.tsx, which replaces the whole page including the shell the user was already reading. *Trade-offs.* Fine-grained boundaries mean more files and more boilerplate, and each boundary's fallback is a design decision (skeleton vs spinner vs "keep old data"). A single top-level boundary is simpler but sacrifices the streaming benefit, because one slow query then blocks everything. *Failure scenario.* A flaky third-party feed fails; the app has no error.tsx under that segment, so the user's entire dashboard is replaced by a generic error page, discarding the stats they were reading, and the incident looks like "the dashboard is down" when only one widget was. *Prevention.* One <Suspense> + one error boundary per independent data region by default; a design-system skeleton per fallback; log boundary name and request id with the error; test the failure path by making the query reject.

When does streaming hurt rather than help?
Does streaming work with static export?

How do you debug "the spinner flashes on every navigation"?

topics.title: Route handlers
topics.description: app//route.ts files define HTTP endpoints using exported functions named after methods, replacing pages/api/*.
keyConcepts: All methods
Streaming responses
Static vs dynamic route handlers
When a route handler is the wrong tool
It's an internal mutation called only by your own UI → Server Action (less boilerplate, typed args, progressive enhancement).

It's a webhook from a third party → route handler is right, but disable CSRF/origin expectations for it, verify the signature, allow POST from any origin, and reply fast with the raw body before doing async work.
It's a file upload or long job → presigned upload to object storage + queue; the handler should not proxy bytes.
It's an HTML page → page.tsx with RSC, not a string of markup.
It's a static asset → put it in public/ or serve from a CDN, not a handler.
It's a cross-origin API consumed by a separate SPA → route handler, and be deliberate about CORS (OPTIONS preflight, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, never * with credentials).
commonMistakes: trusting request.json() to succeed; returning 200 with an error body; missing Vary: authorization on a per-user response; forgetting runtime and shipping a Node-only API to the edge; proxying uploads through the server; duplicating auth logic instead of sharing it with actions; relying on implicit GET caching.
practiceTasks: build /api/products with GET (cursor pagination, Vary), POST (schema validation, 201 + location), PATCH (partial update, 404 vs 409 semantics), DELETE (idempotent, 204), and an OPTIONS handler for CORS. Then add a ReadableStream CSV export endpoint, a per-IP rate limit using a token bucket, and a webhook endpoint that verifies an HMAC signature with a timing-safe compare and enqueues work after responding.

interviewQuestions.text: How do you define a route handler and which methods exist?
How do you return a stream from a handler?
How do you choose runtime per route?
Are GET handlers cached? (State your version and how you control it.)
What happens if a route.ts and page.tsx share a path?
Why can't you return per-user data from a static GET handler?
When is a Server Action better than a route handler?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Route handlers are the right tool when the caller is not my own UI — a mobile app, a webhook, a third-party integration, or anything that needs the HTTP contract to be explicit and stable. Server Actions are better when the caller *is* my own UI: the arguments are typed, I skip the fetch boilerplate and the serialization layer, I get validation-friendly form integration and progressive enhancement, and I get a reference-based call instead of a URL I have to keep in sync. The rule of thumb: if the only consumer is a component in this repo, use an action; if the endpoint has an external contract, use a handler."

Why use keyset pagination instead of offset?

topics.title: Middleware
topics.description: middleware.ts (or src/middleware.ts) runs before a matched request is handled — before pages, route handlers, and rewrites — on the Edge runtime by default.
keyConcepts: Ordering
What middleware can and cannot do
Auth in middleware: the pattern and its limits
The classic redirect loop
Broad matcher including /login. Fix: exclude auth routes explicitly (matcher regex or next.config).

Cookie present but invalid. Middleware checks presence only; the page's requireUser() sees an invalid session and redirects to /login; middleware sees the cookie still present and redirects to /dashboard; infinite loop. Fix: middleware must delete the cookie when it rejects, and the deep check must cookies().delete() on failure.

Param-aware routes. Middleware uses pathname only, so /login?next=/login or an i18n prefix mismatch loops. Fix: normalize with the same prefixes your routes use and validate next to prevent open redirects.
Trailing slash / case mismatch producing /Login which doesn't match your exclusion.
Rewrite loops: rewriting to a path that matches your own matcher again.
commonMistakes: doing DB authorization in Edge middleware; mutating req.nextUrl in place instead of cloning; matching everything and slowing every request; treating middleware as the only auth check; forgetting that middleware can run on RSC/prefetch requests and must be cheap; using redirect() in middleware when you meant an internal rewrite.
practiceTasks: implement middleware with a narrow matcher, a presence-only session gate, a safe next redirect parameter (validate it is a same-origin relative path), and a debug header x-mw: allowed|redirected. Then deliberately create each of the five loop causes above, observe the redirect chain with curl -I -L, and fix each by editing only middleware or requireUser(). Add a test asserting exactly one redirect for an invalid cookie.

interviewQuestions.text: When does middleware run in the request lifecycle?
What does the `config.matcher` do and why prefer it over pathname checks?
Can middleware do authorization? Why not?
What is the redirect loop bug and what causes it?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* A /dashboard route 307s to /login and the browser reports "too many redirects". *Decision.* Trace the two redirect sources as separate actors: the middleware gate and the data-layer session check, and find out which pair is disagreeing. *Reasoning.* The canonical cause is a split-brain: middleware validates *presence* of the session cookie while the page calls requireUser(), which validates the session *value*. When the session is expired, revoked, or signed with a rotated key, the cookie still exists. Middleware therefore admits the request, requireUser() rejects it and redirects to /login, middleware sees the cookie still present and redirects back to /dashboard. Neither component is wrong in isolation; the missing invariant is that the cookie's presence must imply its validity, or that rejection must clear the cookie. *Trade-offs.* Full verification in middleware (JWT signature check, session lookup) is cheap for stateless JWTs and expensive for database sessions on the Edge; verifying fully makes every request pay that cost and still leaves object-level authorization undone. *Failure scenario.* A key rotation invalidates all sessions; 100% of authenticated traffic 307-loops, error monitors fill with 3xx chains, and login itself appears broken. *Prevention.* Clear the cookie on rejection at every layer; make the matcher exclude /login and static assets; keep one requireUser() used by pages, handlers, and actions; add a synthetic check that requests a protected route with an invalid session cookie and asserts a single redirect to /login, plus a loop detector alert on repeated redirect chains.

interviewQuestions.text: What runtime does middleware use, and what are the limits?
Middleware ordering with rewrites in `next.config`?

How do you debug a loop — what do you log?

topics.title: Image/font optimization
topics.description: next/image and next/font are build/serve-time optimizers that change the *default output* of images and fonts — formats, dimensions, responsive srcset, preload hints, self-hosting, and layout-shift prevention — without changing your markup API much.
keyConcepts: Why next/image exists
Bytes: modern formats (AVIF/WebP) cut image weight substantially at similar quality.

Layout shift: an image with unknown dimensions shifts content when it loads, which directly hurts CLS. The optimizer reserves space using width/height (and fill + aspect ratio) and emits the right srcset/sizes.
Responsiveness and laziness: one cannot serve the right resolution per device; next/image generates a srcset and can defer non-critical images.
When optimization is worth it
commonMistakes: priority on many images; missing sizes with fill; serving a 4 MB original because remotePatterns wasn't configured so it silently fell back; loading a full CJK font unsubsetted; dangerouslyAllowSVG for user-uploaded SVGs; ignoring alt.
practiceTasks: build a gallery page with 24 remote images. Measure total transferred bytes and CLS. Convert to next/image with sizes, priority on exactly one image, and placeholder="blur". Re-measure. Then swap next/image for a plain with a CDN srcset and confirm the numbers converge — then write the argument for which you'd keep.

interviewQuestions.text: Why does `next/image` exist? What are its three main benefits?
What prevents layout shift for images?
What does `priority` do and when should you use it?
What are `remotePatterns` and why are they required?
When is a plain `` acceptable?
What does `next/font` do better than a Google Fonts `<link>`?
What is `font-display: swap` and what is the trade-off?
How do you handle CJK fonts?
What is the risk of `dangerouslyAllowSVG`?
Self-hosting: what's the caching gotcha with the image optimizer?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* We self-host Next.js behind nginx on two instances, and users intermittently see placeholder-quality images. *Decision.* Stop relying on the default in-memory image cache; run the optimizer with a shared cache (or an external image CDN) and set explicit Cache-Control on /_next/image. *Reasoning.* The image optimizer caches transformed variants in the Node process by default. With multiple instances behind a round-robin load balancer, each instance has a different cache, so the same URL is transformed repeatedly, and cold instances are slow — which is exactly what "sometimes blurry/slow" looks like. The fix is not to disable optimization but to make the cache shared and the headers correct: immutable, long-lived caching for content-addressed URLs, and a stable cache key. *Trade-offs.* A shared cache adds latency (one hop) and operational cost; disabling optimization and using loses AVIF/WebP and responsive srcset and reintroduces CLS risk on any image you forget to size. *Failure scenario* to avoid: someone "fixes" flakiness by setting unoptimized: true, which removes the flakiness and the CLS regression returns quietly a month later, now attributed to the redesign. *Prevention.* Monitor optimizer cache hit rate and p95 transform latency, budget image bytes per page in CI, and keep CLS in the release gate.

interviewQuestions.text: What does `sizes` do and when do you need it?
How do you prove image optimization helped?

tradeoffs: next/image costs CPU and memory per transform, and on self-hosted Node it adds a caching layer you must operate (/\_next/image responses are cacheable but the cache is local to your instance).
priority (formerly priority/loading="eager") should be used for the LCP image and nothing else — it disables lazy loading and preloads, and misusing it on many images hurts.

is fine when: you already have a CDN doing AVIF/WebP with srcset (Cloudinary, imgix, Fastly), the image is user-uploaded and served from a signed URL on your own CDN, you need /art direction you don't want to fight the API for, the file is an inline SVG or a tiny icon (use SVG sprite or CSS), or the content is truly static and tiny. In those cases a plain with explicit width/height and loading="lazy" is simpler and just as good.
Do not lazy-load the LCP image. Do not forget alt; use alt="" for decorative images (accessibility: canonical entry: PHASE 3 Part 2 → Accessibility).
SVG needs dangerouslyAllowSVG for remote SVGs, which is an XSS risk; prefer serving SVGs yourself or sanitizing. Treat any remote SVG as untrusted input.

topics.title: Edge vs Node runtime
topics.description: Every route, page, layout, and middleware in Next.js runs on a runtime. nodejs (the default) gives you the full Node API surface; edge runs on a lightweight V8-based isolate with Web APIs and much smaller APIs.
keyConcepts: Edge when the work is: a redirect/rewrite, a cookie or geo check, a JWT verify, a small fetch to a globally distributed API, a response transformation, or an image/asset decision. All of it is latency-bound and stateless.
Node when the work touches: a database with a driver, fs, crypto (hashing, bcrypt), long CPU, big payloads, WebSocket servers, native modules, or anything needing connection pooling.
The hybrid is normal: middleware (edge) for cheap gating + a Node route handler for the real work. Or an edge route handler that calls a Node API.

Watch out for: middleware calling a regional database from an edge PoP (adds 100–300 ms and burns invocations); next/image optimization running on the edge (supported, but capacity-limited); heavy npm packages pulled into an edge bundle (build-time failure or a runtime shim that misbehaves); streaming large responses through edge memory limits.
commonMistakes: putting a DB query in middleware; using the Edge runtime for CPU-heavy work; pulling native modules into an edge bundle; assuming streaming behaves identically on both; not noticing that the same route can have different runtimes in different environments.
practiceTasks: create the same /api/report route twice — once runtime: 'edge' with an HTTP-based DB call, once runtime: 'nodejs' with a pooled driver. Measure cold and warm latency for both from a client far from the DB region, and compute cost per 1000 requests. Write the recommendation with numbers.

interviewQuestions.text: What's the difference between the Node and Edge runtimes in Next?
When would you choose Edge for a route handler?
Why is an edge middleware calling a database a problem?
interviewQuestions.answer: "An edge function runs in a PoP near the user but your database lives in one region. Every edge invocation that queries the DB crosses an ocean and opens a connection that a pool cannot keep warm across PoPs, so you pay 100–300 ms of network latency on *every* request plus connection exhaustion risk and per-invocation billing. The rule is: edge for stateless, latency-critical decisions (redirects, JWT verification, cookie gating, a global CDN API call); Node for anything that touches a regional resource. If you need both, gate in edge middleware and do the data work in a Node route handler or a separate API."

interviewQuestions.text: What's missing in the Edge runtime?
How does the cost model differ?
Middleware: which runtime, and can you change it?
When does Edge hurt more than help?
How do you check which runtime a route uses?

topics.title: SEO and metadata
topics.description: Metadata API — export const metadata / generateMetadata — plus Open Graph/Twitter cards, JSON-LD structured data, sitemap.ts, robots.ts, and canonical URLs.
keyConcepts: Why CSR-only content is a problem for crawlers
commonMistakes: relying on <title> in a client component; forgetting canonical URLs with query-param variants; dangerouslySetInnerHTML with interpolated user text in JSON-LD (XSS); indexing ?page=2 duplicates; assuming crawlers render.
practiceTasks: build /products/[slug] with generateMetadata (title template, canonical, OG image, robots: noindex for discontinued items), JSON-LD Product with offers, sitemap.ts generated from the DB, and robots.ts disallowing /admin. Then curl the HTML and confirm every tag is in the *initial* response, not added by JS. Finally, run a Google rich-results-style validator or a structured-data linter and fix what it flags.

interviewQuestions.text: How do you set page metadata dynamically?
What are Open Graph and Twitter cards for?
How do you generate a sitemap without hand-writing it?
Why does CSR-only content hurt SEO?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* A marketing page renders its content only after a client-side fetch; traffic is fine but organic traffic is flat and link previews are blank. *Decision.* Server-render or prerender anything indexable, and treat client fetching as an enhancement. *Reasoning.* Crawlers vary in whether and how well they execute JavaScript; social scrapers generally do not execute it at all; and even JS-capable crawlers allocate limited rendering budget and penalize failures or errors during hydration. Content that depends on hydration is therefore discovered later, indexed less reliably, and never seen at all by non-executing scrapers. The specific failure here — blank link previews — is a direct consequence: the OG tags that would produce the preview are either absent from the initial HTML or the preview scraper sees an empty body. *Trade-offs.* Server-rendering the content costs TTFB and server compute versus a static shell; prerendering (SSG/ISR) gets most of the SEO benefit at near-zero cost but requires build-time or revalidation-time data access, which means a build can fail on stale or unavailable data and dynamic segments need generateStaticParams. *Failure scenario.* A redesign converts every page to CSR with useEffect fetching; rankings drop 30% over two months, and the diagnosis is confusing because "it works in the browser" and Core Web Vitals in the field are fine. *Prevention.* Put indexable content in the server/prerendered path, assert in CI that key pages contain the expected text in the raw HTML response, keep generateMetadata server-side, and monitor crawler logs for 5xx/JS errors.

topics.title: Meta-Frameworks, React 19 Interplay, and Partial Prerendering
topics.description: Meta-Frameworks, React 19 Interplay, and Partial Prerendering within Next.js and Meta-Frameworks.
keyConcepts: What "meta-framework" means
The honest comparison
React 19 interplay
useActionState replaces useState + manual pending for form actions: you get a state object that includes pending, the returned state, and the error.
useFormStatus gives pending inside a child of the form (also data, method, action), so you can build a submit button that knows it is submitting.

Form action prop: <form action={fn}> where fn can be a Server Action or a client function. Server Actions *are* React 19 form actions, which is why progressive enhancement works: without JS the browser posts to the action endpoint.

useOptimistic for optimistic UI driven by an action's pending state — the framework gives you a temporary optimistic value that reverts if the action fails, which is a better default than hand-rolled rollback.
use() reads a promise (including one created during render) and suspends — the basis for reading data without async in the component, useful in client components.
Streaming and transitions are more capable in React 19: <Suspense> boundaries can be revealed out of order, and transitions are more interruptible, which is what makes Next's navigation feel instant.
Partial Prerendering (PPR) — awareness
commonMistakes: declaring one framework universally best; ignoring that migrations cost behavior, not just syntax; over-claiming PPR as stable; treating useOptimistic as a substitute for a server-authoritative re-read.
practiceTasks: build the same CRUD "notes" app twice: once in Next.js App Router with Server Actions and ISR, once in React Router 7 framework mode with a loader and an action. Diff them on: lines of data-fetch code, where caching lives, how a mutation invalidates a read, and how hard it is to reason about staleness. Then write one paragraph justifying your choice for a specific product, citing evidence from the exercise.

interviewQuestions.text: What is a meta-framework?
How does React Router 7 framework mode differ from Next's data model?
When is Astro the right choice?
What does React 19 add for forms and actions?
What is `useActionState` and how does it differ from `useFormStatus`?
What does `useOptimistic` do, and is it safer than manual rollback?
What is `use()` for?
What is Partial Prerendering and what problem does it solve?
Why is "which framework is best" a bad interview answer?
What would make you leave Next.js for another meta-framework?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* I'm the frontend lead on a large React/TypeScript product with heavy e-commerce traffic, a small team, and an existing Next.js codebase. *Decision.* I would not migrate on preference; I would migrate only if a specific, measurable blocker appears. *Reasoning.* The migration cost is not the framework — it is re-deriving caching semantics, auditing every data access, retraining the team, and re-tuning SEO and Core Web Vitals with a real regression budget. That cost is justified only when a capability we need is unavailable or a specific defect is unfixable: for example, if we need a data model we can fully understand and audit (React Router's loader/action split makes every request's data flow explicit and greppable, whereas Next's caching is rule-based and has changed defaults across versions), or if the App Router's implicit caching has repeatedly produced production staleness incidents we cannot prevent. *Trade-offs.* On the other side: React Router gives up the managed edge/CDN/image/ISR integration and the hiring pool; keeping Next means living with its abstractions and version churn. *Failure scenario.* A rewrite "because the framework is wrong" ships three months late, misses the holiday traffic window, and the new app has worse LCP because nobody carried over image and streaming work. *Alternative.* Incremental mitigation inside Next: add explicit caching documentation, tag discipline, and staleness alerts; adopt new features route by route; evaluate a *carve-out* (a docs or marketing site in Astro, a widget in React Router) rather than a whole-app rewrite. *Signals I would actually act on:* repeated data-leak or staleness incidents, a framework limitation blocking a roadmap item with real revenue behind it, or hiring/velocity data showing the framework is the constraint.

interviewQuestions.text: How does the App Router's implicit caching compare with React Router's explicit loaders?

topics.title: Redux Toolkit
topics.description: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is an opinionated layer over Redux that (a) removes the boilerplate that made Redux unpopular, (b) makes the store a *single immutable state tree* changed only through serialisable actions, and (c) ships two libraries on top: createAsyncThunk for imperative async workflows and RTK Query for declarative server-state fetching with caching, deduplication, invalidation, and normalised caching. RTK 2.x targets Redux 5 and React 18+.
keyConcepts: Store shape — the contract you are signing
Typed hooks — non-negotiable
createSlice — one file per feature
createAsyncThunk — the thunk middleware in a typed wrapper
RTK Query — the modern answer for "Redux + server state"
queryKey = (endpointName, serialisedArgs). Two hooks with equal args = one request, one cache entry. Different but overlapping args = two cache entries (the classic "list and detail drift" bug).
providesTags describes what the entry depends on; invalidatesTags invalidates. This is a *dependency graph*, coarse-to-fine, and it is the whole invalidation story.

Cached data is returned for a subscription and re-fetched when stale (keepUnusedDataFor governs eviction of *unsubscribed* entries; refetchOnMount/refetchOnFocus/refetchOnReconnect govern revalidation of used ones).
transformResponse is for shaping one shape into another. Never use it to merge two caches; use providesTags.
onQueryStarted is the optimistic-update hook. It gets { dispatch, queryFulfilled, getState } and its returned promise resolves when the query settles.

.selectFromResult narrows what a component subscribes to, which is the single most effective RTK Query performance lever (selectFromResult: ({ data, isLoading }) => ({ users: data?.users, isLoading })).
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Hand-rolled fetch in a thunk *and* RTK Query in the same app — two caches, two staleness policies.
Passing a class instance or Date in an action payload and disabling the serialisable check instead of fixing it.
Mutating outside a reducer (a reducer that mutates the action payload, or store.getState().x = 1 anywhere).
useSelector(s => s.users.items) where items is an array rebuilt on every state change — the component re-renders forever (see 4.3.4).
returning a fresh object from a selector: useSelector will loop under useSyncExternalStore.
Using combineReducers with a top-level array of "panes" instead of keyed slices — the array becomes the bottleneck and the reducer non-deterministic.
Assuming store.getState() is fresh inside a reducer (it is not — use the state argument).

using Redux for everything "because it scales"; writing fetch logic by hand when RTK Query exists; believing createSlice makes mutation impossible (Immer handles it, but only *inside* reducers); storing secrets in the store.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain store shape — the contract you are signing and when you would use it.
Explain typed hooks — non-negotiable and when you would use it.
Explain createslice — one file per feature and when you would use it.
Explain createasyncthunk — the thunk middleware in a typed wrapper and when you would use it.
Explain rtk query — the modern answer for "redux + server state" and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Redux's costs are real: ceremony (file per slice), an indirection between a click and a render, dispatch typing overhead, and a bundle cost you do not pay with Zustand. Its benefits are also real: one mutation path, one DevTools timeline, deterministic replay, serialisability as an architectural constraint, and RTK Query's cache and invalidation graph. Net verdict that a senior engineer would give: *Redux pays for itself in codebases with many writers of shared state and a real DevTools dependency; it is overkill for a five-screen app with two forms.*

topics.title: Zustand
topics.description: Four "minimal global state" libraries that all try to beat Redux's ceremony while keeping a global store. They differ in the *unit of state*: a store with selectors (Zustand), an atom graph (Jotai), observable objects with a reaction system (MobX), and atom graphs with dependency tracking + selectors (Recoil).
keyConcepts: Mechanical comparison

Team familiarity and hiring. The single biggest factor. A bespoke Zustand store is 40 lines of convention; a MobX codebase needs someone who can reason about observability. Optimise for the five people who will maintain it.

Do you need to *derive* state reactively and often? Jotai's derived atoms or MobX computed earn their keep if you have chained derivations. If derivations are one-liners in useMemo, plain Zustand is fine.

Do you need fine-grained reactivity on large collections? MobX tracks per-property reads inside a render and re-runs only what depends on what changed — the best model for a virtualised list or a spreadsheet-like grid. Zustand's selector is per-component, which is nearly as good with a good selector.

Do you need middleware, devtools time travel, and a big team on a large app? Redux Toolkit. It is the only one of the four with a first-party DevTools timeline, serialisability enforcement, and a documented answer to "who dispatched this".
Do you need cross-cutting async workflows (4.3.5)? Redux Toolkit, or RTK Query. Zustand can do it (store.getState().doThing()) but there is no equivalent of predicate/effect/cancelActiveListeners.
Do you need the smallest possible bundle? Zustand (~1.5 kB gz) ≲ Jotai (~3 kB) ≪ MobX (~15 kB) ≪ Recoil (~25 kB).

Bundle + SSR? Jotai and Recoil need Provider with an initial-state prop; Zustand's vanilla store makes SSR hydration explicit; MobX needs enableStaticRendering(typeof window === 'undefined') on the server.
"Compare Zustand, Jotai, MobX and Redux Toolkit; what would you pick for *this* app and why?"
"What is Recoil's status today?"
"How does MobX know what to re-render?"

topics.title: Server state
topics.description: State taxonomy is the practice of *classifying every piece of state in the app* into exactly one of five kinds, each with a different owner, lifetime, persistence rule, and tool. Getting the classification right removes most state-management debate, because each kind has a defensible home and the home is not negotiable by preference.
keyConcepts: The mechanics of why the classification matters
Local UI state fails when you *lift it too far*. The classic symptom is prop drilling six levels to set a boolean. Fix: composition, a custom hook with its own state, or colocate the state.

Derived state fails when you *store* it in useState and keep it in sync with an effect. This creates a second source of truth that is wrong for exactly as long as the effect takes to run — and wrong forever if the dependency is missed. Fix: delete the state and compute it.
Server state fails when you store it in useState. Then you own caching, deduplication, staleness, garbage collection, retries, and cross-component sharing, badly. Fix: use a query cache.
URL state fails when you keep it in a store. Then the back button breaks, the page cannot be shared, refresh loses it, and SEO/analytics cannot see it. Fix: put it in the URL.
Global client state fails when it becomes a dumping ground for layer 2 and 3. Fix: enforce the boundary — a store must not hold server data.

Local UI state: default for anything one subtree cares about. Do not use for: anything two distant components need (that is lifted, or a store, or the URL), anything derivable, or anything another engineer will need to find (put it in a feature folder, not scattered useStates).
Derived state: always prefer computing. The only reason to useMemo is cost; the only reason to keep it in state is that it is *not* actually derived (it was user input).
Server state: always via a query library or a framework loader. "Always" except in throwaway demos and tests.
URL state: anything shareable, bookmarkable, or that should survive refresh; also anything that changes what the *server* renders (SEO). Not: secrets, and not transient hover/animation flags.
Global client state: last resort after lifting and Context fail. Justify it with a concrete requirement ("five routes deep, changes at 60 Hz, and never persisted").
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Storing a *filtered list* in state next to the unfiltered list ("keep the same reference when unchanged" is a symptom of a duplication bug).
Storing isLoading / error next to the data instead of using the query's own status object — you now have three places that can disagree.
Keeping page/filter state in a store "just for the session", so it survives navigation into a route that should have been fresh.
Using useState + useEffect to mirror a prop into state instead of using a key or the prop.
Classifying a WebSocket buffer as local UI state.
naming five kinds and then putting all five in one store; calling derived state "state"; using a store as a cache without a staleness policy; URL state that includes anything the user should not see.

The cost is that you sometimes route trivial values through the URL (verbose URLs) or keep tiny state in a store (global mutable surface). Both are acceptable; debugging two sources of truth for one fact is not.

topics.title: Redux middleware (thunk, saga)
topics.description: middleware.ts (or src/middleware.ts) runs before a matched request is handled — before pages, route handlers, and rewrites — on the Edge runtime by default.
keyConcepts: Ordering
What middleware can and cannot do
Auth in middleware: the pattern and its limits
The classic redirect loop
Broad matcher including /login. Fix: exclude auth routes explicitly (matcher regex or next.config).

Cookie present but invalid. Middleware checks presence only; the page's requireUser() sees an invalid session and redirects to /login; middleware sees the cookie still present and redirects to /dashboard; infinite loop. Fix: middleware must delete the cookie when it rejects, and the deep check must cookies().delete() on failure.

Param-aware routes. Middleware uses pathname only, so /login?next=/login or an i18n prefix mismatch loops. Fix: normalize with the same prefixes your routes use and validate next to prevent open redirects.
Trailing slash / case mismatch producing /Login which doesn't match your exclusion.
Rewrite loops: rewriting to a path that matches your own matcher again.
commonMistakes: doing DB authorization in Edge middleware; mutating req.nextUrl in place instead of cloning; matching everything and slowing every request; treating middleware as the only auth check; forgetting that middleware can run on RSC/prefetch requests and must be cheap; using redirect() in middleware when you meant an internal rewrite.
practiceTasks: implement middleware with a narrow matcher, a presence-only session gate, a safe next redirect parameter (validate it is a same-origin relative path), and a debug header x-mw: allowed|redirected. Then deliberately create each of the five loop causes above, observe the redirect chain with curl -I -L, and fix each by editing only middleware or requireUser(). Add a test asserting exactly one redirect for an invalid cookie.

interviewQuestions.text: When does middleware run in the request lifecycle?
What does the `config.matcher` do and why prefer it over pathname checks?
Can middleware do authorization? Why not?
What is the redirect loop bug and what causes it?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* A /dashboard route 307s to /login and the browser reports "too many redirects". *Decision.* Trace the two redirect sources as separate actors: the middleware gate and the data-layer session check, and find out which pair is disagreeing. *Reasoning.* The canonical cause is a split-brain: middleware validates *presence* of the session cookie while the page calls requireUser(), which validates the session *value*. When the session is expired, revoked, or signed with a rotated key, the cookie still exists. Middleware therefore admits the request, requireUser() rejects it and redirects to /login, middleware sees the cookie still present and redirects back to /dashboard. Neither component is wrong in isolation; the missing invariant is that the cookie's presence must imply its validity, or that rejection must clear the cookie. *Trade-offs.* Full verification in middleware (JWT signature check, session lookup) is cheap for stateless JWTs and expensive for database sessions on the Edge; verifying fully makes every request pay that cost and still leaves object-level authorization undone. *Failure scenario.* A key rotation invalidates all sessions; 100% of authenticated traffic 307-loops, error monitors fill with 3xx chains, and login itself appears broken. *Prevention.* Clear the cookie on rejection at every layer; make the matcher exclude /login and static assets; keep one requireUser() used by pages, handlers, and actions; add a synthetic check that requests a protected route with an invalid session cookie and asserts a single redirect to /login, plus a loop detector alert on repeated redirect chains.

topics.title: Context: the right use, the wrong use, and the performance cliff
topics.description: Context is a *push-based* dependency-injection and read-through-broadcast channel: a provider publishes one value; every descendant that calls useContext for that context is notified when the published value changes identity. It solves "get a value to a distant descendant without prop drilling". It is not a state manager, and using it as one is the single most common React performance incident.
keyConcepts: Subscription is by context, not by prop. When a Provider's value prop changes (Object.is fails against the previous render's value), React walks its subtree and marks *every fiber that reads that context* for re-render. React.memo is irrelevant: memo compares props, and a context broadcast is not a props change.

Propagation is a tree walk, not a subscription registry. With many providers/consumers this is why React can start tearing across concurrent rendering — hence useSyncExternalStore (see below) as the safe way to expose an *external* mutable store.

value identity is the change signal. value={{ user }} creates a new object every render, so *every* consumer re-renders on *every* provider render, regardless of whether user changed. This is the performance cliff.
The escape hatch: context over an external store
Production and operational
"Explain exactly why memo does not protect a context consumer."
"Your theme provider wraps the whole app; the app feels sluggish on the settings page. Diagnose."
"When would you *not* reach for Context even though you could?"
"How does useSyncExternalStore change Context's behaviour, and what does getServerSnapshot do?"
"What is the difference between a stable context value and a memoised one?"
commonMistakes: value={{ ... }} without useMemo — the cliff, in its purest form.
One context holding both items and dispatch, so dispatch-only consumers re-render on every item change.
Context for server data: no dedupe, so ten components using the same context fire ten requests, or one request whose result nobody can refresh.
Setting state on the context *value object* (ctx.items.push(...)) — mutating a shared reference that Object.is considers unchanged.
Reading a context in a component you do not control just to get a theme, when CSS custom properties would do it with no re-render at all.

assuming Context is scoped to a "component boundary" (it is not — it is subtree-wide); forgetting that reading a context makes the component a consumer even if the read is conditional; using Context as a cache.

tradeoffs: Context is ~zero-dependency, type-safe, built in, and the right answer for roughly 30% of "shared state" needs. Its costs: broadcast invalidation (a cliff, not a slope), no devtools, no middleware, no time travel, no persistence, and no way to subscribe to a *slice*. The upside of a store is the mirror image: precise subscriptions and tooling, paid for with a dependency and a ceremony that small apps do not need.

topics.title: Redux Toolkit: store shape, slices, createSlice, createAsyncThunk, RTK Query
topics.description: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is an opinionated layer over Redux that (a) removes the boilerplate that made Redux unpopular, (b) makes the store a *single immutable state tree* changed only through serialisable actions, and (c) ships two libraries on top: createAsyncThunk for imperative async workflows and RTK Query for declarative server-state fetching with caching, deduplication, invalidation, and normalised caching. RTK 2.x targets Redux 5 and React 18+.
keyConcepts: Store shape — the contract you are signing
Typed hooks — non-negotiable
createSlice — one file per feature
createAsyncThunk — the thunk middleware in a typed wrapper
RTK Query — the modern answer for "Redux + server state"
queryKey = (endpointName, serialisedArgs). Two hooks with equal args = one request, one cache entry. Different but overlapping args = two cache entries (the classic "list and detail drift" bug).
providesTags describes what the entry depends on; invalidatesTags invalidates. This is a *dependency graph*, coarse-to-fine, and it is the whole invalidation story.

Cached data is returned for a subscription and re-fetched when stale (keepUnusedDataFor governs eviction of *unsubscribed* entries; refetchOnMount/refetchOnFocus/refetchOnReconnect govern revalidation of used ones).
transformResponse is for shaping one shape into another. Never use it to merge two caches; use providesTags.
onQueryStarted is the optimistic-update hook. It gets { dispatch, queryFulfilled, getState } and its returned promise resolves when the query settles.

.selectFromResult narrows what a component subscribes to, which is the single most effective RTK Query performance lever (selectFromResult: ({ data, isLoading }) => ({ users: data?.users, isLoading })).
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Hand-rolled fetch in a thunk *and* RTK Query in the same app — two caches, two staleness policies.
Passing a class instance or Date in an action payload and disabling the serialisable check instead of fixing it.
Mutating outside a reducer (a reducer that mutates the action payload, or store.getState().x = 1 anywhere).
useSelector(s => s.users.items) where items is an array rebuilt on every state change — the component re-renders forever (see 4.3.4).
returning a fresh object from a selector: useSelector will loop under useSyncExternalStore.
Using combineReducers with a top-level array of "panes" instead of keyed slices — the array becomes the bottleneck and the reducer non-deterministic.
Assuming store.getState() is fresh inside a reducer (it is not — use the state argument).

using Redux for everything "because it scales"; writing fetch logic by hand when RTK Query exists; believing createSlice makes mutation impossible (Immer handles it, but only *inside* reducers); storing secrets in the store.

tradeoffs: Redux's costs are real: ceremony (file per slice), an indirection between a click and a render, dispatch typing overhead, and a bundle cost you do not pay with Zustand. Its benefits are also real: one mutation path, one DevTools timeline, deterministic replay, serialisability as an architectural constraint, and RTK Query's cache and invalidation graph. Net verdict that a senior engineer would give: *Redux pays for itself in codebases with many writers of shared state and a real DevTools dependency; it is overkill for a five-screen app with two forms.*

topics.title: Selectors, reselect, memoisation, and normalized state
topics.description: A *selector* is a pure function from state to a value. *Reselect* is a memoisation library that makes selectors cheap by caching on their inputs. *Normalized state* is the shape where entities live in a keyed map (byId: Record<Id, T>) plus an array of ids, instead of being duplicated inside every parent object.
keyConcepts: The problem selectors solve
Why "cache size 1" is usually right
Parameterised selectors in components — the React version
Normalized state — the shape that makes everything else possible
Which one
When to normalise and when not to
Production and operational

RTK Query already returns normalised results internally (result.ids / result.entities) — do not duplicate that work by normalising again. If you need a different shape, use transformResponse and keep the adapter as the only writer.
Enforce the shape in review or lint: a createEntityAdapter slice plus a no-restricted-syntax rule banning .find( on entity arrays.

Log selector recomputation counts in dev (a console.count in a development-only branch) to find accidental createSelector calls inside components — creating a selector per render defeats all memoisation.
For very large normalised collections, Object.freeze in dev (RTK does this in development) so accidental mutation fails loudly.
"Why does useSelector re-render constantly here, and what are the two possible fixes?"
commonMistakes: Calling createSelector *inside* a component (new cache every render).
A selector that takes state and returns state.a.b.filter(...) — a new array per call.
Mixing shapes: usersById plus a users array that can disagree.
Deep-cloning in a selector to "fix" mutation (structuredClone in a selector destroys identity and perf).

Using useSelector(shallowEqual) from React Redux as a universal fix instead of memoising — it is correct but costs a full shallow comparison per store update for every subscriber; a memoised selector is cheaper and narrower.
Using normalizr where you only need one level (a plain Map and two reducers are enough).
treating reselect as a correctness mechanism rather than a performance one; normalising lists where order is the data; writing selectors in components; returning object literals from useSelector.

tradeoffs: Normalisation costs indirection: every read is byId[id], every write is one function, and a component that wants a tree needs a denormalize/join step (which must itself be memoised). The payoff is that a single write updates every view, entity updates can be subscribed to per-id (useAppSelector(s => s.users.entities[id]) — one user's change does not re-render a list of a thousand), and list operations stop being O(n²) find/includes calls. Selectors trade a memory cost and a dependency list for "recompute only when inputs changed"; the failure mode is a wrong dependency, which returns stale data — so keep input selectors trivially correct (one property access each) rather than clever.

topics.title: Middleware: thunk vs saga vs listener middleware, and when you need any
topics.description: Redux middleware is a function that wraps dispatch and can do work before, after, or instead of passing the action along:
keyConcepts: The three flavours
Listener middleware — the modern default for "when X happens, do Y"
Sagas — when the flow genuinely is a sequence of events
Which one to pick
Production and operational
"What is the middleware signature and what can it do?" (read state, delay, abort, swallow or intercept, and return a value from dispatch)
"Difference between thunk, saga and listener middleware — when each?"
"How do you debounce an action with cancellation?" (listener middleware cancelActiveListeners + delay, or saga takeLatest.)
"Why not do all async in components?"
"How do you test middleware?"
"What happens if a middleware throws?"
commonMistakes: Using middleware to do things during the render cycle (it runs on dispatch, not on render).
Writing the same analytics event in a component and in middleware — double counting.
takeEvery for a submit button (allows 20 double-charges) — you want takeLeading or a thunk condition.
Assuming middleware can short-circuit a reducer; it can *intercept* the action (don't call next) but then the reducer never sees it.
Writing saga effects without try/finally, leaking calls on cancel.
Middleware ordering forgotten: RTK Query's middleware must be added; a custom middleware that reads a slice which RTK Query's middleware has not yet hydrated reads undefined.
putting data fetching in middleware *and* in RTK Query; deep chains of dispatching middleware; assuming getState() sees pre-reducer state in a listener effect.

tradeoffs: Middleware is invisible to junior developers: an action that triggers a fetch that triggers three dispatches that trigger a listener is a hard trace. It is also the *best* place for cross-cutting concerns because it is applied uniformly and testable outside React. The risk of middleware is a hidden cascade: three layers of middleware that each dispatch two actions is unmaintainable. Keep middleware shallow: at most one listener per action domain, and log dispatches in development so cascades are visible.

topics.title: Zustand, Jotai, MobX, Recoil: comparison and selection criteria
topics.description: Four "minimal global state" libraries that all try to beat Redux's ceremony while keeping a global store. They differ in the *unit of state*: a store with selectors (Zustand), an atom graph (Jotai), observable objects with a reaction system (MobX), and atom graphs with dependency tracking + selectors (Recoil).
keyConcepts: Mechanical comparison

Team familiarity and hiring. The single biggest factor. A bespoke Zustand store is 40 lines of convention; a MobX codebase needs someone who can reason about observability. Optimise for the five people who will maintain it.

Do you need to *derive* state reactively and often? Jotai's derived atoms or MobX computed earn their keep if you have chained derivations. If derivations are one-liners in useMemo, plain Zustand is fine.

Do you need fine-grained reactivity on large collections? MobX tracks per-property reads inside a render and re-runs only what depends on what changed — the best model for a virtualised list or a spreadsheet-like grid. Zustand's selector is per-component, which is nearly as good with a good selector.

Do you need middleware, devtools time travel, and a big team on a large app? Redux Toolkit. It is the only one of the four with a first-party DevTools timeline, serialisability enforcement, and a documented answer to "who dispatched this".
Do you need cross-cutting async workflows (4.3.5)? Redux Toolkit, or RTK Query. Zustand can do it (store.getState().doThing()) but there is no equivalent of predicate/effect/cancelActiveListeners.
Do you need the smallest possible bundle? Zustand (~1.5 kB gz) ≲ Jotai (~3 kB) ≪ MobX (~15 kB) ≪ Recoil (~25 kB).

Bundle + SSR? Jotai and Recoil need Provider with an initial-state prop; Zustand's vanilla store makes SSR hydration explicit; MobX needs enableStaticRendering(typeof window === 'undefined') on the server.
"Compare Zustand, Jotai, MobX and Redux Toolkit; what would you pick for *this* app and why?"
"What is Recoil's status today?"
"How does MobX know what to re-render?"
"Why does useStore with an object selector loop?"
commonMistakes: useStore((s) => ({ a: s.a, b: s.b })) without useShallow → infinite re-render.
Persisting functions or Date objects with zustand/persist (JSON round-trip destroys them silently).
Using useAtom (read+write) where useAtomValue/useSetAtom would do, subscribing to reads you never use.
MobX without runInAction after an await, or with enforceActions: 'observed' and mutation inside a render.
Using MobX/Jotai to cache server data.
Writing to the same key from two stores in an app that has "one store per team" as a rule — the merge problem.
citing bundle sizes you have not verified; proposing Recoil for a new build; using any of them as a cache; evaluating on "Redux vs Zustand" tribalism instead of requirements.

tradeoffs: Zustand: least ceremony, most examples, best default; costs: no built-in devtools time travel, patterns emerge by convention. Jotai: the cleanest derived-state story and the best TypeScript inference; costs: a second mental model (atoms vs stores) and a smaller ecosystem. MobX: the most powerful and least-buggy reactive model once you understand it; costs: bundle size, decorator-era baggage in docs, and a class-based store that some teams dislike. Redux Toolkit: the most explicit and most inspectable; costs: files and ceremony. Recoil: superseded.

topics.title: XState and state machines: when a finite state machine beats booleans
topics.description: A finite state machine (FSM) models a system as a *finite set of states* plus a *finite set of transitions* between them, where transitions may be guarded and may perform effects. XState is the reference implementation for React/TS. It replaces "a pile of booleans that can contradict each other" with "one state value that cannot".
keyConcepts: The bug an FSM eliminates
state.matches({ playing: {} }) tests the state value. state.matches('playing') for a top-level string. There is no way to be "half in a state".
Events are the only input. The machine is a pure function of (state, event). Side effects happen only in actions and invoke.
assign is the only way to change context, and it must be written as a function of (context, event) so it stays serialisable and pure. assign({ x: 5 }) is sugar for a constant assignment.
Guards are predicates evaluated *before* a transition is taken; the first matching entry in an array of transitions wins, so order matters.
States can be nested ({ idle: { on: { FOCUS: 'editing' } }, editing: { initial: 'clean', states: { clean: {...}, dirty: {...} } } }), giving compound states without multiplying values.
invoke ties a service's lifetime to a state: when the machine leaves loading, the fetch is aborted (onError with an abort must be filtered, or use the signal).
after is a delayed transition, cancelled if the state is left first — the built-in answer to "clear this timeout in cleanup".
always transitions are evaluated on every event while in a state (guards that fire immediately); history states let you resume where you were; choice picks one of N transitions.
When a machine beats booleans, precisely
Production and operational
"When is a state machine better than booleans? Give a case where it is worse."
commonMistakes: Modelling a machine with on: { EVENT: ... } transitions that don't have targets (side-effect-only transitions), which makes the state chart a lie.
Using guard to mutate instead of guard + assign.
Forgetting that invoke's promise keeps running after you leave the state unless you pass the signal through.
Deep nesting states so that state.matches('editing') is true for six visually different screens.
Building an FSM for a resource that has no interesting transitions.
Writing machines inside components (recreated every render); define them at module scope.
over-applying FSMs; treating a machine as async-by-default; assuming matches() handles nested states without care; not persisting long flows.

tradeoffs: You gain: impossible states rendered impossible, explicit and testable logic, guaranteed cleanup via state-scoped invoke/after, a single place to see every legal transition, and trivially inspectable debugging (state.value is a data value). You pay: a steeper learning curve, a second mental model (event/action/service), serialisation if you want to resume a machine mid-flow (persisted State), heavier code for simple cases, and a smaller talent pool. The judgement call is about *transition complexity*, not state count.

topics.title: URL as state, localStorage persistence, and hydration-safe storage
topics.description: Two persistence mechanisms with opposite visibility. URL state is state the user can see, copy, bookmark, share, and go back from — it lives in location, survives everything, and requires zero storage. Client storage (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, a cookie) is state the user cannot see, which survives a refresh, is scoped to an origin, and is *not* part of the document.
keyConcepts: URL as state — the mechanics and the rules
Anything a user might want to send someone goes in the search params. Not in a store, not in localStorage.

push vs replace is a product decision, per interaction. Typing in a search box, changing a filter, paginating: replace, so the back button leaves the *page* rather than walking through 40 filter states. Following a result, opening an item, submitting a form: push.

Params must be canonical. /invoices?page=1 and /invoices should be the same screen; parse to defaults on read, serialise by omitting defaults on write. Non-canonical URLs split analytics funnels and create duplicate-content SEO issues.
Server-renderable. Query params must decide *what the server returns* (pagination, filters), otherwise SEO and share-links show page 1 while the URL says page 3.
Never put a secret in a URL — query strings appear in Referer, browser history, and server logs (cross-ref 4.6.9).
Parse, don't spread. Validate params into a typed object at the route boundary with a schema (Zod, 4.4.8) so ?page=abc cannot become NaN.
localStorage — the API and its limits
Versioned persistence with migration
Cookies as the third option
What belongs where — a table you can defend
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Writing to localStorage during render (side effect in render; StrictMode double-writes).
Reading localStorage during render on the server path → ReferenceError or hydration mismatch.
Persisting the entire store (including server cache) with no version and no migration.
pushing every keystroke of a search box into history (back button becomes unusable).
Storing tokens in localStorage (any XSS exfiltrates them for the life of the token).
Expecting cross-tab listeners to fire in the writing tab (they do not).
Copying URL params straight into a query key without validation (NaN, Infinity, __proto__).
treating the URL bar as decoration; persisting unvalidated blobs; assuming storage is per-tab; using push for every filter tweak.

tradeoffs: URL state costs verbosity (?tab=history&sort=-created), requires you to parse/validate/serialise, and can produce unfriendly URLs that you must design (path vs query, short keys vs readable keys). It buys shareability, back-button correctness, SSR/SEO, analytics attribution, and survival across devices — five things localStorage cannot buy. localStorage costs synchronous main-thread reads, cross-tab coupling, an untrusted-by-your-own-app JSON blob, XSS exposure, and versioning burden. It buys survival across reloads for *invisible preferences*.

topics.title: Optimistic updates and rollback
topics.description: An optimistic update applies the expected result of a write to the client cache *before* the server confirms it, so the UI responds immediately; if the server rejects the write, the client rolls the cache back to the previous snapshot and re-syncs. It trades a small correctness window for perceived latency. It is a *decision about user-visible risk*, not a performance trick.
keyConcepts: The mechanics — five moving parts, and all five are required
A complete TanStack Query implementation, including the failure path
Making it robust
Production and operational
"Walk me through the full lifecycle of an optimistic mutation."
"Why is cancelQueries needed in onMutate?"
"How do you roll back correctly when two mutations touch the same list?"
"When would you *not* be optimistic, and what would you show instead?"
"How do you handle an optimistic create when the server assigns the id?"
"What is idempotency and where does it live?"
commonMistakes: Forgetting cancelQueries in onMutate, so a background refetch overwrites the optimistic value and the UI flickers back.
Snapshotting by reference (prev = getQueryData(...)) without structuredClone, so "rollback" restores the object you already mutated.
Rolling back and *not* invalidating, leaving the cache in its pre-mutation (possibly stale) state.
Optimistic create without a clientId, so a retry duplicates.
Optimistic update on a list while a refetchInterval poll is running.
Disabling the button on submit *and* being optimistic — the user sees the change but no sign it has not been saved.
Treating isPending from useMutation as per-row; you need per-item pending state (a Set of ids).

optimism without a failure path; rollback without refetch; optimism on irreversible actions; assuming onMutate's returned context survives a component unmount (it does — the mutation owns it, which is a feature).

tradeoffs: Optimistic updates cut perceived latency to zero and make the UI feel instant; they also introduce a class of bugs that are hard to see — a wrong prediction (the server rejects with a validation error you never predicted), a partial apply (two mutations touching the same list concurrently, second snapshot taken *after* the first applied), a stale rollback (snapshot was already stale), and a flash of wrong data for other users if you broadcast optimistically to a shared cache. Mitigations: cancelQueries before mutating, snapshot with structuredClone, always invalidateQueries on settle, and make every optimistic mutation *narrow* — one entity, not a whole collection.

topics.title: The state-management decision flowchart
topics.description: A deterministic procedure that, given a piece of state and its requirements, names the tool — and justifies it in one sentence. Interviewers use this to test *decision-making under constraints* rather than library recall. The value is in the questions you ask before you pick.
keyConcepts: The flowchart
The three questions that resolve 90% of ambiguity

Who is allowed to write it, and what is the order of writes? One writer → useState. Many writers with no ordering requirement → a store. Many writers where B must not run until A resolves → useReducer or an FSM. Interruption/cancellation requirements → an FSM (4.3.7).

What makes it stale, and who is allowed to refresh it? Nothing (client state, never stale) → store/URL. A TTL → query cache. A server event → query cache invalidated by a subscription. A user action → invalidation with a scope.

What is the blast radius of a wrong value? Cosmetic (hover, animation) → be liberal. Visible and recoverable → be conservative. Money/permissions/irreversible → never optimistic, never client-authoritative.
Decision table for the common interview scenario
A migration playbook
"Here are 6 pieces of state in my app — classify each and justify."
"Why is 'one store for everything' a red flag?"
"How would you migrate this codebase to a query library incrementally?"
"When would you *add* a store to an app that has none?"
"What would make you choose MobX over Zustand here?"
commonMistakes: Choosing a library before classifying the state; asking "Redux or Zustand?" instead of "what is this state's writer and lifetime?"; putting derived state in the store "for performance" (which is backwards — it is the one thing that costs); a store used as a cache; refusing context because "context is slow" without checking whether the problem is an unmemoized value; and treating a flowchart as a decision tree that yields one answer when the right answer is often "this is layer 2, not a state-management question at all".
a flowchart without the "what makes it stale" question; assuming a bigger library is a bigger win; skipping the classification step entirely.
topics.referenceMarkdown:
```

                        │

Layer 5 (global client state) hygiene rules that apply wherever you land:
```

topics.title: Pagination and infinite scroll
topics.description: Pagination is the policy for reading a bounded window of a large collection. Two families exist: offset pagination (?page=2 / ?offset=50&limit=20, computed by the database) and cursor (keyset) pagination (?after=<opaque> / ?before=<opaque>, walking a sort key). Infinite scroll is a UI pattern that repeatedly extends a cursor-paginated collection; infinite *queries* are the cache structure that supports it.
keyConcepts: The mechanics and the failure each family has
Bidirectional scroll — the part most implementations skip
maxPages and the memory model
Offset pagination done properly
Production and operational

Every cursor must be validated server-side and scoped to the filter set (a cursor from filter A is nonsense for filter B) — encode the filter hash into the cursor and reject mismatches, or you get leaked pages.
Log the number of pages fetched per session; a long-tail tail means maxPages is wrong or the sentinel margin is too small.

Watch the DB: OFFSET 400000 shows up as a sequential scan; a missing composite index on (created_at, id) shows up as slow cursor queries. Cursor pagination is only fast if the index exists *in the sort order*.
Track "duplicate row seen" rate in analytics as a data-integrity signal — offset pagination on a mutating table shows up in product metrics as engagement oddities nobody can explain.
"Offset vs cursor: give the exact failure of each."
"How do you handle a post inserted while the user pages?"
"How do you load older messages when scrolling up?"
commonMistakes: Infinite scroll as the only path to content. No maxPages. Forgetting to dedupe by id. Offset pagination on a mutating feed. Cursor sort key not being unique. No "Load more" button. Restoring scroll by pixel offset after a prepend (it jumps). Using the sentinel with rootMargin: '0px' and a fast scroll, causing request storms — use a margin and a isFetching guard.
assuming infinite scroll is free; keepPreviousData forgotten on page changes; a cursor that leaks filter state; no dedupe.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the mechanics and the failure each family has and when you would use it.
Explain bidirectional scroll — the part most implementations skip and when you would use it.
Explain maxpages and the memory model and when you would use it.
Explain offset pagination done properly and when you would use it.
Explain production and operational and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Cursor pagination is the correct choice for correctness and index efficiency, and it costs you page numbers and total counts (both need either a second query or an approximate count — say "1,200+" rather than an exact number, which is what good products do). Infinite scroll removes pagination UI but harms: find-in-page, returning to a position, the back button, and accessibility (no page boundaries). The senior answer is that infinite scroll is a *UI* decision that should be paired with (a) a URL-representable anchor for restoration, (b) a keyboard-reachable "Load more", and (c) maxPages + virtualisation so memory is bounded. Server-side aggregation for huge tables beats client pagination entirely: if a user only sees 25 rows, never fetch 100k.

topics.title: Polling vs WebSockets
topics.description: Three ways to learn that remote data changed. Polling asks on a timer. Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a one-way server→client stream over HTTP. WebSockets are a bidirectional, persistent, upgradeable protocol with framing. The choice is about *push capability vs* complexity, cost, and failure modes — and it should be driven by how fresh the data must be.

topics.title: File upload UX
topics.description: File upload is not a form field; it is a resumable, observable, retryable, cancellable transfer that a user is watching. The design problem has five parts: the UX states (idle → validating → uploading with progress → processing → done/failed), the transport (single POST vs multipart vs direct-to-object-storage), the preview, the queue (concurrency), and the failure/retry path.

tradeoffs: Direct-to-storage saves the most money of anything in this section. A 2 GB/day video product that proxies uploads pays double egress and needs serverless with huge timeouts; presigned PUTs make the app server stateless.

Presigned URLs are capabilities: short expiry, exact key, exact content type, pinned content length, and a quarantine/ prefix that only your worker can promote. Never let the client choose the key freely (path traversal, overwriting other users' objects, serving XSS from your domain).
Timeouts and proxies: an upload through your server dies at 30–60 s on most ingress. That alone is the reason to move large uploads off your server.

Resumability requires persisting { key, uploadId, parts: [{ PartNumber, ETag }] } in IndexedDB; on resume, call ListParts and upload only what is missing. This is a real feature users notice on mobile.

Never trust File.type — it is whatever the OS reported, and on some platforms it is empty. Sniff magic bytes server-side (file-type), re-encode images, strip EXIF, and transcode video (an uploaded "video" can be a 4 GB decompression bomb).

Serving uploads: serve user content from a *different domain* than your app (so an XSS in an HTML upload cannot touch your session), with Content-Disposition: attachment for non-media, a strict Content-Type, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

Mobile: capture="environment" for camera, accept="image/*" for the picker (accepts HEIC on iOS), and remember iOS may downscale the video before it reaches you.

topics.title: The data-fetching model: loaders vs effects, and the waterfall problem
topics.description: A *loader* fetches data as part of a navigation or a render's dependency graph, before the consuming UI renders. Unnecessary requests on every mount. Back-and-forth navigation re-fetches everything. Fix with a cache and a staleness policy.
Missing cleanup. No abort means a setState after unmount and a wasted connection.
Request cancellation on unmount — the same abort controller.
Prefetching: turning navigations warm
Production and operational

Fetching the same resource in a parent and passing it down as a prop *and* having the child fetch it too.

topics.title: TanStack Query: queryKey, cache lifecycle, staleTime vs gcTime
topics.description: TanStack Query (formerly React Query) is a *server-state* cache for asynchronous data. It owns: a keyed cache of query results, in-flight request deduplication, staleness with staleTime, background revalidation, garbage collection with gcTime, retries with backoff, mutations with a lifecycle, and derived/cache state via select. Its central abstraction is a QueryKey: a stable, serialisable, structural descriptor of a request, hashed to identify a cache entry.

The cache lifecycle — the whole thing on one page
staleTime vs gcTime — the distinction interviewers always probe
The other features worth knowing in one line each
Infinite queries (useInfiniteQuery, getNextPageParam) — 4.4.5.
Suspense: useSuspenseQuery throws a promise; combine with <Suspense> for a route-level skeleton instead of per-hook if (isPending).
queryClient.ensureQueryData / prefetchQuery — await the first, fire-and-forget the second; call both in a router loader for a warm navigation.

invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] }) being a no-op because your keys start with 'todosList'.

Retrying mutations (double charges).
Forgetting signal in queryFn so cancelled queries still consume bandwidth.

select returning a new array each call inside selectFromResult (loops).

tradeoffs: You get an enormous amount of correct behaviour for ~13 kB gz and a 10-line config, plus DevTools showing every key, its observers, and its timings. topics.title: SWR and the compare-and-swap revalidation model
topics.description: SWR is a data-fetching hook built on stale-while-revalidate: serve cached data immediately, then revalidate in the background; accept a newer response only if it is actually newer (compare-and-swap). topics.description: A mutation is an intentional write to the server. Unlike a query (implicitly re-fetched by anything), a mutation only runs when you ask for it, and its aftermath — which caches are now wrong, and what the user sees while it runs — is an explicit design decision. topics.title: Pagination: offset vs cursor, infinite queries, bidirectional scroll
topics.description: Pagination is the policy for reading a bounded window of a large collection. Two families exist: offset pagination (?page=2 / ?offset=50&limit=20, computed by the database) and cursor (keyset) pagination (?after=<opaque> / ?before=<opaque>, walking a sort key). Every cursor must be validated server-side and scoped to the filter set (a cursor from filter A is nonsense for filter B) — encode the filter hash into the cursor and reject mismatches, or you get leaked pages.
