Why the client copy is not a security control
Structural rules you must encode deliberately

z.object strips unknown keys (v3) — a client sending { role: 'owner', isAdmin: true } has isAdmin silently dropped. That is usually *desirable* (mass-assignment defence), but use .strict() when you want a loud failure instead of silence.

Coercion is a security-relevant decision. z.coerce.number() turns "" into 0 and null into 0. For numbers that must be present, use z.number() and validate the string first, or use z.preprocess with an explicit empty check. Same for z.coerce.boolean(): "false" coerces to true in JS. This is a classic real bug.
z.string() does not trim. .trim() is a transform; order matters (z.string().trim().min(1)).

Optional vs nullable are different types. z.string().optional() accepts undefined but not null; .nullable() accepts null. Omitting the modifier is the most common source of "why does my optional field fail validation".
Dates: validate as strings with a format check at the boundary, then convert to Date/Temporal inside — never accept a Date from JSON.parse (it arrives as a string).
Enums vs literals: z.enum([...]) gives a union type and rejects unknown values; that is exactly what you want for a role.
partial() vs a new schema: .partial() is for updates where every field is optional; then remember that undefined means "don't change" while null must be a separate path.
File and URL fields: validate on the *server* with content sniffing and size limits; a client File type check is a hint, not a control.
commonMistakes: Validating on the server with a *different* shape than the client (the drift this pattern exists to prevent). z.coerce.boolean() silently inverting "false". Using .optional() where the API sends null. Only validating in the client. Showing a generic "invalid input" instead of mapping field errors. A schema per component so the same field is validated three ways. Leaking server policy details to the client and then treating them as enforced.
two schemas that drift; coercion without checking; stripping unknown keys when you wanted rejection; schema errors surfaced as one big red banner.

tradeoffs: One shared schema means one place to change the contract, but it also couples your client bundle to the server contract (a heavy schema with a big enum costs bundle size) and it forces you to decide what *not* to share (password policy details, rate limits). The pragmatic split: share *shape* and *user-facing* messages; keep *policy* (rate limits, permission, uniqueness) on the server. Zod v4 improved tree-shaking via a modular core (zod/mini) and added better error maps; if bundle size matters, check the current docs rather than assuming v3 behaviour — and the same for z.email() (v4 made top-level string formats, z.string().email() is deprecated in v4). Always verify against the version you have installed.

topics.title: File upload UX: progress, previews, multipart, presigned URLs
topics.description: File upload is not a form field; it is a resumable, observable, retryable, cancellable transfer that a user is watching. The design problem has five parts: the UX states (idle → validating → uploading with progress → processing → done/failed), the transport (single POST vs multipart vs direct-to-object-storage), the preview, the queue (concurrency), and the failure/retry path.
keyConcepts: Why you cannot use fetch for progress
The transport decision — this is the real engineering
Previews — the part that looks easy and is not
The upload queue UX
"Why can't you get upload progress with fetch?"
"Presigned vs multipart: when and why?"
"What must the server do after a presigned upload, and why?"
"How do you make a 2 GB upload resumable?"
"How do you avoid leaking memory with previews?"
"What are the security risks of client uploads?"
commonMistakes: fetch for a progress bar (no progress events). Revoking an object URL while it is still displayed. Trusting file.type server-side. Presigning without ownership scoping or with a 24-hour expiry. Uploading through the app server for multi-GB files. No concurrency limit (20 parallel 100 MB uploads). Announcing every percent to a live region. Losing the queue on refresh.
URL.createObjectURL without revoke; unbounded concurrency; no server-side verification of the uploaded object; assuming a presigned PUT means the file is validated.

tradeoffs: Direct-to-storage saves the most money of anything in this section. A 2 GB/day video product that proxies uploads pays double egress and needs serverless with huge timeouts; presigned PUTs make the app server stateless.

Presigned URLs are capabilities: short expiry, exact key, exact content type, pinned content length, and a quarantine/ prefix that only your worker can promote. Never let the client choose the key freely (path traversal, overwriting other users' objects, serving XSS from your domain).
Timeouts and proxies: an upload through your server dies at 30–60 s on most ingress. That alone is the reason to move large uploads off your server.

Resumability requires persisting { key, uploadId, parts: [{ PartNumber, ETag }] } in IndexedDB; on resume, call ListParts and upload only what is missing. This is a real feature users notice on mobile.

Never trust File.type — it is whatever the OS reported, and on some platforms it is empty. Sniff magic bytes server-side (file-type), re-encode images, strip EXIF, and transcode video (an uploaded "video" can be a 4 GB decompression bomb).

Serving uploads: serve user content from a *different domain* than your app (so an XSS in an HTML upload cannot touch your session), with Content-Disposition: attachment for non-media, a strict Content-Type, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
Cost/UX: for large files, show an estimated time, run uploads while the user does something else, and support paste-from-clipboard (onPaste) and drag-from-Finder.
Mobile: capture="environment" for camera, accept="image/*" for the picker (accepts HEIC on iOS), and remember iOS may downscale the video before it reaches you.

topics.title: Loading, empty, and error states as a first-class design problem
topics.description: Every asynchronous surface has at least five states, not two: *initial loading* (nothing on screen yet), *refreshing* (data present, new data coming), *empty* (the request succeeded and there is nothing), *partial* (some parts failed / some data missing), and *error* (the request failed). UIs that only handle loading + data are incomplete, and the missing states are what users report as bugs.
keyConcepts: The five (really seven) states, and what each must look like
Loading strategies, and the threshold that decides between them
Empty states have three flavours and they are different products
"How many states does an async UI have? Name them."
"Why not show a spinner immediately?"
"How do you handle partial failure?"
"What belongs in an empty state copy?"
"How do skeletons affect CLS and INP?"
commonMistakes: Only handling loading + data. Treating isLoading as "spinner" when data already exists (it wipes good data). Showing the empty state on an error. A full-page spinner for a 200 ms sidebar. role="alert" on the loading container (announces constantly). Skeletons with a different layout from the content. A retry button that refetches with the same broken parameters. No error correlation id shown to support.
two-state thinking; skeleton layout mismatch; error states that leak exceptions; live-region spam.

topics.title: Cache invalidation strategies and the stale-write problem
topics.description: Invalidation is the policy that decides *which cached reads become wrong after a write, and how they learn about it*. The stale-write problem is the specific failure where two writes race — or where a write succeeds but the cache still shows the old value — and it is the reason "just invalidate everything" is a temporary answer, not a strategy.
keyConcepts: The four sources of cache invalidation
A strategy matrix
The stale-write problem, precisely
Making staleness visible and bounded
A concrete, defensible policy you can present in an interview
Production and operational
Log invalidations in development: wrap invalidateQueries in a helper that console.logs the key and the caller. Half of "my data is stale" bugs become obvious immediately.
Test the invalidation graph: for each mutation, a unit test that asserts the expected keys are invalidated and that an unrelated key is *not*. This is the cheapest high-value test in a data layer.

Alert on refetch volume (requests per user-minute). A sudden rise usually means a refetch loop: refetchInterval too low, an invalidate inside an effect, or staleTime: 0 with refetchOnFocus on a route users tab between constantly.
Clear the cache on identity changes: logout, tenant switch, permission downgrade (queryClient.clear()), and on a 401 broadcast from another tab (via BroadcastChannel).
Bound the cache: track queryCache.getAll().length and total serialised size; set gcTime deliberately for high-cardinality keys.
Never trust the client cache for authorisation. It is a UX optimisation over server checks (4.6.9).
commonMistakes: Invalidating with a key that matches nothing. Invalidating in a useEffect (an infinite refetch loop). Not cancelling queries before an optimistic write. staleTime: Infinity plus a new read path that forgets to invalidate. Forgetting that a queryKey missing a filter makes two cache entries for one logical view. React Query's refetchOnMount default being true while assuming it means "always refetch".
invalidateQueries from an effect; no key discipline; treating the cache as authoritative for permissions; rolling back without refetching.

tradeoffs: Broad invalidation is simple and correct and costs a request storm that grows with your app — it is a *deferred architecture bill*. Precise invalidation is efficient and requires a mental model of every dependent read, which is real ongoing cost and is invisible in code review (a new component with a new query key silently becomes a missed dependent). Push invalidation is the most correct and the most operationally expensive (4.4.6). staleTime: Infinity is the best performance and the worst failure mode (permanent wrongness from a missed invalidation) — reserve it for data you fully own.

topics.description: Client routing intercepts navigation, renders a different component tree without a full document load, and keeps the URL bar in sync using the History API — history.pushState(state, '', url), history.replaceState(state, '', url), and the popstate event. It is what makes a single-page app feel like a multi-page app while only loading the shell once.

topics.title: Lazy loading
topics.description: Route-level code splitting is the discipline of making each route's *component module* a separate bundle, downloaded when that route is first needed. topics.title: File-based routing
topics.description: File-based routing derives the route table from the directory tree — the filesystem *is* the router configuration. Add a file, get a route; delete a file, the route is gone; move a file, the URL changes. Nothing declares a path, a layout chain, or a param list in JS, because there is no second place where the URL can be written down and drift out of sync. The important part is that a convention is only as good as its escape hatches: route groups, layout files, dynamic segments, optional catch-alls, and a documented way to opt out (routes.ts).

It costs: a build step you did not write, a learning curve for the conventions (group vs folder, [id] vs :id vs $id), the fact that moving a file changes a URL (so "just reorganise" becomes a production incident without redirects), limited expressiveness for anything irregular (deeply conditional matching, versioned APIs with a custom ranking function — which is exactly why TanStack Router lets you drop to a code-defined route, and why Next lets you write a route.ts handler outside the tree). The rule of thumb I give teams: convention for the 90%, an explicit escape hatch for the 10%, and never both for the same route.

topics.title: Hash vs history mode
topics.description: Two URL schemes. History mode uses real paths (/invoices/42) with the History API. Hash mode puts the route inside the fragment (/#/invoices/42), which is never sent to the server and fires hashchange instead of popstate.
keyConcepts: The decisive technical differences (beyond aesthetics)

Server visibility. The fragment is never sent in an HTTP request. So: no server-side auth check on #/admin, no server-side redirect of #/login?next=/billing, no per-route HTTP caching, no ability to give a deep link its own server-rendered payload. If you need any of these, hash routing is the wrong tool.

When the fragment is available to client code. It arrives *after* the document loads, so a hash router needs a hydration-safe read (useEffect/useLayoutEffect, not render) or you get a flash of the wrong route. History mode has the path from the first byte.

Failure mode. History mode fails loudly if the server rewrite is missing (a 404 on every deep link). Hash mode "just works" anywhere — which is why it dominated the pre-2015 era and why some internal tools still use it.
Analytics. pageview tools that read location.pathname see one page forever in hash mode; you must parse the hash yourself and fire synthetic pageviews.
Where hash routing is still the right answer

Non-SPA contexts where you cannot configure the server: opening file:// pages, embedding inside an iframe served by another team, a static host where the fallback is fixed, a browser extension, a desktop app using a custom protocol.

Fragments used as *data* or *state*, not as routes: OAuth implicit-grant return values (#access_token=... — legacy, do not build new flows on this; use PKCE, PHASE 7), or a client-side deep-link target for a native app (myapp://open/#/invoice/42).
In-page anchors (#section) — the ordinary, boring, correct use of the fragment.
When it is the wrong answer

The migration from hash to history is usually "never", because URLs are already in the wild — plan for a redirect map if you ever migrate (/#/invoices/42 → /invoices/42 via a small script on the hash page).

topics.title: Protected routes with auth
topics.description: A route guard is code that decides whether the current navigation may proceed. The critical, security-relevant distinction: client and router guards are UX; enforcement is server-side. A guard can stop a user from seeing a screen; only the server can stop them from *doing the thing*. Interviewers who probe this distinction are looking for whether you understand that the ID in the URL is attacker-controlled input.
keyConcepts: Three layers, and what each one can do
The next parameter — the vulnerability everyone forgets
The client router must also not render the protected component
Token storage, briefly (full treatment in PHASE 7 and 4.6.9)
Production and operational

Centralise: one requireUser/requirePermission per route module, and a lint/review rule that a route with data access must have a loader that calls it. Route-level guards are the most commonly forgotten security control in SPAs because there is no compile error when you skip one.
Cache-Control: private, no-store and Vary: Cookie on authenticated responses; a CDN-cached authenticated page is a data breach (4.6.5 scenario 9).
Guard the *server actions* and *API handlers* too — a route guard protects the UI, not the endpoint. This is Broken Access Control / IDOR territory in OWASP (PHASE 7).
Session expiry mid-session: an API layer that detects a 401 broadcasts to all tabs (BroadcastChannel) and triggers one redirect, rather than N tabs each redirecting.
Log denials with user + resource + permission: 403 spikes are the signal for a privilege-escalation attempt or a broken role mapping.

Test: for every protected route, an integration test that asserts (a) unauthenticated → redirect, (b) authenticated but unauthorised → 403, (c) authorised → data, and (d) *authenticated as user A requesting user B's resource → 403* — that last one is the test most teams do not write and it is the one that catches real breaches.
"You hid the admin button. Is the app secure?" (No — explain the three layers and where enforcement lives.)
commonMistakes: Guarding only in components; a role check where an object check was needed; validating next insufficiently; caching authenticated HTML; not guarding the server action/API; redirect loops from a loader that fetches without cookies.
component-only guards; broad middleware matchers; no object-level checks; unvalidated next; authenticated HTML in a shared cache.

tradeoffs: Edge guards are fast and prevent disclosure but are limited by what they can read (cookies/headers, no DB), and a broad matcher adds latency to every request. Router guards are precise and can make authorisation decisions with full context, but only after the app is loaded. Component guards are pure UX. The correct architecture uses all three with one rule: the server check is the only one that matters; the other two reduce wasted requests and avoid embarrassing flashes.

topics.title: Deep linking
topics.description: Deep linking is the ability to open any state of the app by URL alone, on a cold load, in a new tab, shared with someone else, months later. URL design is deciding which state belongs in the path, which in the query string, which in neither, and how to make all of it canonical.
keyConcepts: The URL contract — the design decisions, in order

Identity in the path, view state in the query. The path says *what exists*; the query says *how you are looking at it*. A URL in the query should never be the only way to identify a resource (an id in the query can be shared incorrectly and is invisible to crawlers).

The URL must decide what the server returns. ?page=3 must fetch page 3 server-side, or a shared link shows page 1 (the classic "deep link loads the wrong page" bug). Similarly for filters and sorting on any indexable page.

Canonicalise. Omit defaults (?page=1 → /tasks), normalise parameter order, one canonical spelling of a filter (status=open not statuses=open&open=true), and redirect non-canonical URLs with a 301/308 so link equity and analytics do not split. Never have two URLs render identical content.
One spelling per thing, forever. Renaming a path segment means a redirect map (old → new, permanent) — do it once, keep it forever.

URLs are a public API. They appear in emails, support tickets, QR codes, printed receipts, and Slack messages. They must be readable, stable, and free of secrets (4.6.9). Human-readable slugs for public content (/blog/optimistic-updates-rollback) with a numeric id hidden behind them.

Pagination state is URL state, and its format is a product decision: page numbers for admin tables (?page=3), cursor for feeds (?after=… — visible but ugly; some products keep the cursor out of the URL and accept losing back-navigation within a feed). Be explicit about which you chose and why.

Tabs and wizards: ?tab=history is deep-linkable (good for support and for emails linking to "the invoices tab"); a wizard step is usually URL state too (/checkout/2/payment) so Back works and a reload does not lose progress — but that means you must validate which steps the user may reach (4.3.7/4.5.5).
Sort direction: use an explicit prefix (sort=-due) rather than a separate param (dir=desc) so a sort is one atomic value; or use sort=due&dir=asc if you need both — pick one and be consistent.
Deep-link correctness checklist
Interaction with the query cache
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Filters in a store instead of the URL. Defaults left in the URL. Two URLs for the same view. A deep link that fetches page 1 regardless of ?page=. Search text pushed on every keystroke. ?q= in a path with unescaped special characters. Analytics counting a filter change as a pageview.
store-based filters; no canonical form; page=1 shipped in links; unvalidated params reaching the API.

tradeoffs: Rich URLs cost verbosity (a 90-character query string), require validation and canonicalisation, and force you to think about which state is durable — but they buy shareability, Back-button correctness, SSR/crawlability, analytics attribution, reduced server state (nothing to persist per user), and supportability ("open this URL and you'll see what I see"). topics.title: Parallel and intercepting routes
topics.description: Parallel routes render multiple independent route slots into the *same layout at the same time* — so one layout can host, say, a feed and an authenticated sidebar that load and refresh independently. Intercepting routes render one slot *in place of* its normal position when the navigation came from a specific origin (a <Link> from the feed, a form submission) while falling back to the normal position on a hard navigation (a direct URL load, a refresh, a paste). Together they give you the "modal routing" pattern that makes a photo lightbox feel instant while keeping the URL shareable and the deep link correct.

Slot content duplicated across slots (double fetch). Intercepting a route that should have been a real page.

It is what makes a single-page app feel like a multi-page app while only loading the shell once.

tradeoffs: Client routing gives instant transitions, preserved app state (a query cache, a scroll position, an open composer), and no full reload. topics.title: Dynamic, optional-catch-all, and nested segments
topics.description: The path-pattern vocabulary: static segments (/settings), dynamic segments (/invoices/:id), splat/catch-all (/files/*path), optional catch-all (/docs/:lang?/*path), and nested segments that render a parent layout with an Outlet for the child. Optional catch-all segments exist so /docs and /docs/getting-started/install match one route without an ambiguous second definition.
keyConcepts: The matching algorithm, and why route order matters
Why optional catch-all exists
Nesting mechanics

Layout nesting (shared chrome persists): a parent route element renders <Outlet />. In Next.js App Router this is layout.tsx; the parent does not re-render on child navigation, which is the performance win.
Path nesting (the child path is *relative to* the parent): children: [{ path: 'edit', ... }] inside path: '/invoices/:id'. The child's full path is concatenated.
When to nest and when to flatten

"What are the two kinds of nesting in App Router?"

"When is a splat segment dangerous?"

ordering-dependent matching; unvalidated params; nesting for styling.

tradeoffs: Ranked matching means you rarely get ordering wrong — but ambiguity still hurts readability and some routers (Next.js) *do* rely on filesystem layout rather than ranking, where page.tsx and [id]/page.tsx in the same folder is an error. Know which model your router uses.

Params are strings and untrusted. Validate them at the boundary (above) before using them in a query key or a fetch. :id in the URL is user input (4.6.9: IDs in URLs are untrusted; authorisation is per object).

Optional catch-all and generateStaticParams: with SSR, [...slug] and [slug] generate different params shapes ({ slug: ['a','b'] } vs { slug: 'a' }), and forgetting to handle both is a 500 on a deep link.
Splats are a security surface: a splat param feeds filesystem lookups, path joins, or globs. Normalise (.., duplicate slashes, absolute paths) and never pass it to fs unchecked.
basename for apps served from a subpath (/admin/app) — set it once on the router; forgetting it breaks every asset-relative URL.

topics.title: Data loaders and actions in the routing layer
topics.description: A loader is a function the router runs *before* rendering a route, receiving the request (params, search, request object) and returning data for that route. An action is the same contract for mutations: it receives submitted data, performs the write, and returns a result. Both are the router's data layer, and both are the place where "fetch before render" becomes a framework feature instead of a useEffect.
keyConcepts: The loader contract, end to end
Subtle but important mechanics
Next.js equivalents
Production and operational
"What is the difference between a loader and an action?"
"How do loaders avoid waterfalls?"
"What is defer for?"
"When does a loader re-run, and how do you stop it?"
"Why would you use a query library inside a route that has a loader?"
commonMistakes: Calling your API without forwarding auth headers (redirect loops). Using useEffect + fetch inside a route component anyway. Expecting useNavigation().state to identify which route. Revalidating on every query-string change. Loaders that ignore shouldRevalidate and hammer the API. Throwing new Error instead of a Response for expected states (everything becomes a 500).
mixing the two data models without a rule; unauthenticated loader fetches; no shouldRevalidate tuning.

tradeoffs: Loaders: explicit, no waterfall, SSR-capable, progressive enhancement, and impossible to render with the wrong data (fetch-before-render is a *guarantee*, not a convention). Costs: you must learn a second data model; loaders run on *every* navigation unless you tune shouldRevalidate; data is not shared with non-router components (a modal rendered outside the route tree cannot use useLoaderData); and client-side-only caching of loader data requires extra work (dehydrate/hydrate, 4.4.2). Effects/queries: better caching and sharing, worse guarantees. The honest senior position: *use the router's loader for the route's data (it is the only thing that can SSR and stream it correctly), and use a query cache for incremental and shared client-side data.*

topics.title: Route guards and protected routes with auth
topics.description: A route guard is code that decides whether the current navigation may proceed. The critical, security-relevant distinction: client and router guards are UX; enforcement is server-side. A guard can stop a user from seeing a screen; only the server can stop them from *doing the thing*. Interviewers who probe this distinction are looking for whether you understand that the ID in the URL is attacker-controlled input.
keyConcepts: Three layers, and what each one can do
The next parameter — the vulnerability everyone forgets
The client router must also not render the protected component
Token storage, briefly (full treatment in PHASE 7 and 4.6.9)
Production and operational

Centralise: one requireUser/requirePermission per route module, and a lint/review rule that a route with data access must have a loader that calls it. Route-level guards are the most commonly forgotten security control in SPAs because there is no compile error when you skip one.
Cache-Control: private, no-store and Vary: Cookie on authenticated responses; a CDN-cached authenticated page is a data breach (4.6.5 scenario 9).
Guard the *server actions* and *API handlers* too — a route guard protects the UI, not the endpoint. This is Broken Access Control / IDOR territory in OWASP (PHASE 7).
Session expiry mid-session: an API layer that detects a 401 broadcasts to all tabs (BroadcastChannel) and triggers one redirect, rather than N tabs each redirecting.
Log denials with user + resource + permission: 403 spikes are the signal for a privilege-escalation attempt or a broken role mapping.

Test: for every protected route, an integration test that asserts (a) unauthenticated → redirect, (b) authenticated but unauthorised → 403, (c) authorised → data, and (d) *authenticated as user A requesting user B's resource → 403* — that last one is the test most teams do not write and it is the one that catches real breaches.
"You hid the admin button. Is the app secure?" (No — explain the three layers and where enforcement lives.)
commonMistakes: Guarding only in components; a role check where an object check was needed; validating next insufficiently; caching authenticated HTML; not guarding the server action/API; redirect loops from a loader that fetches without cookies.
component-only guards; broad middleware matchers; no object-level checks; unvalidated next; authenticated HTML in a shared cache.

tradeoffs: Edge guards are fast and prevent disclosure but are limited by what they can read (cookies/headers, no DB), and a broad matcher adds latency to every request. Router guards are precise and can make authorisation decisions with full context, but only after the app is loaded. Component guards are pure UX. The correct architecture uses all three with one rule: the server check is the only one that matters; the other two reduce wasted requests and avoid embarrassing flashes.

topics.title: Lazy loading routes and code splitting at the route boundary
topics.description: Route-level code splitting is the discipline of making each route's *component module* a separate bundle, downloaded when that route is first needed. It is the single highest-leverage performance technique in a routed SPA, because routes are the natural boundaries of both code and data.

Where to put the boundaries (and where not to)
The chunk-loading failure modes in production
Verification

"Why can you not split a dynamically computed route table?"
"What is ChunkLoadError and how do you handle it?"
"How do you avoid a spinner on every route navigation?"
"Why can lazy break hydration?"
commonMistakes: lazy on the shell. Splitting above-the-fold content (hurts LCP). No prefetch, so every route navigation shows a spinner. No ChunkLoadError handling. Forgetting to include route-level *loaders* in the split. Suspending without a boundary or with a boundary at the root (one slow route blanks the app). manualChunks splitting so aggressively that a shared import is duplicated.

The failure mode of over-splitting is worse than under-splitting on a fast connection and better on a slow one — so measure on the slowest network your users actually have (4.6.8 RUM, not lab).

topics.description: Navigation hooks are the router's imperative API for programmatic navigation (navigate), the current location (useLocation), params (useParams), and navigation state (useNavigation, useNavigationType). topics.title: Deep linking, URL design, and query-param state
topics.description: Deep linking is the ability to open any state of the app by URL alone, on a cold load, in a new tab, shared with someone else, months later. URL design is deciding which state belongs in the path, which in the query string, which in neither, and how to make all of it canonical.
keyConcepts: The URL contract — the design decisions, in order

Identity in the path, view state in the query. The path says *what exists*; the query says *how you are looking at it*. A URL in the query should never be the only way to identify a resource (an id in the query can be shared incorrectly and is invisible to crawlers).

The URL must decide what the server returns. ?page=3 must fetch page 3 server-side, or a shared link shows page 1 (the classic "deep link loads the wrong page" bug). Similarly for filters and sorting on any indexable page.

Canonicalise. Omit defaults (?page=1 → /tasks), normalise parameter order, one canonical spelling of a filter (status=open not statuses=open&open=true), and redirect non-canonical URLs with a 301/308 so link equity and analytics do not split. Never have two URLs render identical content.
One spelling per thing, forever. Renaming a path segment means a redirect map (old → new, permanent) — do it once, keep it forever.

URLs are a public API. They appear in emails, support tickets, QR codes, printed receipts, and Slack messages. They must be readable, stable, and free of secrets (4.6.9). Human-readable slugs for public content (/blog/optimistic-updates-rollback) with a numeric id hidden behind them.

Pagination state is URL state, and its format is a product decision: page numbers for admin tables (?page=3), cursor for feeds (?after=… — visible but ugly; some products keep the cursor out of the URL and accept losing back-navigation within a feed). Be explicit about which you chose and why.

Tabs and wizards: ?tab=history is deep-linkable (good for support and for emails linking to "the invoices tab"); a wizard step is usually URL state too (/checkout/2/payment) so Back works and a reload does not lose progress — but that means you must validate which steps the user may reach (4.3.7/4.5.5).
Sort direction: use an explicit prefix (sort=-due) rather than a separate param (dir=desc) so a sort is one atomic value; or use sort=due&dir=asc if you need both — pick one and be consistent.
Deep-link correctness checklist
Interaction with the query cache
Production and operational

Search text pushed on every keystroke. ?q= in a path with unescaped special characters. Analytics counting a filter change as a pageview.
store-based filters; no canonical form; page=1 shipped in links; unvalidated params reaching the API.

topics.title: Router comparison: React Router, TanStack Router, Next.js App Router, Remix
topics.description: A router comparison is a set of decisions about *where the route table lives*, *who owns data loading*, *how caching works*, *how much framework is imposed*, and *what you must know about rendering*. These four options are not interchangeable: two are routers you mount in your own app, two are frameworks that own the whole application.
keyConcepts: The comparison
How to choose, in the order a staff engineer actually uses it

Do you need server rendering, SEO, or a CDN-cached public site? If yes → a framework (Next.js App Router, Remix). If no → a library (React Router, TanStack Router) and you keep your own deploy story. *This single question eliminates half the options.*

Are you already on Next.js? Stay on Next.js unless you have a named, measurable blocker. Migration cost is the dominant term, and Next's weaknesses (implicit caching) are now well-documented and cacheable.

Do you want compile-time route/param/search typing across a large app? → TanStack Router. It is the strongest typing story in React routing, and defaultPreload: 'intent' gives you prefetching for free.

Do you want maximum control and the smallest surface, and are you already rendering your own HTML or using a non-standard renderer? → React Router. It is a router, not a framework, and it composes with anything.
Do you want explicit data flow, progressive enhancement, and no magic caching? → Remix / RR7 framework mode. Every request's data flow is visible in one file.
Do you need parallel/intercepting routes (modal-over-feed at scale)? → Next.js App Router (or build it yourself, which is real work).
"Compare these four routers and tell me which you would pick for *this* product."
"What does Next's implicit caching cost you, and how do you mitigate it?"
"What is the strongest argument for TanStack Router?"
"What does 'progressive enhancement' mean here, and which router gives it to you for free?"
commonMistakes: choosing by popularity; ignoring who owns the cache; treating a router as if it also solved data fetching; migrating for a framework preference rather than a named defect.

tradeoffs: Next.js: implicit, rule-based caching that has changed defaults across versions and is the single largest source of "why is my data stale" incidents; a client/server boundary you must reason about constantly ('use client' at the top of a file is a big hammer); a large runtime; and a fast-moving release cadence. Mitigation: keep data access in server components, make cache policy explicit and documented per route, and pin versions.

React Router: you own the cache, the SSR strategy, the error handling, and the file conventions — which is freedom and also work. Mitigation: adopt a data layer with opinions (TanStack Query), a route-error-boundary convention, and a lazy-route policy (4.5.6).
TanStack Router: the plugin/codegen is a new moving part, and the type inference is a build-time cost; in exchange you get params/search typed end to end and excellent preload/intent behaviour.
Remix: its loader/action model is its greatest strength and its main constraint — you must learn to think per-request, and nested-route data dependencies take a moment to internalise.

topics.title: File-based routing and route organisation
topics.description: File-based routing derives the route table from the directory tree — the filesystem *is* the router configuration. Add a file, get a route; delete a file, the route is gone; move a file, the URL changes. Nothing declares a path, a layout chain, or a param list in JS, because there is no second place where the URL can be written down and drift out of sync. The important part is that a convention is only as good as its escape hatches: route groups, layout files, dynamic segments, optional catch-alls, and a documented way to opt out (routes.ts).
keyConcepts: Production and operational
"What do route groups do, and when do you need one?"
"How do you keep a route rename from breaking production?"
"What does codegen buy you that a JS route array cannot?"
"Where do you draw the line between convention and configuration?"
"How would you audit which routes exist and which are protected?"
commonMistakes: Two files resolving to the same URL without a group; assuming a group creates a path segment (it does not); putting request state in a layout and wondering why it survives navigation; using (group) for auth instead of a real check; renaming a folder without redirects; mixing generated and hand-written routes without a documented single writer; and relying on the folder name for security.
treating the convention as enforcement; no redirect discipline on moves; two writers for the route tree; ignoring that optional catch-all can swallow its siblings' URLs.

tradeoffs: File-based routing buys: no config file to merge-conflict, an enumerable route set, automatic per-route code splitting, and — when codegen is involved — compile-time checking of paths, params, and search. It costs: a build step you did not write, a learning curve for the conventions (group vs folder, [id] vs :id vs $id), the fact that moving a file changes a URL (so "just reorganise" becomes a production incident without redirects), limited expressiveness for anything irregular (deeply conditional matching, versioned APIs with a custom ranking function — which is exactly why TanStack Router lets you drop to a code-defined route, and why Next lets you write a route.ts handler outside the tree). The rule of thumb I give teams: convention for the 90%, an explicit escape hatch for the 10%, and never both for the same route.

topics.title: Design systems and component libraries (shadcn, MUI, Radix)
topics.description: A design system is a versioned, cross-product collection of decisions — tokens, primitives, components, patterns, documentation — plus the governance that keeps those decisions consistent. Canonical entry for design principles and visual language: PHASE 1 → Communication; here we talk engineering.
keyConcepts: What a design system is
A single source of truth for visual and interaction decisions, encoded as code where possible (tokens, components, lints).
A contract with a versioning policy: consumers declare which major version they are on and get a migration path.
A product of an organisation: it exists because five teams were solving the same modal focus-trap bug five different ways.
An accessibility enforcement point: primitives are where keyboard and screen-reader behaviour is proved once.
What a design system is NOT
Not a Figma file with a colour palette. Designers' files are an input, not the deliverable — code is where behaviour lives.
Not a "component library with nice buttons". It includes *patterns* (how components combine to accomplish a task), *content guidelines* (empty states, error copy), and *governance*.
Not a monolith of 200 exported components. A system that nobody can navigate is a system nobody adopts.
Not a marketing term for "we use Tailwind". Tailwind is a styling mechanism; a design system is the decisions plus the contract.
The anatomy: token → primitive → component → pattern → page
Design tokens
commonMistakes: calling Figma the design system; letting product code reference primitives; assuming dark: class variants scale past a handful of components; adding props instead of slots; deprecating without a codemod or a migration deadline; treating accessibility as a checklist at the end; versioning by "how big the diff looks" instead of by API compatibility; measuring adoption by "did we write it" instead of "is it used".
practiceTasks: build a token pipeline: author 40 tokens in JSON, emit CSS custom properties + a TS object + a markdown table; define a light and a dark theme; write the tier-boundary lint; then implement Button, Input, and Dialog consuming only semantic tokens, with axe passing and a --brand switch at runtime with no rebuild. Measure the CSS output size for one theme and justify whether you shipped both or generated one at build time.

interviewQuestions.text: What is a design system, and what is explicitly not one?
Explain the token → primitive → component → pattern → page anatomy with an example.
Primitive vs semantic vs component tokens: why does the distinction matter operationally?
How do you enforce "product code never touches primitive tokens"?
How do you theme with CSS custom properties? Why not Sass variables?
Multi-brand and dark mode at the same time — where do the overrides live?
What does `oklch()` give you over hex, and what are the caveats?
Why is contrast not symmetric between light and dark themes? Give failing examples.
Controlled vs uncontrolled components: why support both?
How do you prevent boolean-prop explosion? Show the API you would design.
Escape hatches: what do you expose and why is removing them harmful?
Polymorphic `as`: what problems does it solve and what does it cost?

topics.title: Storybook
topics.description: A workshop for UI components in isolation — a static site per component, where every variant, state, and edge case is a *story* that can be rendered, reviewed, tested, and diffed.
keyConcepts: Stories vs stories of stories
A story is one named, parameterised state of a component (Primary, WithError, Loading, LongLabel, RTL, ZeroItems).

A story of stories is the *coverage requirement*: the argument that a component's stories must enumerate its state space, not just its happy path. A mature component library has a story per state (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty, over-long content, RTL, high-contrast, reduced-motion) — that is the real contract.

Docs pages group stories and add prose; autodocs generate the API table (props, types, defaults, descriptions) from the component's TypeScript types plus JSDoc. Autodocs means your docs table rots less than a hand-written props table — the machine-reads-types part is the win; the descriptions still need a human.
MDX mixes prose with live stories, which is how you document "when to use / when not to use" with an example rather than a screenshot.
Interaction testing with play
The a11y addon, and what it cannot catch
Keyboard operability of a custom widget (does Tab order make sense? does Escape close?).
Focus visibility and focus-trap correctness in dynamic content.
Screen-reader announcement quality and reading order (e.g. a live region that exists but announces nothing useful).
Whether the accessible name is *meaningful* ("Click here").
Timing and motion problems, or zoom/reflow at 400%.
commonMistakes: treating Storybook as documentation only, or as documentation that lives in a wiki; writing one story per component instead of one per state; live API calls in stories; flaky visual baselines papered over with tolerance thresholds; assuming axe means accessible; a Storybook per app in a monorepo.
practiceTasks: write Dialog and Select with full state stories, add a play test per state that asserts focus behaviour, add axe, then run everything in CI on a deliberately broken version (remove the focus trap, remove the label) and confirm the pipeline catches each defect. Finally, set up visual regression, deliberately introduce a flaky story, and write down what caused the flake and how you fixed it.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem does Storybook solve that unit tests do not?
What is a "story of stories" and why does it matter?
How do args and argTypes differ, and what does autodocs take from your types?
Why does a `play` function test something a jsdom unit test cannot?
What fraction of accessibility problems does the axe addon catch, and what does it miss?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: axe-core automates a well-defined subset of accessibility rules, and it is excellent at that subset. Decision: run it on every story in CI as a blocking gate for critical and serious violations, and pair it with a mandatory manual keyboard and screen-reader pass per component release. Reasoning: the addon catches mechanical failures — missing accessible names, invalid ARIA, missing labels, some contrast — which are numerous and entirely mechanical, so automation gives immediate value at near-zero marginal cost. What it cannot judge is interaction: whether a custom listbox's arrow-key behaviour matches the ARIA pattern, whether focus moves into a dialog and returns to the invoker on close, whether the focus ring is visible against the actual background, whether a live region announces a change meaningfully, or whether the accessible name is any good at all. Failure scenario: we ship a combobox that passes axe with a correct role and aria-expanded but does nothing on ArrowDown, so a keyboard or screen-reader user cannot reach any option — green pipeline, unusable product. Trade-offs: full manual testing per component is expensive and inconsistent, which is why I want one documented manual checklist per component archetype (dialog, combobox, tabs, table) and a shared vocabulary, rather than 'test accessibility' as a slogan. Alternative: shift automated effort to keyboard-interaction assertions inside play, which mechanises part of the manual check by simulating a real user with userEvent."

interviewQuestions.text: How do you make visual regression baselines stable? Give four concrete causes of flake and their fixes.
Should visual regression block a merge?
How do you run one Storybook for a monorepo?
How do you document a *published* component package so docs cannot drift from versions?
Storybook build time is 8 minutes. What do you measure first?
How do you stop stories rotting when nobody is motivated?
When would you deliberately *not* use Storybook?

topics.title: Micro-frontends
topics.description: An architectural pattern where a single-page application is decomposed into independently built, deployed, and owned sub-applications that are composed at runtime into one user-facing product. Canonical backend-side treatment: PHASE 11 → Architectural Styles → Microfrontends; here the *frontend mechanics and costs*.
keyConcepts: Real motivations
Independent deploy cadence. Multiple teams must ship on their own schedules through one shared release train without coordinating merges. This is the strongest legitimate driver.

Organisational autonomy at scale. Team boundaries *caused by* code ownership need: "if you can't deploy it alone, you can't be on call for it alone." At ~50+ engineers across overlapping surfaces, deployment coupling is the real cost of a shared frontend repo.
Legacy incremental migration. A 400k-line Angular app gets a new React surface without a rewrite. Strangler-fig the frontend (PHASE 11).

Domain boundaries that genuinely differ. Billing is a checkout with a totally different UX and lifecycle from an analytics dashboard; merging them into one bundle and one deploy is a merge of risk profiles, not just code.

Technology heterogeneity as a *by-product*, never as a goal. "We use React in the new thing because the new thing is React" is fine; "we split so each team picks its own framework" is a cost with no user benefit and enormous tax.
Real costs

Runtime inconsistency: the shell and remotes were built at different times against different dependency versions. Two copies of React → hooks errors; two copies of a token system → visual mismatch; two router versions → navigation bugs.
Dependency duplication and bundle bloat. If each MFE is independently built and each bundles its own framework, you ship 3× React. Sizing becomes a first-class concern (see sharing/singletons).

CSS isolation is genuinely hard. Options are: CSS Modules or scoped styles per MFE (works, but you lose cross-MFE overrides like theming and typography), Shadow DOM (real isolation, but breaks global design-token inheritance, form controls, fonts, and is awkward for SSR), BEM naming discipline, or a strict "no global CSS outside the shell" rule. Every real implementation picks one and suffers its trade-off.

Cross-team coordination cost. Contract changes, shared component releases, and release-order dependencies reappear as distributed-systems problems: you need versioning, compatibility windows, and deprecation.
Testing. End-to-end tests must test the *composition*, which is now nondeterministic and version-skewed. Unit/component tests stay inside the MFE; integration tests need both sides deployed.
commonMistakes: adopting micro-frontends for "scalability" or "team autonomy" without a release-cadence problem; leaving routing unowned; ignoring the React singleton; assuming client-side composition is SEO-safe; migrating the shell before one remote works end to end; not budgeting the runtime dependency.
practiceTasks: build a shell with two routes, each loading a separately built "remote" (two Vite builds with a tiny federated-style loader), sharing a singleton React, a shared token stylesheet, and a typed postMessage event bus. Then break it on purpose: ship remote v2 with a changed shared-component prop and no shell release, and document the failure and the compatibility fix. Add a trace-id breadcrumb in both apps and show the correlated Sentry issue.

interviewQuestions.text: What problems do micro-frontends genuinely solve? Which one is strongest?
List the costs. Which do teams underestimate?
Build-time vs runtime composition: when each?
How does the shell own routing, and what breaks if two MFEs disagree about routes?
How do you share React across MFEs, and what fails if you get it wrong?
How do you isolate CSS between remotes? What does Shadow DOM break?
Design cross-MFE communication. When is URL state enough?
Auth across three apps on the same parent domain: your approach?
Your shell v2 ships while remote v1 is still deployed. What are the failure modes and mitigations?
What is a compatibility contract between a shell and a remote?
How do you trace one user action across four codebases?
Migrate a monolith: order the steps and pick the first slice.

topics.title: Error monitoring (Sentry)
topics.description: A client/server error-reporting service that captures unhandled exceptions and (optionally) traces, enriches them with release/environment/user context, groups them into *issues*, and routes alerts. Canonical observability material: PHASE 8 → monitoring, logging, metrics; here is the frontend-specific craft.
keyConcepts: What to capture
Context that makes a report actionable
Attach feature flag state to every event (4.6.7). When a bug appears only for 5% of users, the flag values in the event are the difference between a five-minute and a five-hour investigation.
Attach the trace id so you can jump to the trace (Phase 8) for the timeline of fetches and spans around the failure.
Sampling and error quotas
Session replay and PII
Mask by default: all input, textarea, select, and contenteditable (set maskAllText: true and blockAllMedia: true, then unmask only specific selectors you have reviewed).
Never replay: payment fields, national IDs, health data, free-text notes containing customer data, anything on a page behind authentication you have not reviewed.
Legal/privacy review is mandatory before enabling, and record it (retention period, DPA, where data is stored, who can access). Cross-reference PHASE 7 → GDPR/privacy practices.
Sampling: record a fraction of *sessions* (or only sessions that contain an error), which cuts cost and data volume while keeping the useful correlation ("replay the session where this happened").
Treat replay as a debugging tool with short retention (7–14 days) and access controls, not as an analytics product.
Performance tracing and Web Vitals
commonMistakes: deploying without uploading source maps for that exact release; no release tag so every stack is unminified; sending Authorization headers; enabling replay without masking and legal review; alerting on every new issue; relying on breadcrumbs you never added; "it only happens locally" treated as a monitoring gap rather than an environment difference.
practiceTasks: Browser SDK for client errors/traces; server SDK for your API; framework/framework-agnostic wrappers (React Router, Next.js, SvelteKit) add routing context and automatic route transaction names — use one, because free contextual data is better than manual breadcrumbs.
Source maps must reach Sentry. They never go in the public bundle. Upload them from CI, per release, and delete/ignore them for the deployed artifact. Framework: sentry-cli sourcemaps upload.

Release and build identity. Every build gets a unique release id ($CI_COMMIT_SHA, or ${semver}+${sha}), reported by the SDK and written onto uploaded source maps. Without a matching release, stack traces are useless — this is the single most common integration failure. Also set a dist (or build id) so the Sentry release matches your asset fingerprint exactly.

integrate Sentry into an app with release tagging, CI map upload, beforeSend scrubbing of headers and query params, flag tags, and a custom fingerprint on your API client. Then deliberately ship three distinct bugs (a type error on a rare flag path, a network 500, and a slow fetch) and verify each lands as a grouped, actionable issue with the right release, flags, and trace link. Then delete one issue from the noise and justify it.

interviewQuestions.text: What is the single most important Sentry integration detail, and why?
How do you wire release and source maps in CI? Why does order matter?
What is the difference between unhandled and handled error capture, and which is more valuable?
Where exactly should `captureException` live in a React app?
What context makes an error report actionable? Name five fields.
How do you sample without losing visibility of new issues?
What must be masked in session replay, and who approves it?
How do traces and Web Vitals connect to a user-reported "the page is slow"?
An issue has 4,000 events from six different bugs. Fix the grouping.
How do you decide what pages you?
What is the difference between `beforeSend` and an ignore list, and when is each right?
When do you alert on an error, and how do you connect that to SLOs?

topics.title: Feature flags
topics.description: A remote configuration mechanism that lets you change runtime behaviour without shipping code. Cross-reference PHASE 8 → CI/CD → feature flags for the delivery side; here is the frontend correctness side.
keyConcepts: Types of flag, with the frontend consequence
Targeting rules
User id (stable, precise, but only usable after login — so pre-login experiences need something else).
Tenant/organisation (the usual choice for B2B: one rollout decision per customer).
Cohort/attribute (country, plan, app version, device class) — needs a stable bucketing hash of a *stable* attribute; changing the attribute reassigns users and destroys your experiment data.
Percentage (0–100%) via a deterministic hash of a stable id (user id, or anonymous id before login), not Math.random():
Gradual rollout: ramp 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, advancing on an SLO/metric gate rather than on a date.
Exposure events and experiment analysis
Emit exposure once per (flag, variant, user/session) with a stable id, and only when the variant was actually rendered.

Gate analysis on exposure, not assignment. Filtering on assignment dilutes results with users who never reached the UI — usually a large and *biased* fraction (they may have bounced early or errored).
Sticky assignment plus a shared id across devices is what makes results trustworthy; without it, users flip variants between sessions and your metrics become noise.
Flag lifecycle (the part teams skip)
commonMistakes: using Math.random() for bucketing; logging assignment and calling it exposure; no owner or expiry; baking flag values into build-time env; caching HTML without the variant in the key; assuming client flags are trustworthy for access control; leaving 100%-rolled-out flags forever.
practiceTasks: implement a flag SDK over a static JSON config with deterministic hash bucketing, an useFlag hook, an exposure logger with dedupe, and typed definitions including owner/expires. Then write a CI script that fails on expired flags and prints a report of flags by age and usage, and reproduce the hydration-mismatch bug by evaluating a flag differently on server and client — then fix it.

interviewQuestions.text: What kinds of feature flags exist, and which ones should never expire?
How should percentage rollouts be bucketed so assignment is sticky and independent?
Where should a flag be evaluated, and what goes wrong if you evaluate on the wrong side?
Explain assignment vs exposure and why analysis must gate on exposure.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: experiment analysis has to attribute an outcome to the variant a user actually saw. Decision: emit one exposure event per flag, variant, and user id at the moment the variant is rendered, and define the analysis population as users with an exposure event, not users with an assignment event. Reasoning: assignment happens at evaluation time — which might be at app boot, on a route the user never visits, on a payload the client discards, or in a code path that throws before render. Users in the assigned-but-unexposed group are systematically different from exposed users: they are the ones who bounced early, hit an error, or never reached the UI at all. Including them biases the experiment toward whatever the unexposed population does, and it dilutes effect size toward zero, so you can easily fail to detect a real win. Exposure also gives the denominator you actually need for funnel conversion. Trade-offs: exposure logging is extra client work and needs dedupe by (flag, variant, user) so page navigation does not inflate counts; it also means you must handle a variant that renders conditionally inside an error boundary, where an exposure may be logged for something the user did not perceive. Failure scenario: we ship a pricing-layout experiment, assign 50/50, log assignment at boot, and read a 2% conversion lift as real — but exposure logging shows only 20% of assigned users ever reached the pricing table, and the lift was entirely inside the wrong population; the team ships a change that does nothing. Alternative: define exposure at a well-chosen semantic point (the component that actually differs) rather than at the flag read, and validate the exposure rate per arm as a sanity check — an exposure rate near zero or near 100% means the measurement point is wrong."

interviewQuestions.text: Describe the flag lifecycle, including the owner and expiry requirements.
What is expand/contract and why does a flag not migrate data?
Give three flag-induced bugs and their root causes.
Your CDN serves the wrong experiment variant. Diagnose.
How do you keep flags from becoming a configuration swamp?
When would you use a kill switch, and how do you test it?
A hydration mismatch appears only for 5% of users. Explain the mechanism.
How do you make E2E tests deterministic with flags in the picture?

topics.title: Analytics
topics.description: The deliberate collection of product and performance events, with a governed taxonomy, that answers product questions you cannot answer from server logs alone.
keyConcepts: Client vs server event collection
Event taxonomy and naming

Pick one convention and enforce it. Two that work: past-tense object.action (order_completed, report_exported) or verb-noun (completed_order). Past-tense object.action reads better in SQL-ish pipelines and groups related events alphabetically; verb-noun is more common in the wild. Whatever you pick, consistency beats preference.
Properties: snake_case, lowercase, documented, no PII, and low-cardinality where you group by them (a user_email property destroys your dashboards; a plan value is fine).
Versioned schemas. Events change; consumers (dashboards, warehouses, downstream ML) do not deploy with you. Put a schema version in every event and never repurpose a name:
Reserved property names: common ones like page_url, session_id, user_id, timestamp, app_version, release are added by the collector so you never hand-write them inconsistently.
Client vs server duplication and identity
anonymous_id assigned on first visit (persisted in a first-party cookie or localStorage), rotates with consent state.
On login/identify, stitch by calling the platform's identify(anonymous_id, user_id). Historical anonymous activity attaches to the user.

Handle the awkward cases honestly: shared devices, logouts, multi-account households, and clearing cookies. These are real data-quality limits; say so in an interview rather than claiming a perfect identity graph.
Use your internal user id, never email or phone (PII, and it changes).
Consent and privacy
commonMistakes: one-off event names with no registry; money as floats; relying on the load event for page views; awaiting analytics in event handlers; fetch without keepalive for critical events; collecting before consent; no sampling policy; treating client-side revenue as authoritative.
practiceTasks: build a consent-gated collector with sendBeacon + batching, a schema validator for 8 events, a debug mode, and a CI test that fails on unknown event names or PII-shaped properties. Then simulate a navigation right after an event and prove no loss; add a visibilitychange flush and measure the added INP impact (should be ~0).

interviewQuestions.text: Client events vs server events: who owns which truth?
Pick and defend an event naming convention.
How do you version an event schema, and why must names never be repurposed?
What is a tracking plan and who signs off on it?
Explain identity stitching from anonymous to user id, and where it breaks.
What is the consent gate and why must it live in the collector?
What is the reality of `Do Not Track`?
How do you define a page view and a session in a SPA, and why does the definition matter?
Capture Core Web Vitals in a way that is useful in a dashboard.
Funnels vs retention vs cohorts: which question does each answer?
Why are client events insufficient for revenue, and how do you join the two sources?
Sampling: what must be sampled deterministically, and what must never be sampled?

topics.title: Frontend security
topics.description: Frontend security within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Framing for the whole section
The React escaping model — where it helps and where it stops
Opt out of escaping with dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

Pass URLs to href/src/action/formaction — React 16.9+ warns on javascript: URLs, but data: URLs, blob: and unusual schemes, or an unvalidated path are still your problem, and a data:text/html link is an XSS vector in some contexts.
Spread user-controlled props onto DOM elements (<div {...userProps} />), which can inject dangerouslySetInnerHTML, onError, style, or event handlers.
Render third-party or user-authored rich content (markdown, HTML comments, WYSIWYG output).
Build DOM yourself — innerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval, new Function, template strings into style/href.
Set style from user data (CSS injection can exfiltrate via background: url(//evil/?token) in older engines, and can always do UI redress).
Third-party embeds/widgets that are, by design, script injection points.
postMessage handlers that trust the message's origin and payload shape.
DOM clobbering
postMessage and origin checks
commonMistakes: sanitizing only some of a subtree; sanitizing on write instead of on output; trusting author/trust flags; regex "sanitising"; allowing javascript: and data:text/html URLs; postMessage with '*'; CSP with unsafe-inline; secrets in VITE_/NEXT_PUBLIC_ env vars; treating hidden UI as authorization; no rate limiting on the server because the UI disables the button.
practiceTasks: build a component that renders user markdown with a safe pipeline, then attempt five XSS payloads against it (script tag, javascript: link, data: URL, SVG onload, mXSS via noscript, and a prop-spread attack) and show each failing safely. Then add a nonce-based CSP in report-only mode, run your app with a third-party tag, and record the violations you must fix before enforcing.

interviewQuestions.text: What does React's escaping protect against, and where does it stop?
Your app renders user markdown. What is the safe pipeline?
`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` alternatives: what do you use when you cannot sanitize?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: we need to render a rich description field that users can format, and we cannot sanitize because we do not control all producers — some content is created by an internal tool and some is imported. Decision: never pass untrusted strings to dangerouslySetInnerHTML; render user-authored rich content through a parser that emits a constrained AST (markdown-it in CommonMark mode, or a ProseMirror/Tiptap schema where the source is the editor), map that AST to React elements, and drop anything outside the allowlist. Reasoning: dangerouslySetInnerHTML hands the string to the HTML parser, and once the parser is in play, the attacker controls an entire parser surface, including mutation XSS where a sanitized string re-parses differently in a different context (inside SVG, noscript, or an attribute). Escaping-by-default is the whole value of React and opting out of it throws that away. The AST approach keeps text as text, keeps attributes as props where React escapes them, and makes link handling (rel, scheme allowlist) a property of my renderer rather than of the content. Trade-offs: I lose arbitrary HTML — product has to accept the subset the renderer supports, which is a real product conversation — and markdown tables/embeds need explicit renderer support. I also need to normalise at render time rather than write time, because content already stored before the sanitizer existed must be safe on output, which costs CPU on read and means a stored-XSS cleanup job. Failure scenario: someone adds a 'feature' to the renderer that renders raw HTML for 'trusted' authors, and because trust was defined by an author flag rather than by role plus a sanitiser, one support-agent account turns into stored XSS on every customer page. Alternative: if a WYSIWYG HTML field is genuinely required, sanitize at render with a mature allowlist sanitiser, sanitise the entire subtree in one pass, and combine it with a strict CSP so a sanitiser bypass is not a full compromise."

interviewQuestions.text: How do you safely handle a user-supplied URL in `href`?
What is DOM clobbering and how do you defend against it?
Write a `postMessage` listener that is actually safe.
Why does `'unsafe-inline'` defeat CSP?
Explain nonce-based CSP with `'strict-dynamic'`. How do you keep third-party scripts?
How do you roll out CSP without breaking production?
`style-src` is fighting your app. What are your options?
What is the risk profile of an analytics/chat widget, and how do you contain it?

topics.description: Awareness of Vue — part of Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem in Frontend Frameworks.

topics.title: Angular
topics.description: Angular within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Purpose
Vue 3

Reactivity: ref for primitives, reactive for objects, both implemented with ES Proxy; reads inside a *reactive scope* (the render effect created by watchEffect/computed, which a component's render function is) are tracked, writes trigger re-runs. computed values are cached and lazily invalidated; watch/watchEffect are side-effect hooks with flush timing ('pre', 'post', 'sync').
Effect scope / lifecycle: effectScope collects effects for disposal (this is why component unmount is clean), plus onMounted/onUnmounted.

Template compiler: SFC templates compile to render functions; the compiler tracks *static* vs *dynamic* nodes and hoists static content, so it knows at build time what can be skipped. v-memo is the escape hatch for expensive subtrees.

Fragmentation insight: Vue re-renders a component when any reactive value it touched during render changed (a "dynamic dependency" set), not a top-down re-render of the subtree. This is finer-grained than React's default top-down re-render and needs no manual memo.
Data fetching: @tanstack/vue-query is the community standard; there is no first-party framework data layer (contrast React Query, which is also third-party but React-first — be accurate).
Routing: Vue Router (official). State: Pinia (official, store pattern).
Model: single-file components; template + scoped styles + script; templates are the recommended way to write UIs (and the compiler's static analysis is part of the performance story).
SFC <style scoped> rewrites selectors with a data attribute, which is a *build-time* isolation strategy — closer to "CSS Modules" than to Shadow DOM.
Angular

Reactivity/change detection: zone-based change detection by default (the zone patches async APIs so the framework knows when to check), with OnPush components for targeted checks; the newer signals (signal, computed, effect, and signal inputs/outputs) give fine-grained graph-based updates and can be used to reduce reliance on zones. markForCheck/detectChanges are the manual escape hatches.
commonMistakes: declaring a universal winner; arguing from personal taste; not knowing what <script setup>/runes/signals are; claiming React is "faster" without a workload; implying you could rewrite a production app in a different framework in a quarter; being unable to name what transfers framework-agnostically.
practiceTasks: implement the same accessible combobox (4.6.11 drill 1) in React, Vue 3, and Svelte, and compare bundle size, LOC, and the a11y behaviour you get from the platform's native primitives. Write one paragraph per framework on what the framework gave you for free versus what you reimplemented — this is the real answer to "why X".

interviewQuestions.text: Explain Vue 3's reactivity in two sentences and when it re-renders.
What is `reactive` vs `ref`, and what breaks if you forget which to use?
What does `computed` guarantee that a plain function does not?
Explain Angular's change detection and what `OnPush` changes.
What does Angular's DI give you that React lacks?
Where does RxJS help and where does it hurt in Angular?
What are Svelte runes and why were they introduced?
Why does Svelte have no virtual DOM, and what do you trade away?
Which React concepts transfer to every framework, and which are React-specific?
Why does an Angular app have a different performance profile than a React app?
Why React? Give an honest answer with counter-cases.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: 'why React' is a test for whether my reasoning is evidence-based. Decision: React, framed as an ecosystem and hiring decision rather than a technical superiority claim, with the constraints that would flip my answer stated up front. Reasoning: unidirectional data flow gives traceable state ownership; the component-per-function model keeps rendering a pure function of props and state, which is what makes unit testing cheap; the breadth of mature libraries (routing, server state, forms, testing, RN) removes work we would otherwise own; React Native shares components, hooks, and types with the native app, which is a leverage argument no other web-first framework can make. React's concurrent model and the compiler are the trajectory for keeping large trees responsive without hand-tuning. Trade-offs I accept: React's escape hatches mean we must build and enforce our own conventions — a design system, boundary rules, a state strategy — which is real cost; the hooks model has genuine footguns (dependency arrays, stale closures) that require discipline; and the churn is real. Where React is the wrong answer: a small bundle-sensitive product (Vue/Svelte ship less runtime), a very large org that benefits from Angular's enforced conventions and DI, or a codebase whose only requirement is web with a small team that will be faster with less ceremony. Failure scenario: we choose React for ecosystem depth, inherit three state libraries and two routers from merge conflicts, and spend a year untangling conventions — the flexibility we bought is exactly the ambiguity we got. Mitigation: standardise on one of each at the start, adopt the community defaults, and enforce boundaries in CI. Alternative: if the team has 10 years of Angular and a working platform, staying on Angular is the professional answer and I would say so."

topics.title: Svelte
topics.description: Svelte within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Purpose
Vue 3

Reactivity: ref for primitives, reactive for objects, both implemented with ES Proxy; reads inside a *reactive scope* (the render effect created by watchEffect/computed, which a component's render function is) are tracked, writes trigger re-runs. computed values are cached and lazily invalidated; watch/watchEffect are side-effect hooks with flush timing ('pre', 'post', 'sync').
Effect scope / lifecycle: effectScope collects effects for disposal (this is why component unmount is clean), plus onMounted/onUnmounted.

Template compiler: SFC templates compile to render functions; the compiler tracks *static* vs *dynamic* nodes and hoists static content, so it knows at build time what can be skipped. v-memo is the escape hatch for expensive subtrees.

Fragmentation insight: Vue re-renders a component when any reactive value it touched during render changed (a "dynamic dependency" set), not a top-down re-render of the subtree. This is finer-grained than React's default top-down re-render and needs no manual memo.
Data fetching: @tanstack/vue-query is the community standard; there is no first-party framework data layer (contrast React Query, which is also third-party but React-first — be accurate).
Routing: Vue Router (official). State: Pinia (official, store pattern).
Model: single-file components; template + scoped styles + script; templates are the recommended way to write UIs (and the compiler's static analysis is part of the performance story).
SFC <style scoped> rewrites selectors with a data attribute, which is a *build-time* isolation strategy — closer to "CSS Modules" than to Shadow DOM.
Angular

Reactivity/change detection: zone-based change detection by default (the zone patches async APIs so the framework knows when to check), with OnPush components for targeted checks; the newer signals (signal, computed, effect, and signal inputs/outputs) give fine-grained graph-based updates and can be used to reduce reliance on zones. markForCheck/detectChanges are the manual escape hatches.
commonMistakes: declaring a universal winner; arguing from personal taste; not knowing what <script setup>/runes/signals are; claiming React is "faster" without a workload; implying you could rewrite a production app in a different framework in a quarter; being unable to name what transfers framework-agnostically.
practiceTasks: implement the same accessible combobox (4.6.11 drill 1) in React, Vue 3, and Svelte, and compare bundle size, LOC, and the a11y behaviour you get from the platform's native primitives. Write one paragraph per framework on what the framework gave you for free versus what you reimplemented — this is the real answer to "why X".

topics.title: infinite feed
topics.description: infinite feed within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: State model

Cursor pagination, not offset. offset pagination duplicates and skips items when the feed mutates (a post deleted or a new post inserted above you) — the single most important sentence in this design. Cursors are stable but "load older posts" is *prepending*, which needs a *backward* cursor.
Dedupe by id on insert, always. Under realtime insertion, the server may return an item you already have; mergeById(newItems, existing) keeps order and uniqueness.
Dedupe on re-render is about keys: use stable key={item.id}, never key={index} — with prepend-heavy feeds, index keys produce the classic "input resets / items appear to shuffle" bug.
Key flows

Load next: IntersectionObserver on a sentinel with rootMargin: '800px' (prefetch before visible), disabled while a page is in flight, and a guard that hasNextPage is false (otherwise the sentinel re-triggers forever).
Load previous: a *second* observer near the top with rootMargin: '-200px' or an explicit "New posts" button (better a11y, and it avoids surprise jumps).

Scroll restoration is the hard part. Two-part approach: (1) store the id of the top visible item plus its pixel offset when leaving the route; (2) on return, render until that id exists, then scrollTo(id.offset - measuredOffset). Restoring by raw scrollY breaks because the DOM height differs while items are still loading. Combine with history.scrollRestoration = 'manual' so the browser does not fight you.
Prefetch on pointerenter of a visible card (or on IntersectionObserver at 50% visibility) to warm the detail API — cheap and invisible.
Refresh: re-fetch page one, merge by id, and diff to decide whether to keep the user's scroll position (if the top items are unchanged, do not move; if they changed, show a "N new posts" pill).

topics.title: image carousel
topics.description: image carousel within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Layout decisions (state this first)
State
Key flows

LCP discipline: the *first* image is fetchpriority="high", not lazy, with a known width/height (or aspect-ratio) so there is zero CLS. Everything after is loading="lazy". Never lazy-load the hero (3.6).

Preload strategy: prefetch the next and previous at loading="lazy"-with-intent once the first is painted; prefetch the next two, not all 50; cancel preloads on rapid navigation (<link rel="prefetch"> has no cancel, so use new Image().src and drop the reference).

Transitions: animate only transform/opacity. Slide via a translate3d on a track with will-change applied just before and removed after (transform animation of thousands of images janks; virtualise the track to ±1 slides).

Swipe: pointerdown/move/up with a direction lock (if |dx| > |dy| then it's a swipe; otherwise let the page scroll), a 15% threshold to commit, and velocity-based flinging. touch-action: pan-y on the track so vertical scroll still works. Do not implement swipe with touchstart/touchmove if you can use pointer events (mouse + pen + touch unified, and no passive-listener problems).

Zoom/lightbox: open a dialog with the full-resolution image, trap focus, restore focus to the trigger, Escape to close, arrow keys to move between images, and a download/open in new tab escape. Use <dialog> or a properly-built modal (4.6.2 primitives) — never a bare fixed div.
Performance budget
Loading / empty / error
Accessibility
The stage is a group with an accessible name and aria-roledescription="carousel", each slide is role="group" with aria-roledescription="slide" and aria-label="3 of 12".
