topics.title: chat UI
topics.description: chat UI within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Optimistic messages get a clientId generated locally and a status: 'sending' | 'sent' | 'failed'. On server ack, replace by clientId (this is the dedupe rule). Reconnect resends unacked items with the *same* clientId so the server can dedupe (idempotency key) — this is the difference between "mostly works" and "works".

Ordering is by server sequence (seq, monotonically increasing per conversation), not by client timestamp. Client timestamps are for display only, because clock skew between devices is a guaranteed source of misordering. Sort by (seq ?? localCreatedAt).
Typing indicators must expire (2–4 s TTL, cleared on a timer or on message arrival) or they lie forever.
Key flows

WebSocket lifecycle: connecting → open → (heartbeat every 25–30 s) → closing → closed → reconnect with exponential backoff + jitter (1 s, 2 s, 4 s … cap 30 s). On each successful (re)connect: resubscribe, then resync — issue a GET /messages?since=<lastSeq> to fetch anything missed while offline, then reconcile the outbox. Resuming a subscription without a resync is the classic "messages from the gap are gone forever" bug. Handle visibilitychange (close when hidden on mobile to save battery, reopen on visible), online/offline events, and page unload (send a presence-leaving beacon).

Optimistic send: append immediately, mark sending, POST; on success mark sent and stamp seq; on failure mark failed with a Retry affordance, and keep the text in the input? No — keep it in the message (with retry), which is what real apps do.
Offline queue: persist the outbox to IndexedDB so a refresh does not lose an unsent message; flush on reconnect; show a clear "1 message not sent" affordance rather than silently retrying forever.

Read receipts: server-authoritative (the server records lastReadSeq per user per conversation), so it works across devices. Show "Seen" for the other user's last message only when the conversation is open and the document is visible.

Scroll behaviour: stick to the bottom only when the user is already near the bottom; if they scrolled up, show a "jump to latest" pill with an unread count. Never yank the viewport when a message arrives while the user is reading history.

Virtualisation is mandatory for long histories: window the message list, keep the scroll height stable while older messages load above (measure and adjust scrollTop by the delta), and preserve focus across prepends.

topics.title: Google Docs-style editor
topics.description: Google Docs-style editor within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Goroutines are cheap (a few KB of stack, multiplexed onto OS threads by the runtime). Spawning thousands is normal and idiomatic. They have no preemption guarantee in older versions (since Go 1.14, async preemption exists via signals).

Channels are the coordination primitive. Always size the buffer when the producer can outrun the consumer, or the producer blocks; and never close from the send side if senders may still be running. Prefer errgroup for a bounded group of goroutines with automatic error propagation and Wait.

context.Context is the cancellation and deadline mechanism, threaded through every call as the first parameter. It is how you propagate a client disconnect, a request timeout, and a deadline down to the database driver — which is why context.WithTimeout plus defer cancel() on every function that creates one is the single most important Go habit.
errgroup + SetLimit gives you a bulkhead for free:

net/http: the standard library server is production-grade. http.Server has ReadHeaderTimeout (set it or you have a Slowloris vulnerability), ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout, and MaxHeaderBytes. Middleware is plain wrapping of http.Handler. Graceful shutdown is srv.Shutdown(ctx) plus closing the listener, waiting for in-flight requests.
Errors are values: no exceptions; wrap with %w for errors.Is/errors.As; a missing error is a programming error. Error strings are lowercase and without punctuation because they compose into messages.
Interfaces are implicit and small: define the interface at the consumer, keep it to one or two methods (io.Reader, error).

Single static binary: cross-compiles with CGO_ENABLED=0 to a few megabytes, no runtime, no dependency manager at deploy time. Containers start in milliseconds and images stay small — an operational advantage that shows up in cold-start scale-out and in distroless/security-scanning terms.

Compile-time safety: static typing with no null, exhaustive-ish error handling, and a language that is small enough to hold in your head. Structs are value types by default; slices and maps are reference types, which is the classic aliasing bug.
Weaknesses to be honest about
Error-handling verbosity: if err != nil everywhere is a real productivity and readability cost; the ecosystem is converging on wrapped errors and helper packages rather than on magic.

Generics are still less pleasant than TypeScript or Java: no higher-kinded types, no Stream-style pipelines, still awkward for higher-order abstractions. Go 1.18+ generics help for containers but have ergonomics complaints (no method constraints on the type-parameter set in some cases).
commonMistakes: not defer cancel()ing contexts; unbounded goroutines without SetLimit; forgetting ReadHeaderTimeout; unbuffered channels between many senders and one receiver; assuming Go's GC solves tail latency by default.
practiceTasks: write a Go service with net/http, errgroup with a concurrency limit of 8, context deadline propagation, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM, and a load test at 20k rps with p99 reported; then repeat in Node and compare.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 Why is `context.Context` conventionally the first parameter?
🟡 What is the cost of spawning a goroutine compared to a thread?
🟡 Why must channels be buffered when a producer can outrun the consumer?
🔴 What is the loop-variable capture bug in older Go and how does Go 1.22+ change it?
🔴 Explain `errgroup.WithContext` and `SetLimit` and why the limit is a feature.
🔴 Why must you set `ReadHeaderTimeout` on an `http.Server`?
🔴 What's the equivalent of graceful shutdown, and what breaks if you skip it?
🔴 Compare `sync.WaitGroup` and `errgroup` for error propagation.
🔴 When would you choose Go over Node and over Java?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a new internal service that must handle 20k requests per second with p99 under 20ms, where the team has strong Node and Java experience. Decision: I would pick Go for the service and give a short, explicit list of reasons, while naming the real costs. Reasons for Go: goroutines and channels make high IO-bound concurrency simple without an async framework or reactive types; the single static binary means no runtime dependency and fast container starts, which matters for scale-out; context gives first-class cancellation and deadline propagation all the way to the database driver, which is genuinely excellent; and the language surface is small enough that a new engineer is productive in a week. Costs I would state plainly: error handling is more verbose than TypeScript, generics ergonomics are worse, GC tuning for extreme tail latency is less flexible than the JVM's, and the hiring pool is smaller than Java's by a wide margin, so I would only assign people who want to work in Go. Reasoning: the decision hinges on the *shape of the workload*, not on a preference. If this service were mostly blocking JDBC with complex transactional queries, Java with virtual threads would be the better fit; if the team were strongest in Python and this was an ML-adjacent service, Python would win on velocity. Trade-offs: choosing Go means the on-call rotation needs Go expertise, and if we later need complex ORM-style domain modelling we are outside Go's strengths. Failure scenario: we pick Go for throughput, then the real requirement turns out to be heavy transactional domain logic with an existing team fluent in Spring — now we are paying a language-learning tax for throughput we did not need. Prevention: state the bottleneck and the constraint that drives the choice before committing, and validate the throughput assumption with a load test on a realistic handler in week one rather than trusting a hello-world benchmark. Alternative: Node, if the service is thin and the constraint is delivery speed rather than concurrency."

topics.title: Design systems
topics.description: A design system is a versioned, cross-product collection of decisions — tokens, primitives, components, patterns, documentation — plus the governance that keeps those decisions consistent. Canonical entry for design principles and visual language: PHASE 1 → Communication; here we talk engineering.
keyConcepts: What a design system is
A single source of truth for visual and interaction decisions, encoded as code where possible (tokens, components, lints).
A contract with a versioning policy: consumers declare which major version they are on and get a migration path.
A product of an organisation: it exists because five teams were solving the same modal focus-trap bug five different ways.
An accessibility enforcement point: primitives are where keyboard and screen-reader behaviour is proved once.
What a design system is NOT
Not a Figma file with a colour palette. Designers' files are an input, not the deliverable — code is where behaviour lives.
Not a "component library with nice buttons". It includes *patterns* (how components combine to accomplish a task), *content guidelines* (empty states, error copy), and *governance*.
Not a monolith of 200 exported components. A system that nobody can navigate is a system nobody adopts.
Not a marketing term for "we use Tailwind". Tailwind is a styling mechanism; a design system is the decisions plus the contract.
The anatomy: token → primitive → component → pattern → page
Design tokens
commonMistakes: calling Figma the design system; letting product code reference primitives; assuming dark: class variants scale past a handful of components; adding props instead of slots; deprecating without a codemod or a migration deadline; treating accessibility as a checklist at the end; versioning by "how big the diff looks" instead of by API compatibility; measuring adoption by "did we write it" instead of "is it used".
practiceTasks: build a token pipeline: author 40 tokens in JSON, emit CSS custom properties + a TS object + a markdown table; define a light and a dark theme; write the tier-boundary lint; then implement Button, Input, and Dialog consuming only semantic tokens, with axe passing and a --brand switch at runtime with no rebuild. Measure the CSS output size for one theme and justify whether you shipped both or generated one at build time.

topics.title: Component libraries: shadcn/ui, Radix, MUI, Ant Design, Chakra
topics.description: Component libraries: shadcn/ui, Radix, MUI, Ant Design, Chakra within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: The landscape
Headless vs styled
Why "copy the source into your repo" changed the ecosystem
Customisation cost drops to near zero, because customisation is a diff you control.
No runtime abstraction: fewer layers between your code and the DOM, better tree-shaking, no version conflicts.
You inherit responsibility: accessibility fixes, React 19 compatibility, security patches, dependency updates are now *your* backlog. The MIT license makes this legal; the engineering cost is real.

The trade-off that people gloss over: with 60 copied components you now have 60 files to keep in sync with React and Radix. Mitigations: keep the copied set small, keep a components/ui/ convention, and re-run the CLI deliberately during dependency upgrades rather than pretending files are a package.
License and maintenance realities
When to adopt a library vs build primitives

Adopt when the component is commodity (date picker, data grid, rich text, combobox with async, file upload), the library is actively maintained, and its defaults match your design language reasonably.
Build/wrap when the component is core to your brand's differentiation, when you need behaviour the library does not support, or when the library's a11y has a known gap you cannot work around.

Never rebuild a date picker or data grid from scratch for a product; the edge cases (locale, keyboard, RTL, ranges, a11y) are a multi-month project. Copy-source libraries solve this because you get the hard logic and own the pixels.
commonMistakes: naming a library without knowing its distribution model; saying a component library "handles accessibility for you" without caveats; comparing them on aesthetics only; reaching for a specific library as a brand signal; proposing to wrap a component while leaking its types and props; ignoring license and maintenance reality.
practiceTasks: take one third-party component (a date picker or a select), write a wrapper with your own types and states (loading, empty, error, disabled, RTL), and write a "swap the library" test that imports only your component. Then bundle-analyze your app with and without the library and quantify what you would save by hand-rolling it — and defend whether you would.

interviewQuestions.text: Compare shadcn/ui, Radix, MUI, Ant Design, and Chakra on distribution model and ownership.
Headless vs styled: what are you actually choosing between?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: the choice is behaviour-versus-pixels ownership. Decision: headless primitives when our visual language is a differentiator and we can fund CSS work; a styled library when speed-to-finished-UI matters more than pixel-level control and our product can live with a house style. Reasoning: headless gives correct keyboard and ARIA behaviour, which is genuinely hard and slow to re-derive — Radix or React Aria encode a decade of fixes — and lets us own every pixel, theming token, and bundle byte. Styled systems give a coherent look immediately and a theme model, which is often the difference between shipping in a week and in a quarter. Trade-offs: headless means we own the visual states (hover, focus, active, disabled, loading) for every component and we own accessibility regressions after adoption; styled means we pay bundle and SSR cost, fight theme override systems when we need something non-standard, and accept the library's opinionated UX. Failure scenario: a headless choice with no design investment — we ship a primitive with no hover or focus-visible state and fail a WCAG audit that we had assumed was handled. Alternative: a hybrid — headless behaviour with a small in-house styled layer (the shadcn model) — which is where most mature product teams land."

topics.title: Frontend project structure and boundaries
topics.description: Frontend project structure and boundaries within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Feature-based vs type-based folders
Layering and dependency direction
Dependencies point downward only. shared/lib never imports from features; a feature never imports from another feature's internals.
features are private by default. Another feature wanting your code goes through your feature's public index.ts, or you promote the shared piece to shared/.
app is composition only: providers, routing, error boundaries, layout. It should contain no business logic — if app/ has if (user.role === 'admin'), that belongs in a feature or a permission module.
shared/lib is framework-free if you want to test it without a renderer and reuse it in workers.
Enforcing boundaries mechanically
Circular dependency detection
Module boundaries vs folder names
Barrels (index.ts) and why they hurt

Tree-shaking degrades. With sideEffects metadata and proper ESM, unused exports *can* be shaken, but barrel files create large re-export graphs that some bundlers resolve poorly, and any barrel member with a side effect (a polyfill, a window guard) is retained, dragging its whole subtree in. The reliable statement for an interview: barrels make it harder for bundlers to prove a module is unused, and the cost grows with barrel size and import-path depth.
Build/watch cost. In a monorepo or a large app, a barrel re-export of many files turns any change into a large invalidation graph (dev-server restarts, slow type-check, watch-mode thrash).
commonMistakes: mixing type-based and feature-based conventions without a rule; adding barrels "for cleanliness"; relying on review instead of lint for boundaries; promoting a single-consumer helper to a shared package; a big-bang restructure on a live codebase; tests in a mirrored __tests__ tree that drift.
practiceTasks: take an existing app (or scaffold one with 3 features), add feature-based folders, eslint-plugin-boundaries rules, a madge --circular CI step, and alias config across tsconfig/Vitest/ESLint. Then, one file at a time, move code into the new structure with the suite green at every commit, and record the wall-clock time the lint rule saved you versus the time the rules cost on new code.

interviewQuestions.text: Feature-based vs type-based folders: what does each optimise for and break on?
Draw your layering and say which direction imports are allowed.
How do you enforce boundaries without relying on code review?
What creates circular dependencies, and how do you detect them in CI?
Why do barrels hurt tree-shaking and build times? What's the compromise?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: barrels are the reflex fix for 'too many import paths' and they are a real build-performance footgun. Decision: barrels at package and feature boundaries only, never in leaf directories. Reasoning: a barrel creates a re-export graph that the bundler must analyse to decide what is unused; the bigger the barrel, the more of it must be proven side-effect-free before anything can be dropped, and any module in the graph with a side effect (a polyfill, a global registration) is retained along with its imports. On top of that, in watch mode and in monorepo builds, a single changed file invalidates every module that re-exports it, so a barrel at the top of shared/lib turns one edit into a large rebuild. Cycle detection also gets harder because the cycle runs through the barrel entry. Trade-offs: this costs a bit of import ergonomics — consumers write import { formatDate } from '@/shared/lib/dates' rather than '@/shared/lib' — and it means discipline, since one lazy barrel will be added eventually and the rule must be enforced. Failure scenario: a team adds a root barrel for convenience; shared/lib ends up importing a module that touches window for a Node/worker path, so the whole graph lands in the initial chunk for every route, and the app's LCP regresses by 180 kB with no visible cause. Alternative: keep the ergonomic barrel but split per-package with exports maps and sideEffects: false, and verify with the bundler's stats that the initial chunk actually dropped — measure, don't believe."

topics.title: Error monitoring
topics.description: A client/server error-reporting service that captures unhandled exceptions and (optionally) traces, enriches them with release/environment/user context, groups them into *issues*, and routes alerts. Canonical observability material: PHASE 8 → monitoring, logging, metrics; here is the frontend-specific craft.
keyConcepts: What to capture
Context that makes a report actionable
Attach feature flag state to every event (4.6.7). When a bug appears only for 5% of users, the flag values in the event are the difference between a five-minute and a five-hour investigation.
Attach the trace id so you can jump to the trace (Phase 8) for the timeline of fetches and spans around the failure.
Sampling and error quotas
Session replay and PII
Mask by default: all input, textarea, select, and contenteditable (set maskAllText: true and blockAllMedia: true, then unmask only specific selectors you have reviewed).
Never replay: payment fields, national IDs, health data, free-text notes containing customer data, anything on a page behind authentication you have not reviewed.
Legal/privacy review is mandatory before enabling, and record it (retention period, DPA, where data is stored, who can access). Cross-reference PHASE 7 → GDPR/privacy practices.
Sampling: record a fraction of *sessions* (or only sessions that contain an error), which cuts cost and data volume while keeping the useful correlation ("replay the session where this happened").
Treat replay as a debugging tool with short retention (7–14 days) and access controls, not as an analytics product.
Performance tracing and Web Vitals
commonMistakes: deploying without uploading source maps for that exact release; no release tag so every stack is unminified; sending Authorization headers; enabling replay without masking and legal review; alerting on every new issue; relying on breadcrumbs you never added; "it only happens locally" treated as a monitoring gap rather than an environment difference.
practiceTasks: Browser SDK for client errors/traces; server SDK for your API; framework/framework-agnostic wrappers (React Router, Next.js, SvelteKit) add routing context and automatic route transaction names — use one, because free contextual data is better than manual breadcrumbs.
Source maps must reach Sentry. They never go in the public bundle. Upload them from CI, per release, and delete/ignore them for the deployed artifact. Framework: sentry-cli sourcemaps upload.

Release and build identity. Every build gets a unique release id ($CI_COMMIT_SHA, or ${semver}+${sha}), reported by the SDK and written onto uploaded source maps. Without a matching release, stack traces are useless — this is the single most common integration failure. Also set a dist (or build id) so the Sentry release matches your asset fingerprint exactly.

integrate Sentry into an app with release tagging, CI map upload, beforeSend scrubbing of headers and query params, flag tags, and a custom fingerprint on your API client. Then deliberately ship three distinct bugs (a type error on a rare flag path, a network 500, and a slow fetch) and verify each lands as a grouped, actionable issue with the right release, flags, and trace link. Then delete one issue from the noise and justify it.

interviewQuestions.text: What is the single most important Sentry integration detail, and why?
How do you wire release and source maps in CI? Why does order matter?
What is the difference between unhandled and handled error capture, and which is more valuable?
Where exactly should `captureException` live in a React app?
What context makes an error report actionable? Name five fields.
How do you sample without losing visibility of new issues?
What must be masked in session replay, and who approves it?
How do traces and Web Vitals connect to a user-reported "the page is slow"?
An issue has 4,000 events from six different bugs. Fix the grouping.
How do you decide what pages you?
What is the difference between `beforeSend` and an ignore list, and when is each right?
When do you alert on an error, and how do you connect that to SLOs?

topics.title: Vue / Angular / Svelte awareness + "Why React?"
topics.description: Vue / Angular / Svelte awareness + "Why React?" within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Purpose
Vue 3

Reactivity: ref for primitives, reactive for objects, both implemented with ES Proxy; reads inside a *reactive scope* (the render effect created by watchEffect/computed, which a component's render function is) are tracked, writes trigger re-runs. computed values are cached and lazily invalidated; watch/watchEffect are side-effect hooks with flush timing ('pre', 'post', 'sync').
Effect scope / lifecycle: effectScope collects effects for disposal (this is why component unmount is clean), plus onMounted/onUnmounted.

Template compiler: SFC templates compile to render functions; the compiler tracks *static* vs *dynamic* nodes and hoists static content, so it knows at build time what can be skipped. v-memo is the escape hatch for expensive subtrees.

Fragmentation insight: Vue re-renders a component when any reactive value it touched during render changed (a "dynamic dependency" set), not a top-down re-render of the subtree. This is finer-grained than React's default top-down re-render and needs no manual memo.
Data fetching: @tanstack/vue-query is the community standard; there is no first-party framework data layer (contrast React Query, which is also third-party but React-first — be accurate).
Routing: Vue Router (official). State: Pinia (official, store pattern).
Model: single-file components; template + scoped styles + script; templates are the recommended way to write UIs (and the compiler's static analysis is part of the performance story).
SFC <style scoped> rewrites selectors with a data attribute, which is a *build-time* isolation strategy — closer to "CSS Modules" than to Shadow DOM.
Angular

Reactivity/change detection: zone-based change detection by default (the zone patches async APIs so the framework knows when to check), with OnPush components for targeted checks; the newer signals (signal, computed, effect, and signal inputs/outputs) give fine-grained graph-based updates and can be used to reduce reliance on zones. markForCheck/detectChanges are the manual escape hatches.
commonMistakes: declaring a universal winner; arguing from personal taste; not knowing what <script setup>/runes/signals are; claiming React is "faster" without a workload; implying you could rewrite a production app in a different framework in a quarter; being unable to name what transfers framework-agnostically.
practiceTasks: implement the same accessible combobox (4.6.11 drill 1) in React, Vue 3, and Svelte, and compare bundle size, LOC, and the a11y behaviour you get from the platform's native primitives. Write one paragraph per framework on what the framework gave you for free versus what you reimplemented — this is the real answer to "why X".

interviewQuestions.text: Explain Vue 3's reactivity in two sentences and when it re-renders.
What is `reactive` vs `ref`, and what breaks if you forget which to use?
What does `computed` guarantee that a plain function does not?
Explain Angular's change detection and what `OnPush` changes.
What does Angular's DI give you that React lacks?
Where does RxJS help and where does it hurt in Angular?
What are Svelte runes and why were they introduced?
Why does Svelte have no virtual DOM, and what do you trade away?
Which React concepts transfer to every framework, and which are React-specific?
Why does an Angular app have a different performance profile than a React app?
Why React? Give an honest answer with counter-cases.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: 'why React' is a test for whether my reasoning is evidence-based. Decision: React, framed as an ecosystem and hiring decision rather than a technical superiority claim, with the constraints that would flip my answer stated up front. Reasoning: unidirectional data flow gives traceable state ownership; the component-per-function model keeps rendering a pure function of props and state, which is what makes unit testing cheap; the breadth of mature libraries (routing, server state, forms, testing, RN) removes work we would otherwise own; React Native shares components, hooks, and types with the native app, which is a leverage argument no other web-first framework can make. React's concurrent model and the compiler are the trajectory for keeping large trees responsive without hand-tuning. Trade-offs I accept: React's escape hatches mean we must build and enforce our own conventions — a design system, boundary rules, a state strategy — which is real cost; the hooks model has genuine footguns (dependency arrays, stale closures) that require discipline; and the churn is real. Where React is the wrong answer: a small bundle-sensitive product (Vue/Svelte ship less runtime), a very large org that benefits from Angular's enforced conventions and DI, or a codebase whose only requirement is web with a small team that will be faster with less ceremony. Failure scenario: we choose React for ecosystem depth, inherit three state libraries and two routers from merge conflicts, and spend a year untangling conventions — the flexibility we bought is exactly the ambiguity we got. Mitigation: standardise on one of each at the start, adopt the community defaults, and enforce boundaries in CI. Alternative: if the team has 10 years of Angular and a working platform, staying on Angular is the professional answer and I would say so."

interviewQuestions.text: When would you pick Vue? When Svelte? When Angular?

keyConcepts: Scale numbers to say out loud
Client state

One request at a time, identified by an incrementing requestId; responses whose requestId is not the latest are discarded (the canonical stale-response race). Cancel the previous request too — AbortController — because cancelling frees the connection and stops wasted server work.
query (raw), debouncedQuery (after debounce), and results are separate fields. Conflating them is the bug behind "the list flickers while typing".
Cached responses keyed by normalised query (an LRU of 50) make backspace-free navigation instant and turn a repeat query into no network call.
Recent searches in a small store (persisted), popular searches from the server, history cross-device if the user is signed in.

topics.title: Image carousel / gallery
topics.description: Image carousel / gallery within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Layout decisions (state this first)
State
Key flows

LCP discipline: the *first* image is fetchpriority="high", not lazy, with a known width/height (or aspect-ratio) so there is zero CLS. Everything after is loading="lazy". Never lazy-load the hero (3.6).

Preload strategy: prefetch the next and previous at loading="lazy"-with-intent once the first is painted; prefetch the next two, not all 50; cancel preloads on rapid navigation (<link rel="prefetch"> has no cancel, so use new Image().src and drop the reference).

Transitions: animate only transform/opacity. Slide via a translate3d on a track with will-change applied just before and removed after (transform animation of thousands of images janks; virtualise the track to ±1 slides).

Swipe: pointerdown/move/up with a direction lock (if |dx| > |dy| then it's a swipe; otherwise let the page scroll), a 15% threshold to commit, and velocity-based flinging. touch-action: pan-y on the track so vertical scroll still works. Do not implement swipe with touchstart/touchmove if you can use pointer events (mouse + pen + touch unified, and no passive-listener problems).

Zoom/lightbox: open a dialog with the full-resolution image, trap focus, restore focus to the trigger, Escape to close, arrow keys to move between images, and a download/open in new tab escape. Use <dialog> or a properly-built modal (4.6.2 primitives) — never a bare fixed div.
Performance budget
Loading / empty / error
Accessibility
The stage is a group with an accessible name and aria-roledescription="carousel", each slide is role="group" with aria-roledescription="slide" and aria-label="3 of 12".

topics.title: Analytics dashboard
topics.description: Analytics dashboard within Frontend Architecture and Ecosystem.
keyConcepts: Layout and information hierarchy
Data-fetching strategy
KPIs and time series: one aggregate endpoint with from, to, granularity, filters[], compare=true. Aggregates server-side, always. Never ship raw events to the browser to aggregate 100k rows.
Tables: server-side pagination *and* sorting (sort=revenue.desc, cursor) — the browser must never hold 100k rows to sort them. Virtualise the 50 rows it does hold.
Entity detail: route-level fetch on drill-down.
Caching and consistency
Timezones and date ranges
Real-time updates
Polling (e.g. every 30 s on the live tiles only): simple, stateless, works everywhere, slightly stale, costs request volume per viewer.
WebSocket/SSE push: lower latency and cost per viewer at scale, but you now have connection management, ordering, and reconnect (4.6.11.4).
Performance budget for 100k rows

Never transfer 100k rows. Server-side pagination/sorting + aggregation. If a full export is needed, do it server-side as a job (generate a CSV asynchronously, email a signed link) — a 100k-row CSV is not a browser download.
